title: Design a Real-Time Collaborative Document Editor
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a backend system for a Google Docs-like collaborative document editor that supports real-time multi-user editing, conflict resolution, and version history.

**Core Features:**
- Multiple users edit the same document simultaneously
- Changes propagate to all active editors in <500ms
- Automatic conflict resolution when concurrent edits occur
- Full version history with ability to revert to any checkpoint
- Presence indicators showing who is editing and their cursor positions
- Document persistence and offline support recovery

**Scale Assumptions:**
- 1M daily active users
- 500K concurrent documents being edited at any time
- Peak load: 50K documents with 10+ concurrent editors each
- Average document: 2MB of content
- Average edits: 5 operations per second per active document
- Retention: 7-year version history

**Constraints:**
- Latency budget: <500ms for edit propagation
- Strong consistency preferred for document state
- Support offline edits with sync on reconnection

requirements: Real-time bidirectional communication between clients and server
Operational Transformation (OT) or CRDT-based conflict resolution
Distributed session management for presence tracking
Persistent document state with version snapshots
Efficient delta compression for network transmission
Offline queue and reconciliation on reconnect
Access control and collaborative permissions
Activity audit logs for all document changes
required_components: WebSocket server for real-time communication
Conflict resolution engine (OT or CRDT implementation)
Distributed in-memory store (Redis) for active sessions
Document storage layer (PostgreSQL + S3)
Snapshot/checkpoint service for version history
Presence service for cursor tracking
Message queue (Kafka) for edit event streaming
Load balancer with sticky sessions
scalability_signals: Sharding documents by document ID to distribute conflict resolution load
Connection pooling and WebSocket server clustering
Eventual consistency model for presence vs strong consistency for edits
Incremental snapshots to reduce storage footprint of version history
Edge caching for read-heavy version retrieval
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Clients connect via WebSocket to a load-balanced cluster of WebSocket servers. Each server maintains in-memory operation queues backed by Redis. Edit operations flow through a Kafka topic for durability, then to a distributed conflict resolution engine. Document state is persisted in PostgreSQL with snapshots stored in S3. A separate presence service tracks active cursors via Redis pubsub.

title: Design a Real-Time Leaderboard System
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a real-time leaderboard system for a competitive gaming platform where millions of players compete globally. Players earn points through matches, and the leaderboard must instantly reflect score updates, rank changes, and support multiple leaderboard views (global, regional, friends, seasonal).

Players expect:
- Immediate rank updates after a match completes (within 1-2 seconds)
- Fast leaderboard queries showing top 100, user's rank, and nearby players
- Historical leaderboards for past seasons
- Consistent ranking without ties or gaps

You have 50 million total players, with 5 million monthly active players. Peak concurrent matches: 500,000. Average match completion: 100 matches/second, with score updates varying from +10 to +50,000 points.

requirements: Submit match results and update player scores atomically
Query player rank and percentile in real-time
Retrieve top N players globally and by region
Show players ranked around a specific user (e.g., top 50 near me)
Support multiple concurrent leaderboards (global, regional, seasonal, friend groups)
Handle score corrections and disputes with audit trails
Archive and rollover seasonal leaderboards
required_components: Sorted Set Database (Redis or similar for ranking)
Write-ahead Log for durability
Distributed Cache Layer
Leaderboard Aggregation Service
Real-time Notification System (rank change alerts)
Time-series Database for historical rankings
API Gateway with rate limiting
Message Queue for async score processing
Geolocation Service for regional partitioning
scalability_signals: Redis Cluster sharding by region/user-id ranges to handle 100k+ concurrent reads
Batch score updates using message queues to prevent thundering herd
Time-window bucketing to balance consistency vs. real-time latency
Caching hot leaderboards (top 1,000) separately with TTL invalidation
Eventual consistency model for non-top-100 ranks to reduce write contention
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Match completion events flow through a Message Queue (Kafka) → Leaderboard Service validates and updates Redis Sorted Sets (sharded by region). Reads go directly to Redis with a Cache Layer for popular queries. Rank changes trigger notifications via WebSocket. Archive service periodically snapshots to TimescaleDB for historical queries.

title: Design a Distributed Payment Processing System
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a distributed payment processing system that handles transactions across multiple merchants, payment methods, and geographic regions. The system must process payments reliably, prevent fraud, handle disputes, and reconcile transactions in real-time.

Your system should support:
- **Payment Processing**: Credit cards, digital wallets, bank transfers, and cryptocurrency
- **Multi-Currency Support**: Automatic FX conversion with rate locking
- **Idempotency**: Retry-safe transactions to prevent duplicate charges
- **Real-Time Settlement**: Process and settle payments within seconds
- **Dispute Resolution**: Handle chargebacks and refunds with audit trails
- **Fraud Detection**: Rule-based and ML-driven anomaly detection
- **Compliance**: PCI-DSS adherence, KYC/AML verification

**Scale Assumptions**:
- 10,000 QPS peak transaction volume
- 500+ merchants onboarded
- 100+ payment corridors (routes between regions)
- 5+ years of transaction history (petabyte-scale)
- 99.99% uptime SLA with <2 second P99 latency
- Global deployment across 6+ regions

requirements: Process payments from multiple sources (cards, wallets, bank transfers) with idempotent transaction handling
Support multi-currency transactions with real-time FX conversion and rate locking
Implement real-time fraud detection using rule engines and machine learning models
Handle payment disputes, chargebacks, and refunds with complete audit trails
Ensure PCI-DSS compliance with tokenization and encryption of sensitive payment data
Reconcile transactions across multiple payment gateways and settlement partners
Provide real-time transaction status updates and webhook notifications to merchants
Scale horizontally across multiple regions with consistent data and strong eventual consistency
required_components: API Gateway with request validation and rate limiting
Payment Service (orchestrates transaction workflow)
Idempotency Store (deduplicates retry requests using unique keys)
Fraud Detection Engine (rules + ML model scoring)
Payment Gateway Adapters (integrations with external providers)
Distributed Transaction Ledger (immutable transaction log)
Settlement Engine (batch processing for fund transfers)
KYC/AML Verification Service
Webhook Notification System (async merchant updates)
Data Warehouse/Analytics (reconciliation and reporting)
scalability_signals: Idempotency key management across distributed nodes to prevent duplicate transactions
Event sourcing for transaction immutability and audit compliance
Sharding strategy for ledger (by merchant ID or payment corridor) to distribute write load
Async settlement processing with compensating transactions for failures
Cross-region replication with conflict-free reconciliation for multi-currency conversions
Caching layer for FX rates with cache invalidation strategy
Circuit breakers for external payment gateway integrations to handle failures gracefully
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Merchants submit payment requests to an API Gateway. Requests flow through a Payment Service that checks the Idempotency Store, validates KYC/AML, and runs Fraud Detection. Valid transactions are routed to Payment Gateway Adapters (Stripe, PayPal, etc.) or direct bank processors. All transactions are logged in a Distributed Ledger. Successful payments flow to the Settlement Engine for batch processing. Merchants receive webhook notifications. Failed/disputed transactions are tracked separately for chargeback handling. Analytics and reconciliation queries pull from the Data Warehouse.

title: Design a Real-Time Content Moderation System
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a real-time content moderation system for a social media platform that processes user-generated content (text posts, comments, images) and flags potentially harmful material before it reaches other users.

The platform has 50M daily active users generating 200M pieces of content daily. Content moderation decisions must be made within 500ms to avoid user friction. The system should support multiple moderation strategies: automated ML-based filtering, keyword blocking, user reporting workflows, and human review escalation for edge cases.

Content types include short-form text (tweets, comments), long-form text (articles), and images. The system must handle:
- Real-time classification of incoming content
- Appeal workflows for incorrectly flagged content
- Admin dashboards for reviewing flagged items
- Configurable policy rules per region/market
- Historical audit logs for compliance

Design the system to minimize false positives (user frustration), false negatives (safety risk), and latency while handling traffic spikes during viral events.

requirements: Accept content submissions (text/image) with <500ms decision latency
Support multiple classification models (toxicity, NSFW, spam, hate speech)
Provide human review queue for uncertain or appealed items
Enable regional policy customization and A/B testing of rules
Store audit trails for compliance and appeals investigation
Real-time metrics dashboard (flagged rate, appeal rate, model performance)
Graceful degradation when ML services are slow or unavailable
required_components: Content Ingestion Service (API endpoint with load balancing)
ML Classification Pipeline (multiple models, ensemble scoring)
Feature Extraction Engine (text embeddings, image analysis, metadata)
Policy Rules Engine (configurable blocking rules, regional variations)
Content Queue/Store (fast retrieval for review, appeals, analytics)
Human Review Workflow Service (task assignment, reviewer UI, state management)
Caching Layer (model outputs, policy rules, hot content)
Audit Log Storage (immutable, queryable, compliance-ready)
Metrics & Monitoring (false positive rate, latency SLIs, model drift detection)
scalability_signals: Horizontal scaling of classification workers with load balancing
Distributed feature extraction (batch processing for images, streaming for text)
Model serving optimization (quantization, caching, regional inference endpoints)
Asynchronous appeals processing to decouple from real-time path
Time-series database for metrics and model performance tracking across regions

Uncertain items route to Human Review Queue (with appeals feedback loop). All decisions logged to Audit Storage. Metrics streamed to monitoring dashboard.

title: Design a Real-Time Video Recommendation Engine
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a recommendation engine for a video streaming platform that generates personalized content suggestions in real-time. The system must handle millions of concurrent users, each with unique viewing histories, preferences, and interaction patterns.

Users can watch videos, like/dislike content, add items to watchlists, and pause/resume playback. The recommendation engine should surface relevant videos on the home feed, in carousel tiles, and during end-of-video suggestions within 200ms latency.

Key challenges: balancing collaborative filtering with content-based recommendations, handling cold-start problems for new users and videos, avoiding recommendation staleness as user preferences evolve, and preventing recommendation bubbles while maintaining engagement metrics.

**Scale Assumptions:**
- 50M daily active users
- 2B total videos in catalog
- 500K QPS for recommendation requests
- Average user has 200-500 interactions (views, likes, watchlist adds)
- New videos uploaded: 10K/day
- Recommendation freshness required: < 5 minutes for trending shifts

requirements: Real-time personalized recommendations within 200ms SLA
Handle cold-start for new users (< 24h data) and new videos
Support multiple recommendation contexts (home feed, end-of-video, search results, carousel tiles)
Track and incorporate user signals (watches, likes, dislikes, watch duration, watchlist adds)
Detect and prevent recommendation bubbles and echo chambers
A/B test recommendation algorithms with metrics tracking
Handle user preference drift and seasonal content popularity changes
Provide explainability signals for why a video was recommended

Collaborative Filtering Service (user-user and item-item similarity)
Content-Based Ranking Module (video metadata, genres, cast, themes)
Real-Time Signal Ingestion (Kafka/Pulsar for events: views, likes, watch duration)
Embedding Store (vector database like Pinecone/Weaviate for fast similarity search)
Model Serving Layer (low-latency inference for ranking models)
Candidate Generation Service (ALS, matrix factorization, or neural collaborative filtering)
Ranking & Re-ranking Service (combining signals, diversity, freshness, business rules)

title: Design a Multi-Tenant Subscription & Billing Schema
problem_statement_markdown:
You are building a billing platform for a multi-tenant SaaS that supports flexible subscription plans with usage-based charges, plan changes, and prorated billing.

Customers subscribe to plans (e.g., Basic, Pro, Enterprise), each with a base monthly fee. Plans contain features, and customers are granted feature entitlements based on their current plan. Customers can upgrade/downgrade plans mid-cycle, triggering prorated adjustments. Additionally, plans support overage charges—if a customer exceeds usage thresholds for metered features (e.g., API calls), they incur per-unit overage costs.

Each tenant (SaaS customer company) has multiple user accounts, and billing is tracked at the subscription level. Historical plan changes, feature entitlements, and overage charges must be auditable. Soft-deleted subscriptions and plan changes should not affect active billing calculations.

requirements: Support multiple subscription tiers with distinct base pricing and features
Track temporal validity of plan changes (effective dates, cancellation dates) without deleting historical records
Implement M:M relationship between Plans and Features with feature-level entitlements (e.g., API rate limit per feature)
Model usage-based overage charges tied to metered features with aggregation logic
Support mid-cycle plan transitions with prorated billing calculations
Enable soft-deletion of subscriptions and audit historical billing events
Isolate multi-tenant data; each tenant has independent plans, subscriptions, and usage tracking
Track billing cycles, invoice generation triggers, and payment status transitions
modeling_signals: Temporal validity (effective_date, ended_at) on Subscription and PlanChange to track plan history
Soft delete via deleted_at on Subscription to preserve billing audit trail
M:M relationship (Plan ↔ Feature) with attributes (entitlement_value, e.g., API call limit)
M:M relationship (Subscription ↔ Feature) to track active entitlements with temporal scope
Polymorphic or discriminated charge types (base fee vs. overage) in Invoice line items
Multi-tenancy isolation at Tenant level with cascading foreign keys
Usage aggregation: UsageRecord tied to Subscription, Feature, and billing period
metadata.reference_schema_description: Core structure: Tenant → Account (user) and Subscription (with temporal validity). Plan contains Features via M:M with entitlement metadata. Subscription tracks active plan and history via PlanChange records (each with effective_date, ended_at). UsageRecord captures metered consumption per Subscription/Feature/period. Invoice aggregates base fees and calculated overages, with line items linking to Feature and usage totals. Soft-deleted Subscriptions exclude from active billing queries via WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.

title: Design a Healthcare Provider Network & Claims Schema
problem_statement_markdown: You are designing a data model for a health insurance platform that manages provider networks, member enrollments, and insurance claims processing. The system must track which providers (doctors, hospitals, clinics) are in-network for different insurance plans, handle temporal validity of network memberships, process claims with multiple service line items, and support soft deletes for historical audit trails. Providers can offer different specialties and have varying contracted rates by plan. Claims must reference both the provider and the specific plan under which care was delivered, and support rejection reasons with appeal workflows.

requirements: Track provider network membership with effective and termination dates (temporal validity)
Support multiple specialties per provider with many-to-many relationships
Model contracted rates that vary by provider-plan combination with historical tracking
Process claims with multiple service line items, each with its own cost and status
Support soft deletes on all entities with deleted_at timestamps for compliance auditing
Enable claim rejection with reason codes and appeal workflow states
Track claim adjudication history (submitted, in-review, approved, rejected, appealed)
Ensure claims reference both the plan member belongs to and the in-network provider
modeling_signals: Temporal validity: effective_date and termination_date on ProviderNetworkMembership
Soft deletes: deleted_at column on all core entities for audit compliance
M:M with attributes: Provider-Specialty junction with years_of_experience and certification_level
M:M with attributes: ContractedRate joining Provider-Plan with rate_amount, effective_period, and copay_override
Polymorphic state machine: ClaimAdjudication with status enum (submitted, in_review, approved, rejected, appealed) and conditional reason_code
Historical tracking: audit trail of rate changes and membership changes via effective dating

metadata.reference_schema_description: Core schema includes Provider (with NPI, license_state), InsurancePlan (plan_type, coverage_year), and Member (plan_id, effective_enrollment_date). ProviderNetworkMembership bridges Provider-Plan with temporal dates and status. ContractedRate tracks negotiated rates per Provider-Plan pair with valid date ranges. Claim aggregates claim-level metadata (claim_number, member_id, provider_id, plan_id, submitted_date, total_amount). ClaimLineItem breaks down services (service_code, description, quantity, billed_amount, allowed_amount). title: Design a Dynamic Inventory & Fulfillment Schema for Multi-Warehouse E-Commerce
problem_statement_markdown: You are designing the inventory and fulfillment backbone for a multi-warehouse e-commerce platform serving multiple regional brands. The system must track product inventory across distributed warehouses in real-time, handle complex fulfillment rules (split shipments, cross-warehouse transfers, backorders with temporal validity windows), and support polymorphic inventory types (physical stock, pre-orders with release dates, drop-shipped items). Additionally, the schema must audit all inventory mutations (stock movements, holds, reservations) with full traceability, support brand-level inventory isolation, and efficiently query available-to-promise (ATP) inventory across warehouse networks considering in-flight orders and pending transfers. A critical challenge: inventory reservations expire if orders aren't confirmed within a time window, and you must handle race conditions where multiple orders compete for limited stock across asynchronous fulfillment pipelines.

requirements: Track inventory levels across multiple warehouses with real-time availability visibility
Support polymorphic inventory types: physical stock, pre-orders (with release dates), drop-shipped items, and consignment inventory
Implement inventory reservations with temporal expiration windows and cascading release logic
Audit all inventory transactions (receives, transfers, adjustments, holds, releases) with full lineage and reason codes
Enforce brand-level inventory isolation while allowing cross-warehouse fulfillment within authorized networks
Calculate available-to-promise (ATP) inventory accounting for in-flight orders, pending transfers, and safety stock policies
Support backorder queuing with customer priority rules and automatic allocation when stock replenishes
Model fulfillment rules as polymorphic relationships (warehouse rules, carrier rules, product-warehouse rules) with soft-delete history
modeling_signals: Temporal validity: reservation expiration windows, pre-order release dates, backorder FIFO timestamps
Polymorphic relationships: InventoryType hierarchy (Physical, PreOrder, DropShipped, Consignment) with type-specific attributes
Soft deletes on FulfillmentRule with temporal versioning for audit trails
M:M with attributes: InventoryLocation-to-InventoryType junction with quantity, reserved_qty, hold_qty, damaged_qty
Event sourcing pattern: InventoryMovement as immutable audit log with reason codes and linked order/transfer context
Race condition handling: reservation state machine (pending → confirmed → released/expired) with optimistic locking
Hierarchical multi-tenancy: Brand isolation with warehouse network authorization rules
metadata.reference_schema_description: The schema models inventory as a state machine across distributed locations. Core junction table InventoryLocation (Warehouse × Product × InventoryType) tracks quantity variants (available, reserved, on_hold, damaged). InventoryMovement is an append-only ledger capturing every state change with contextual references (order_id, transfer_id, reason_code). InventoryReservation (M:M between Order and InventoryLocation) includes expiration logic and cascading release triggers. FulfillmentRule uses single-table inheritance (rule_type discriminator) to polymorphically attach to Warehouse, Product, or Warehouse-Product pairs. BackorderQueue maintains FIFO priority with allocation triggers on replenishment. ATP queries join across InventoryLocation filtered by type and temporal validity, minus reserved and on-hold quantities. Brand-level isolation enforced via foreign key on Warehouse and row-level filtering on all inventory queries.

title: Design a Social Graph & Content Feed Schema
problem_statement_markdown:
You are designing the data model for a social content platform similar to Twitter/X. Users create posts, follow each other, and engage through likes, reposts, and replies. The platform must support:

Design a schema supporting millions of daily active users, billions of posts, and real-time feed queries without sacrificing data consistency.

Support directional follow relationships with temporal validity (follow_at, unfollow_at timestamps)

Temporal validity (follow_at, unfollow_at, deleted_at for audit trails)
M:M with attributes (FollowRelationship carries follow_at, mutual_follow boolean, notification_muted)

title: Design a Dynamic Pricing & Seat Allocation Schema for Event Ticketing
problem_statement_markdown:
You are designing the data model for a large-scale event ticketing platform that supports concerts, sports, theater, and conferences. The platform must handle dynamic pricing (prices change based on demand, time-to-event, and seat location), complex seat inventories across multiple venue layouts, ticket holds with expiration, and flexible refund/exchange policies that vary by event and ticket type.

metadata.reference_schema_description: Core tables: Events (with deleted_at), Venues, VenueLayouts (layout_version, effective_event_id), SeatSections, Seats (section_id, row, seat_number, status), PricingWindows (event_id, start_date, end_date), PricingTiers (name, section_id, window_id, base_price, effective_from, effective_to), Tickets (seat_id, order_id, status, price_paid, created_at, deleted_at), TicketHolds (ticket_id/seat_id, order_id, hold_expires_at), Orders (user_id, event_id, total_price, status), Transactions (order_id, type: 'hold'/'sale'/'refund'/'exchange', before_state, after_state, timestamp), RefundPolicies (event_id/ticket_type_id, refund_before_days, restocking_fee_pct, exchange_allowed, valid_from, valid_to). title: Warehouse Inventory Reconciliation
problem_statement_markdown:
# Warehouse Inventory Reconciliation

A warehouse manager receives two lists of product IDs: one from the physical inventory count and one from the system records. The manager needs to identify discrepancies to flag items for recount.

Given two lists of integers representing product IDs:
- `physical_count`: IDs counted during the physical inventory audit
- `system_records`: IDs in the warehouse management system

Return a list of product IDs that appear a **different number of times** in the two lists. If a product appears 3 times physically but 2 times in the system, it should be included. Order does not matter in the output.

**Example 1:**
```
physical_count = [101, 102, 101, 103]
system_records = [101, 102, 103, 103]
Output: [101, 103]
```
Explanation: Product 101 appears 2 times physically but 1 time in system. Product 103 appears 1 time physically but 2 times in system.

**Example 2:**
```
physical_count = [5, 5, 5]
system_records = [5, 5, 5]
Output: []
```
Explanation: All products match perfectly.

metadata.reference_approach: Use hash maps (dictionaries) to count the frequency of each product ID in both lists. Iterate through the union of all product IDs present in either list and compare their frequencies. If frequencies differ, add the product ID to the result. Time complexity: O(n + m) where n and m are the lengths of the two input lists. Space complexity: O(n + m) for the frequency maps.

title: Rebuild Playlist from Shuffle Logs
problem_statement_markdown:
You are given a list of song transitions that occurred during a shuffle playback session. Each transition is represented as a tuple `(previous_song, next_song)` indicating that `next_song` was played immediately after `previous_song`.

Your task is to reconstruct the original playlist order from these transitions. The playlist is guaranteed to be a valid linear sequence (no cycles, no branches).

**Return the complete playlist as a list of song IDs in playback order.**

**Constraints:**
- Input is a list of tuples, each containing two distinct song IDs (strings or integers)
- The playlist has at least 1 song
- All transitions form a single valid chain with no missing or duplicate songs
- Song IDs are unique identifiers

**Examples:**

1. Input: `[("B", "C"), ("A", "B")]`  
   Output: `["A", "B", "C"]`  
   Explanation: A played first, then B, then C.

2. Input: `[(2, 5), (5, 7), (1, 2)]`  
   Output: `[1, 2, 5, 7]`  
   Explanation: Song 1 → 2 → 5 → 7.

test_cases.label: Integer song IDs with longer chain

starter_code.python:
def solution(transitions):
    """
    Rebuild the playlist from shuffle transition logs.
    
    Args:
        transitions: List of tuples (prev_song, next_song)
    
    Returns:
        List of song IDs in original playback order
    """
    pass

reference_solution.python:
def solution(transitions):
    if not transitions:
        return []
    
    # Build a graph: next_song_map[song] = following_song
    next_song_map = {}
    all_songs = set()
    songs_with_predecessor = set()
    
    for prev_song, next_song in transitions:
        next_song_map[prev_song] = next_song
        all_songs.add(prev_song)
        all_songs.add(next_song)
        songs_with_predecessor.add(next_song)
    
    # Find the first song (one with no predecessor)
    first_song = None
    for song in all_songs:
        if song not in songs_with_predecessor:
            first_song = song
            break
    
    # Reconstruct the playlist by following the chain
    playlist = []
    current = first_song
    while current is not None:
        playlist.append(current)
        current = next_song_map.get(current)
    
    return playlist

metadata.reference_approach: Use two-pointer-inspired graph traversal: build a hash map of next_song relationships and a set tracking which songs have a predecessor. title: Optimize Meeting Schedule
problem_statement_markdown:
# Optimize Meeting Schedule

A project manager has a list of meetings to schedule with prerequisite constraints. Some meetings must occur before others (e.g., kickoff before design review, design review before implementation review).

Given:
- `n_meetings`: total number of meetings (numbered 0 to n-1)
- `prerequisites`: a list of tuples `(meeting_b, meeting_a)` meaning meeting_a must happen before meeting_b

Return a valid meeting order that respects all prerequisites, or an empty list if scheduling is impossible (e.g., circular dependency: meeting A requires B, B requires A).

**Example 1:**
```
n_meetings = 4
prerequisites = [(1, 0), (2, 0), (3, 1), (3, 2)]
Output: [0, 1, 2, 3] (or [0, 2, 1, 3])
```
Explanation: Meeting 0 must happen first, then 1 and 2 (in any order), then 3 last.

**Example 2:**
```
n_meetings = 2
prerequisites = [(1, 0), (0, 1)]
Output: []
```
Explanation: Circular dependency. Meeting 0 must come before 1, but 1 must come before 0. Impossible.

starter_code.python:
def solution(n_meetings, prerequisites):
    """
    Find valid meeting order respecting prerequisites.
    
    Args:
        n_meetings: int - total meetings (0 to n-1)
        prerequisites: List[Tuple[int, int]] - (meeting_b, meeting_a) means a before b
    
    Returns:
        List[int] - valid schedule, or empty list if impossible
    """
    pass

reference_solution.python:
from collections import defaultdict, deque

def solution(n_meetings, prerequisites):
    # Build adjacency list and in-degree count
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    in_degree = [0] * n_meetings
    
    for meeting_b, meeting_a in prerequisites:
        graph[meeting_a].append(meeting_b)
        in_degree[meeting_b] += 1
    
    # Kahn's algorithm: topological sort
    queue = deque([i for i in range(n_meetings) if in_degree[i] == 0])
    schedule = []
    
    while queue:
        meeting = queue.popleft()
        schedule.append(meeting)
        
        for next_meeting in graph[meeting]:
            in_degree[next_meeting] -= 1
            if in_degree[next_meeting] == 0:
                queue.append(next_meeting)
    
    # If not all meetings scheduled, there's a cycle
    if len(schedule) != n_meetings:
        return []
    
    return schedule

metadata.reference_approach: Model the problem as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where each meeting is a node and prerequisites define edges. Use Kahn's algorithm (topological sort with in-degree counting): (1) Build adjacency list and in-degree for each node, (2) queue all nodes with in-degree 0, (3) repeatedly dequeue a node, add it to result, and decrement in-degree of its neighbors, (4) if a neighbor's in-degree becomes 0, enqueue it. If fewer than n_meetings are scheduled, a cycle exists and the answer is empty. Time complexity: O(n + p) where n is meetings and p is prerequisites. Space complexity: O(n + p) for graph storage.

options.option_text: Constant-time average lookup keeps the join over orders and refunds at O(n+m) time.

options.option_text: Hash maps offer better cache locality on modern CPUs than sorted arrays.
options.explanation: Cache locality is a real hardware consideration, but it actually favors sorted arrays and linear scans over hash maps in many cases. Finally, the outer query filters to only rows where rank ≤ 3, returning the top 3 best-selling products per category. This two-level approach avoids mixing GROUP BY and window functions in the same SELECT clause, which is the key pattern for solving complex ranking problems in SQL.

-- Write your SQL query here
-- For each advertiser, compute their ROI
-- ROI = (conversions × $50 - spend) / spend × 100
-- Use NULLIF to avoid division-by-zero

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT
  a.name,
  SUM(s.spend) AS total_spend,
  SUM(s.conversions) AS total_conversions,
  SUM(s.conversions) * 50 AS estimated_revenue,
  ROUND((SUM(s.conversions) * 50 - SUM(s.spend)) / NULLIF(SUM(s.spend), 0) * 100, 2) AS roi_pct
FROM advertisers a
JOIN ad_spend s ON a.advertiser_id = s.advertiser_id
GROUP BY a.advertiser_id, a.name
ORDER BY roi_pct DESC;

metadata.reference_approach: Group ad_spend records by advertiser and calculate total spend and total conversions. Compute estimated revenue as conversions × $50. Calculate ROI using the formula (estimated_revenue - total_spend) / total_spend × 100, protecting against division-by-zero with NULLIF(SUM(s.spend), 0). Round to 2 decimal places and sort by ROI in descending order. The NULLIF function returns NULL when spend is zero, causing the entire division to yield NULL rather than a database error, which is the expected behavior for advertisers with zero spend.

-- Calculate the 7-day rolling friend request acceptance rate for each day in 2024

reference_solution.sql:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT sent_date,
         COUNT(*) AS sent,
         COUNT(accepted_date) AS accepted
  FROM friend_requests
  WHERE sent_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
  GROUP BY sent_date
)

       SUM(accepted) OVER (ORDER BY sent_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_accepted,
       SUM(sent) OVER (ORDER BY sent_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_sent,

FROM daily
ORDER BY sent_date;

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Calculate percentage of total revenue from promoted vs non-promoted products
-- A product is promoted if it has a matching row in promotions table
-- AND the order_date falls within the promotion date range

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT
  SUM(CASE WHEN pr.promotion_id IS NOT NULL THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount) ELSE 0 END) AS promoted_revenue,
  SUM(CASE WHEN pr.promotion_id IS NULL THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount) ELSE 0 END) AS non_promoted_revenue,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN pr.promotion_id IS NOT NULL THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount) ELSE 0 END)
    / SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)), 2) AS promoted_pct
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN promotions pr ON p.product_id = pr.product_id
  AND o.order_date BETWEEN pr.start_date AND pr.end_date;

test_cases.label: Basic: Promoted vs non-promoted revenue split with percentages
Verify: Date range filtering for promotions (only active on order date)
Edge case: Multiple promotions, mixed discount levels, order-level discounts

metadata.reference_approach: The solution uses conditional aggregation with CASE WHEN to split revenue into two buckets: promoted (where a promotion exists and the order date falls within its active window) and non-promoted. A LEFT JOIN ensures all order items are included, with NULL promotion_id indicating no active promotion. The revenue for each item is quantity × unit_price × (1 − discount). Two SUM(CASE WHEN ...) expressions calculate the separate revenue streams, and a third calculates the promoted percentage relative to total revenue. This avoids multiple queries and computes all metrics in a single pass.

-- Write your SQL query here
-- Use a CTE to compute daily acceptance rates
-- Use another CTE for the platform-wide average
-- CROSS JOIN them to enrich each day with the global average
-- Filter for days below 50% and show the difference

reference_solution.sql:
WITH daily_rates AS (
  SELECT sent_date,
         ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(accepted_date) / COUNT(*), 2) AS acceptance_rate_pct
  FROM friend_requests
  GROUP BY sent_date
),
platform_avg AS (
  SELECT ROUND(AVG(acceptance_rate_pct), 2) AS avg_rate FROM daily_rates
)
SELECT d.sent_date, d.acceptance_rate_pct, p.avg_rate,
       ROUND(d.acceptance_rate_pct - p.avg_rate, 2) AS diff_from_avg
FROM daily_rates d CROSS JOIN platform_avg p
WHERE d.acceptance_rate_pct < 50
ORDER BY d.acceptance_rate_pct;

metadata.reference_approach: Build a CTE (daily_rates) that groups friend_requests by sent_date and calculates the daily acceptance rate as the percentage of requests with a non-NULL accepted_date. -- Write your SQL query here
-- Find the cancellation rate for each property type

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT l.property_type,
       COUNT(b.booking_id) AS total_bookings,
       SUM(CASE WHEN b.status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN b.status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(b.booking_id), 2) AS cancellation_rate_pct
FROM listings l JOIN bookings b ON l.listing_id = b.listing_id
GROUP BY l.property_type
ORDER BY cancellation_rate_pct DESC;

metadata.reference_approach: Join the listings table with bookings on listing_id. For each property type, count the total number of bookings and use a CASE WHEN expression to count only the cancelled bookings. Divide the sum of cancelled bookings by the total count of bookings, multiply by 100.0 to convert to percentage, and ROUND to 2 decimal places. Group by property_type and order by cancellation_rate_pct in descending order to surface the property types with the highest cancellation rates.

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Hint: First aggregate to monthly revenue in a CTE, then apply AVG() with ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

reference_solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT l.host_id, DATE(STRFTIME('%Y-%m-01', b.check_in)) AS month,
         SUM(b.total_price) AS monthly_revenue
  FROM listings l JOIN bookings b ON l.listing_id = b.listing_id
  WHERE b.status = 'completed' AND b.check_in >= '2024-01-01' AND b.check_in < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY l.host_id, DATE(STRFTIME('%Y-%m-01', b.check_in))
)
SELECT host_id, month, monthly_revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(monthly_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY host_id ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS rolling_3m_avg
FROM monthly ORDER BY host_id, month;

test_cases.label: Monthly revenue and 3-month rolling average for all hosts in 2024
Verify rolling average calculation with ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
Edge case: hosts with varying number of completed bookings across months

metadata.reference_approach: Create a CTE named 'monthly' that aggregates total_price from completed bookings by host and month (using DATE_TRUNC equivalent in SQLite). Then apply a window function AVG() with PARTITION BY host_id and ORDER BY month, using ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW to compute the 3-month rolling average. The ROWS frame is more efficient for numeric rolling windows than RANGE, and ensures each row includes itself plus the two preceding months. Finally, order by host_id and month to display results clearly.

reference_solution.sql:
WITH earnings AS (
  SELECT r.city, d.driver_id, d.name,
         SUM(r.fare) AS total_fare,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY r.city ORDER BY SUM(r.fare) DESC) AS city_rank
  FROM rides r JOIN drivers d ON r.driver_id = d.driver_id
  WHERE r.status = 'completed'
    AND r.start_time >= '2024-01-01' AND r.start_time < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY r.city, d.driver_id, d.name
)
SELECT city, name, total_fare, city_rank
FROM earnings WHERE city_rank <= 5
ORDER BY city, city_rank;

metadata.reference_approach: This solution demonstrates the critical pattern of aggregating data in a CTE before applying window functions. First, the CTE computes total fare per driver per city by joining rides with drivers and filtering for completed 2024 rides. Then RANK() with PARTITION BY city creates per-city rankings ordered by descending total_fare. Finally, the outer query filters to rank ≤ 5 and orders results by city and rank. This approach avoids the common mistake of trying to use window functions directly on unaggregated columns in a GROUP BY context.

SELECT m.category,
       COUNT(t.txn_id) AS total_txns,

SELECT s.title,

       SUM(CASE WHEN v.watch_pct >= 80 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_views,

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Find the top 3 most watched shows per genre by total unique viewers
-- Use DENSE_RANK() to handle ties properly

reference_solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT s.genre, s.title,
         COUNT(DISTINCT v.user_id) AS unique_viewers,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY s.genre ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT v.user_id) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM views v JOIN shows s ON v.show_id = s.show_id
  GROUP BY s.genre, s.show_id, s.title
)
SELECT genre, title, unique_viewers, rnk
FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY genre, rnk;

test_cases.label: Top 3 shows per genre by unique viewers
DENSE_RANK handles ties correctly (no rank gaps)
Edge case: multiple genres with varying viewer counts

metadata.reference_approach: Use a CTE with a window function to partition views by genre and rank shows within each genre by count of distinct viewers in descending order. DENSE_RANK() ensures that if two shows tie for 2nd place, both receive rank 2 and the next show gets rank 3 (not rank 4), which is crucial for business logic that requires exactly 'top 3' including ties. Filter to rnk <= 3 and order by genre and rank for clarity.

title: Spotify: Skip Rate Analysis
problem_statement_markdown: What percentage of streams were skipped before 30 seconds for each genre?

starter_code.sql:

-- Calculate the percentage of streams skipped before 30 seconds for each genre

SELECT t.genre,
       COUNT(*) AS total_streams,
       SUM(CASE WHEN s.skipped = 1 AND s.listen_duration_sec < 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS early_skips,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN s.skipped = 1 AND s.listen_duration_sec < 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS skip_rate_pct
FROM streams s
JOIN tracks t ON s.track_id = t.track_id
GROUP BY t.genre
ORDER BY skip_rate_pct DESC;

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Show the 4-week rolling average engagement rate (likes + comments / views) per content type for 2024
-- Aggregate to weekly sums first, then apply rolling SUM window functions

reference_solution.sql:
WITH weekly AS (
  SELECT content_type,
         DATE(posted_at, 'weekday 0', '-6 days') AS week,
         SUM(likes + comments) AS total_engagement,
         SUM(views) AS total_views
  FROM posts
  WHERE posted_at >= '2024-01-01' AND posted_at < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY content_type, DATE(posted_at, 'weekday 0', '-6 days')
)
SELECT content_type,
       week,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(total_engagement) OVER (PARTITION BY content_type ORDER BY week ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
             / NULLIF(SUM(total_views) OVER (PARTITION BY content_type ORDER BY week ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 0), 2) AS rolling_4w_engagement_pct
FROM weekly
ORDER BY content_type, week;

Rolling 4-week engagement rate for Video across multiple weeks
Verify engagement rate calculation with different view volumes

metadata.reference_approach: First aggregate posts to weekly sums of engagement (likes + comments) and views per content type using DATE truncation. Then apply a 4-row window (3 preceding + current) with SUM over both the engagement and views columns, partitioned by content_type and ordered by week. Divide rolling engagement sum by rolling views sum to get the correctly weighted rolling engagement rate, multiplying by 100 for percentage. This ensures weeks with higher view volumes influence the average appropriately, rather than averaging individual weekly rates which would give equal weight to all weeks.

title: Airbnb: Guests Who Booked Multiple Cities

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Find guests who have completed bookings in 3 or more different cities

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT b.guest_id, g.name, COUNT(DISTINCT l.city) AS cities_visited
FROM bookings b
JOIN listings l ON b.listing_id = l.listing_id
JOIN guests g ON b.guest_id = g.guest_id
WHERE b.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY b.guest_id, g.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT l.city) >= 3
ORDER BY cities_visited DESC;

The HAVING clause filters groups where the distinct city count is 3 or more. Finally, order by cities_visited in descending order to show the most-traveled guests first. This is a classic aggregation pattern for identifying customers who have engaged with multiple categories or locations.

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Calculate month-over-month revenue growth rate per merchant category for 2024

reference_solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT m.category,
         DATE(strftime('%Y-%m-01', t.created_at)) AS month,
         SUM(t.amount) AS monthly_revenue
  FROM merchants m 
  JOIN transactions t ON m.merchant_id = t.merchant_id
  WHERE t.status = 'completed' 
    AND t.created_at >= '2024-01-01' 
    AND t.created_at < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY m.category, DATE(strftime('%Y-%m-01', t.created_at))
)
SELECT category, 
       month, 
       monthly_revenue,
       LAG(monthly_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY month) AS prev_month_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (monthly_revenue - LAG(monthly_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY month))
             / NULLIF(LAG(monthly_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY month), 0), 2) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY category, month;

First month has NULL previous month revenue

metadata.reference_approach: Use a CTE to aggregate completed transactions by merchant category and month for 2024. Then apply a LAG window function partitioned by category and ordered by month to retrieve the previous month's revenue within each category. Calculate the month-over-month growth percentage as (current_month - previous_month) / previous_month * 100. The PARTITION BY clause ensures each category's growth is tracked independently, and the first month of each category will have a NULL previous month value.

title: Spotify: Top 5 Artists per Genre
problem_statement_markdown: Find the top 5 most streamed artists per genre this year.

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Find the top 5 most streamed artists per genre in 2024
-- Use a CTE to aggregate streams by genre and artist, then apply RANK()

reference_solution.sql:
WITH artist_streams AS (
  SELECT t.genre, a.name AS artist_name, COUNT(s.stream_id) AS stream_count,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY t.genre ORDER BY COUNT(s.stream_id) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM streams s
  JOIN tracks t ON s.track_id = t.track_id
  JOIN artists a ON t.artist_id = a.artist_id
  WHERE s.streamed_at >= '2024-01-01'
  GROUP BY t.genre, a.artist_id, a.name
)
SELECT genre, artist_name, stream_count, rnk
FROM artist_streams
WHERE rnk <= 5
ORDER BY genre, rnk;

Apply the RANK() window function partitioned by genre and ordered by stream_count descending to rank artists within each genre. Filter the ranked results to keep only the top 5 (rnk <= 5) and sort by genre and rank for readability. This approach ensures aggregation happens before windowing, which is critical for accurate ranking.

title: Repeat Customer Rate

-- Join orders to customers on customer_id AND store_id
-- A repeat order is when order_date > first_order_date

  SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_date > c.first_order_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS repeat_orders,

title: Top 5 Drivers by Total Earnings
problem_statement_markdown: Who are the top 5 drivers by total earnings (fare + tip + incentives) in each city?

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Find the top 5 drivers by total earnings (fare + tip + incentives) in each city
-- Include drivers with no incentives using LEFT JOIN
-- Use RANK() OVER to rank within each city

reference_solution.sql:
WITH earnings AS (
  SELECT r.city, r.driver_id, d.name,
         SUM(r.fare + r.tip) AS ride_earnings,
         COALESCE(SUM(i.amount), 0) AS incentive_earnings
  FROM rides r
  JOIN drivers d ON r.driver_id = d.driver_id
  LEFT JOIN incentives i ON r.driver_id = i.driver_id
    AND strftime('%Y', i.paid_at) = strftime('%Y', r.pickup_time)
  WHERE r.status = 'completed' AND r.pickup_time >= '2024-01-01' AND r.pickup_time < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY r.city, r.driver_id, d.name
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *, (ride_earnings + incentive_earnings) AS total_earnings,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY (ride_earnings + incentive_earnings) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM earnings
)
SELECT city, name, ride_earnings, incentive_earnings, total_earnings, rnk
FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 5 ORDER BY city, rnk;

Top 5 drivers by total earnings in Los Angeles
Drivers with no incentives still included

metadata.reference_approach: Use a CTE to aggregate ride earnings (fare + tip) and incentive earnings per driver per city, applying a LEFT JOIN to incentives to preserve drivers without incentives using COALESCE. In a second CTE, calculate total earnings and apply RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city) to rank drivers within each city. Finally, filter to rank <= 5 and order by city and rank. This ensures drivers with no incentives are included with 0 incentive earnings, and ties are handled correctly with RANK().

title: Over-Budget Campaigns

-- Hint: Pre-aggregate ad_performance by campaign_id first, then join to campaigns

title: High-CTR Campaigns
problem_statement_markdown: Which campaigns have a click-through rate (CTR) above 5%?

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Find campaigns with CTR > 5%
-- Remember: CTR = clicks / impressions
-- Hint: Use HAVING to filter aggregated groups

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT c.name AS campaign_name, a.name AS advertiser,
       SUM(ap.impressions) AS total_impressions,
       SUM(ap.clicks) AS total_clicks,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(ap.clicks) / NULLIF(SUM(ap.impressions), 0), 2) AS ctr_pct
FROM campaigns c
JOIN advertisers a ON c.advertiser_id = a.advertiser_id
JOIN ad_performance ap ON c.campaign_id = ap.campaign_id
GROUP BY c.campaign_id, c.name, a.name
HAVING 100.0 * SUM(ap.clicks) / NULLIF(SUM(ap.impressions), 0) > 5
ORDER BY ctr_pct DESC;

test_cases.label: Verify correct CTR calculation with aggregation
Edge case: campaign with low CTR excluded

metadata.reference_approach: This query demonstrates the GROUP BY & HAVING pattern for filtering aggregated results. First, join the three tables (campaigns, advertisers, ad_performance) to combine campaign metadata with performance metrics. Then GROUP BY campaign to aggregate impressions and clicks across all ad records for each campaign. Calculate CTR as clicks divided by impressions (multiplied by 100 for percentage). The key insight is using HAVING with the full aggregate expression (not the alias) to filter for campaigns with CTR > 5%. NULLIF prevents division by zero. Finally, order by CTR descending to show the best-performing campaigns first.

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Calculate week-over-week conversion rate change per industry for 2024
-- Use LAG() partitioned by industry to compare with previous week's rate

reference_solution.sql:
WITH weekly AS (
  SELECT a.industry, 
         DATE(ap.date, 'weekday 0', '-6 days') AS week,
         SUM(ap.conversions) AS convs, 
         SUM(ap.clicks) AS clicks
  FROM ad_performance ap
  JOIN campaigns c ON ap.campaign_id = c.campaign_id
  JOIN advertisers a ON c.advertiser_id = a.advertiser_id
  WHERE ap.date >= '2024-01-01' AND ap.date < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY a.industry, DATE(ap.date, 'weekday 0', '-6 days')
),
rates AS (
  SELECT industry, 
         week,
         ROUND(100.0 * convs / NULLIF(clicks, 0), 2) AS conv_rate,
         LAG(ROUND(100.0 * convs / NULLIF(clicks, 0), 2)) OVER (PARTITION BY industry ORDER BY week) AS prev_conv_rate
  FROM weekly
)
SELECT industry, 
       week, 
       conv_rate, 
       prev_conv_rate,
       ROUND(conv_rate - COALESCE(prev_conv_rate, conv_rate), 2) AS wow_delta
FROM rates 
ORDER BY industry, week;

First week of each industry has NULL previous rate

metadata.reference_approach: Build a CTE that aggregates conversions and clicks by week and industry. Calculate the conversion rate (conversions/clicks * 100) per week. Apply LAG() window function partitioned by industry and ordered by week to retrieve the previous week's conversion rate. Finally, compute the week-over-week delta by subtracting the previous rate from the current rate. This approach ensures the rate is calculated first, then the LAG comparison is applied to the computed metric, avoiding issues with lagging raw numerators/denominators.

-- Calculate tip rate percentage broken down by vehicle type for completed rides

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT d.vehicle_type,
       COUNT(r.ride_id) AS total_rides,
       SUM(CASE WHEN r.tip > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS tipped_rides,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN r.tip > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(r.ride_id), 2) AS tip_rate_pct,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN r.tip > 0 THEN r.tip END), 2) AS avg_tip_when_tipped
FROM rides r
JOIN drivers d ON r.driver_id = d.driver_id
WHERE r.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY d.vehicle_type
ORDER BY tip_rate_pct DESC;

Additionally, compute the average tip amount only for rides where a tip was given by using CASE WHEN in the AVG function (NULL values from ELSE are automatically ignored). title: Lyft: Top 5 Earners per City
problem_statement_markdown: Who are the top 5 drivers by total earnings (fare + tip + incentives) in each city for 2024?

starter_code.sql:
-- Top 5 Earners per City for 2024
-- Use LEFT JOIN on incentives with COALESCE to preserve drivers with no incentives
-- Use RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city) for per-city ranking
WRITE YOUR QUERY HERE

reference_solution.sql:
WITH earnings AS (
  SELECT 
    r.city,
    r.driver_id,
    d.name,
    SUM(r.fare + r.tip) AS ride_earn,
    COALESCE(SUM(i.amount), 0) AS incent_earn
  FROM rides r
  JOIN drivers d ON r.driver_id = d.driver_id
  LEFT JOIN incentives i ON r.driver_id = i.driver_id AND strftime('%Y', i.paid_at) = '2024'
  WHERE r.status = 'completed' AND strftime('%Y', r.pickup_time) = '2024'
  GROUP BY r.city, r.driver_id, d.name
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT 
    *,
    (ride_earn + incent_earn) AS total,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY (ride_earn + incent_earn) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM earnings
)
SELECT city, name, ride_earn, incent_earn, total, rnk
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 5
ORDER BY city, rnk;

Top 5 earners in Los Angeles by total earnings
Driver with no incentives still appears in ranking

metadata.reference_approach: The solution uses a two-step CTE approach. First, it aggregates ride earnings (fare + tip) and incentives for each driver per city in 2024, using a LEFT JOIN on incentives to preserve drivers with no incentive records via COALESCE(SUM(), 0). Then it applies RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY total DESC) to rank drivers within each city, finally filtering for rank 5 or better and sorting by city and rank for clear per-city breakdowns.

title: Shopify: Top 3 Categories per Plan

starter_code.sql:
-- Find the top 3 product categories by revenue for each Shopify plan tier
-- Use window functions to rank categories within each plan independently

reference_solution.sql:
WITH rev AS (
  SELECT 
    s.plan, 
    p.category, 
    SUM(o.total) AS cat_rev, 
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY s.plan ORDER BY SUM(o.total) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM stores s
  JOIN orders o ON s.store_id = o.store_id
  JOIN products p ON o.store_id = p.store_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY s.plan, p.category
)
SELECT plan, category, cat_rev, rnk 
FROM rev 
WHERE rnk <= 3 
ORDER BY plan, rnk;

title: Shopify: Month-over-Month Store Revenue
problem_statement_markdown: Show month-over-month revenue growth rate per store for 2024.

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Show month-over-month revenue growth rate per store for 2024
-- Use LAG() OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY month) to calculate growth rate

reference_solution.sql:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT 
    store_id,
    DATE(strftime('%Y-%m-01', order_date)) AS month,
    SUM(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed' 
    AND order_date >= '2024-01-01' 
    AND order_date < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY store_id, DATE(strftime('%Y-%m-01', order_date))
)
SELECT 
  store_id,
  month,
  revenue,
  LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
  ROUND(
    100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY month)) / 
    NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY month), 0),
    2
  ) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM m
ORDER BY store_id, month;

metadata.reference_approach: Aggregate monthly revenue per store by grouping completed 2024 orders by store_id and month. Apply LAG() window function with PARTITION BY store_id and ORDER BY month to retrieve the prior month's revenue for each store. Calculate the growth percentage as (current_revenue - previous_revenue) / previous_revenue * 100, using NULLIF to avoid division by zero for the first month of each store. The PARTITION BY store_id is critical—without it, LAG would cross store boundaries and incorrectly compare revenue across different stores.

title: DoorDash: On-Time Delivery Rate
problem_statement_markdown: What percentage of orders were delivered within the restaurant's estimated delivery time?

starter_code.sql:

-- Calculate the percentage of orders delivered within the restaurant's estimated delivery time
-- Compare actual delivery time (delivery_time - order_time) against each restaurant's avg_delivery_time_min
SELECT
  -- Your answer here

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total,
  SUM(CASE WHEN (julianday(o.delivery_time) - julianday(o.order_time)) * 24 * 60 <= r.avg_delivery_time_min THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS on_time,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN (julianday(o.delivery_time) - julianday(o.order_time)) * 24 * 60 <= r.avg_delivery_time_min THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS on_time_rate_pct
FROM orders o
JOIN restaurants r ON o.restaurant_id = r.restaurant_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered';

Count total delivered orders and sum the on-time flagged orders, then calculate the percentage. title: GitHub: Weekly Commit Activity Trend
problem_statement_markdown: For the top 10 repos by stars, show weekly commit count and 4-week rolling average for 2024.

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Hint: Use a CTE to aggregate commits by week first,
-- then apply the 4-week rolling average window function

reference_solution.sql:
WITH top10 AS (
  SELECT repo_id 
  FROM repos 
  WHERE is_public = 1 
  ORDER BY stars DESC 
  LIMIT 10
),
weekly AS (
  SELECT 
    c.repo_id,
    DATE(c.committed_at, 'weekday 1', '-7 days') AS week,
    COUNT(*) AS commits
  FROM commits c
  JOIN top10 t ON c.repo_id = t.repo_id
  WHERE c.committed_at >= '2024-01-01' AND c.committed_at < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY c.repo_id, DATE(c.committed_at, 'weekday 1', '-7 days')
)
SELECT 
  repo_id,
  week,
  commits,
  ROUND(AVG(commits) OVER (PARTITION BY repo_id ORDER BY week ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS rolling_4w
FROM weekly
ORDER BY repo_id, week;

Verify rolling average calculation for repo 1 (highest stars)
Edge case: repo with single week of commits

metadata.reference_approach: The solution identifies the top 10 public repositories by star count, then aggregates commit counts into weekly buckets using a CTE. A window function computes a 4-week rolling average (including the current week and the 3 preceding weeks) partitioned by repository and ordered chronologically. title: Snowflake: Failed Query Rate
problem_statement_markdown: What percentage of queries failed, broken down by account plan?

starter_code.sql:
-- Calculate the percentage of failed queries broken down by account plan
-- Use CASE WHEN to count failures in a single pass
SELECT
  -- plan,
  -- total_queries,
  -- failed,
  -- fail_rate_pct
FROM
  queries q
  JOIN accounts a ON q.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE
  1=1
GROUP BY
  a.plan
ORDER BY
  fail_rate_pct DESC;

reference_solution.sql: SELECT a.plan, COUNT(q.query_id) AS total_queries, SUM(CASE WHEN q.status='failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failed, ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN q.status='failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(q.query_id),2) AS fail_rate_pct FROM queries q JOIN accounts a ON q.account_id=a.account_id GROUP BY a.plan ORDER BY fail_rate_pct DESC;

metadata.reference_approach: This problem demonstrates the efficiency of using a single CASE WHEN expression within aggregate functions to calculate percentages in one pass. Rather than running separate COUNT(*) queries filtered for successes and failures, we use SUM(CASE WHEN status='failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) to count failures and COUNT(query_id) for the total in the same GROUP BY operation. This avoids scanning the queries table multiple times and ensures consistent grouping. The percentage is calculated as (failed/total)*100, rounded to 2 decimal places, and results are ordered by failure rate descending to highlight problem areas by plan type.

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Calculate weekly lead-to-opportunity conversion rate with 4-week rolling average

reference_solution.sql:
WITH weekly AS (
  SELECT 
    DATE(created_at, 'weekday 0') AS week,
    SUM(CASE WHEN lifecycle_stage='lead' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS leads,
    SUM(CASE WHEN lifecycle_stage='opportunity' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS opportunities
  FROM contacts
  WHERE created_at >= DATE('2024-11-09', '-3 months')
  GROUP BY DATE(created_at, 'weekday 0')
)
SELECT 
  week,
  leads,
  opportunities,
  ROUND(100.0 * opportunities / NULLIF(leads, 0), 2) AS conv_rate,
  ROUND(AVG(100.0 * opportunities / NULLIF(leads, 0)) OVER (
    ORDER BY week 
    ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ), 2) AS rolling_4w_avg
FROM weekly
ORDER BY week;

Verify rolling average calculation over 4 weeks
Edge case: weeks with zero leads (division by zero handling)

metadata.reference_approach: First, use a CTE to group contacts by week and count leads vs opportunities for the last 3 months. Then calculate the weekly conversion rate as a percentage (opportunities/leads). Finally, apply a window function with AVG() and a 4-week rolling window (ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) to compute the rolling average of conversion rates, not raw counts. Use NULLIF to handle division by zero.

SELECT

  SUM(CASE WHEN e.opened_at IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS opened,
  SUM(CASE WHEN e.clicked_at IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS clicked,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN e.opened_at IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / NULLIF(COUNT(e.email_id), 0), 2) AS open_rate_pct,

FROM campaigns c
JOIN emails e ON c.campaign_id = e.campaign_id
WHERE e.bounced = 0
GROUP BY c.campaign_id, c.name
ORDER BY open_rate_pct DESC;

title: Snowflake: Top 5 Expensive Queries per Account

starter_code.sql:

-- Filter for successful queries only
-- Return top 5 per account ordered by credits_used descending

reference_solution.sql:
WITH rk AS (
  SELECT account_id, query_id, credits_used, duration_sec, bytes_scanned,

FROM rk

ORDER BY account_id, rnk;

title: Twilio: Hourly Message Volume Trend
problem_statement_markdown: Show the hourly message volume for each account over the last 7 days, with a 3-hour rolling average.

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Show hourly message volume with 3-hour rolling average for each account over the last 7 days

reference_solution.sql:
WITH hourly AS (
  SELECT 
    account_id, 
    STRFTIME('%Y-%m-%d %H:00:00', sent_at) AS hour, 
    COUNT(*) AS msg_count 
  FROM messages 
  WHERE sent_at >= DATE('now', '-7 days')
  GROUP BY account_id, STRFTIME('%Y-%m-%d %H:00:00', sent_at)
)
SELECT 
  account_id,
  hour,
  msg_count, 
  ROUND(AVG(msg_count) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY hour ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS rolling_3h_avg 
FROM hourly 
ORDER BY account_id, hour;

test_cases.label: Multiple accounts appear with their respective hourly volumes
Rolling average increases correctly as window fills from 1 to 3 hours

metadata.reference_approach: First, aggregate messages by account and hour using STRFTIME to truncate sent_at to hourly buckets, filtering for the last 7 days. Then apply a window function with AVG() partitioned by account_id and ordered by hour, using ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW to compute a 3-hour rolling average (current hour + 2 prior hours). The rolling average naturally grows from 1 value in the first hour, to 2 in the second, and stabilizes at 3 thereafter, showing the trend of message volume over time.

title: Salesforce: Cumulative Pipeline by Team

starter_code.sql:

-- Exclude Closed Won and Closed Lost stages
-- Order by team and month

reference_solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT u.team, DATE(o.created_at, 'start of month') AS month, SUM(o.amount) AS new_pipeline
  FROM opportunities o
  JOIN users u ON o.owner_id = u.user_id
  WHERE o.stage NOT IN ('Closed Won', 'Closed Lost')
    AND o.created_at >= '2024-01-01'
    AND o.created_at < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY u.team, DATE(o.created_at, 'start of month')
)

       SUM(new_pipeline) OVER (PARTITION BY team ORDER BY month ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS cumulative_pipeline
FROM monthly
ORDER BY team, month;

title: Twilio: Top 5 Accounts by Total Spend
problem_statement_markdown: Who are the top 5 accounts by total spend (messages + calls) in 2024?

starter_code.sql:
-- Write your SQL query here
-- Find the top 5 accounts by total spend (messages + calls) in 2024

reference_solution.sql:
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT account_id, SUM(cost_usd) AS msg_spend
  FROM messages
  WHERE sent_at >= '2024-01-01' AND sent_at < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY account_id
),
call_spend AS (
  SELECT account_id, SUM(cost_usd) AS call_cost
  FROM calls
  WHERE started_at >= '2024-01-01' AND started_at < '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY account_id
)
SELECT
  a.name,
  COALESCE(s.msg_spend, 0) AS msg_spend,
  COALESCE(c.call_cost, 0) AS call_spend,
  COALESCE(s.msg_spend, 0) + COALESCE(c.call_cost, 0) AS total_spend
FROM accounts a
LEFT JOIN spend s ON a.account_id = s.account_id
LEFT JOIN call_spend c ON a.account_id = c.account_id
ORDER BY total_spend DESC
LIMIT 5;

test_cases.label: Correct total spend calculation with both messages and calls
Account with no activity shows zero spend

metadata.reference_approach: Use two CTEs to aggregate message and call costs separately for 2024, filtered by sent_at and started_at timestamps. LEFT JOIN both CTEs to the accounts table to preserve all accounts even if they have no messages or calls. Use COALESCE to convert NULL values to 0, then calculate total_spend by adding the two components. Order by total_spend descending and limit to 5 rows to identify the top accounts.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
problem_statement_markdown: Given an integer array nums, find a contiguous subarray with the largest product, and return the product.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(nums):
    if not nums:
        return 0
    curr_max = nums[0]
    curr_min = nums[0]
    global_max = nums[0]
    for num in nums[1:]:
        new_max = max(num, curr_max * num, curr_min * num)
        new_min = min(num, curr_max * num, curr_min * num)
        curr_max = new_max
        curr_min = new_min
        global_max = max(global_max, curr_max)
    return global_max

metadata.reference_approach: Maintain two running values: curr_max and curr_min representing the maximum and minimum products ending at the current position. For each number, the new maximum could be the number itself, the number times the previous max (positive * positive), or the number times the previous min (negative * negative flips to positive). Similarly for new minimum. Update global_max after each step. This handles zeros, negatives, and sign flips in O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problem_statement_markdown: Given a sorted array of unique integers that has been rotated between 1 and n times, find the minimum element in O(log n) time.

metadata.reference_approach: Use binary search comparing nums[mid] with nums[right]. If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum must be in the right half (exclusive of mid), so set left = mid + 1. Otherwise, the minimum is in the left half including mid, so set right = mid. Repeat until left == right, which points to the minimum. Time: O(log n) | Space: O(1).

title: Valid Anagram
problem_statement_markdown: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise.

metadata.reference_approach: First check lengths — if they differ, return false immediately. Then build a frequency map by incrementing counts for each character in s and decrementing for each character in t. If any character in t has a zero or missing count when we try to decrement, the strings are not anagrams. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space since there are at most 26 distinct lowercase letters.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problem_statement_markdown: Given a rotated sorted array of unique integers and a target, return the index of target or -1 if not present. Must be O(log n).

metadata.reference_approach: Use a modified binary search. At each step, compute mid and check if nums[mid] equals the target. Then determine which half is sorted by comparing nums[left] with nums[mid]. If the left half is sorted and the target falls within [nums[left], nums[mid]), search the left half; otherwise search the right. If the right half is sorted and the target falls within (nums[mid], nums[right]], search the right half; otherwise search the left. Repeat until the target is found or the search space is exhausted. Time complexity: O(log n), Space complexity: O(1).

title: Trapping Rain Water

metadata.reference_approach: Use two pointers starting at both ends of the array. Maintain left_max and right_max as the maximum heights seen from each side. At each step, if height[left] <= height[right], the water at the left pointer is determined by left_max; add (left_max - height[left]) to the total and advance left. Otherwise, do the same for the right pointer using right_max. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space since no auxiliary arrays are needed.

title: Contains Duplicate

Otherwise, add it to the set. After the loop, return False since all elements were distinct. Time complexity: O(n) for a single pass, Space complexity: O(n) for the set.

title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm)
problem_statement_markdown: Given an integer array nums, find the subarray with the largest sum and return its sum.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(nums):
    max_sum = nums[0]
    current_sum = nums[0]
    for num in nums[1:]:
        current_sum = max(num, current_sum + num)
        max_sum = max(max_sum, current_sum)
    return max_sum

metadata.reference_approach: Kadane's Algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. We maintain two variables: current_sum (the maximum subarray sum ending at the current position) and max_sum (the global maximum seen so far). For each element, we decide whether to extend the existing subarray or start fresh: current_sum = max(num, current_sum + num). If current_sum + num is less than num alone, we reset by starting a new subarray at the current element. We update max_sum at each step to track the overall maximum.

title: Merge Intervals

metadata.reference_approach: Sort intervals by start time in O(n log n). Initialize result with the first interval. Iterate through remaining intervals: if the current interval's start is <= the last merged interval's end, they overlap, so extend the end to the max of both ends. Otherwise, append the current interval as a new non-overlapping entry. This runs in O(n log n) time due to sorting, with O(n) space for the result array.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring

metadata.reference_approach: Use the Expand Around Center technique. For each index i in the string, treat it as the center of both an odd-length palindrome (expanding from i,i) and an even-length palindrome (expanding from i, i+1). Expand outward as long as characters match. Track the start and end indices of the longest palindrome found. Return the substring at those indices. Time complexity: O(n²), Space: O(1).

title: Encode and Decode Strings
problem_statement_markdown: Design an algorithm to encode a list of strings to a single string, and decode it back to the original list. The encoded string is sent over the network and decoded on the other side.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(strs):
    # Encode the list, then decode it back, returning the original list
    # Encode
    encoded = ''.join(f'{len(s)}#{s}' for s in strs)
    # Decode
    result = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(encoded):
        j = encoded.index('#', i)
        length = int(encoded[i:j])
        result.append(encoded[j+1:j+1+length])
        i = j + 1 + length
    return result

metadata.reference_approach: Use length-prefix encoding: for each string in the list, prepend its length followed by a '#' delimiter, then concatenate everything into a single encoded string. To decode, scan for the '#' character starting at the current pointer position, parse the integer before it as the string length, extract exactly that many characters after the '#', append to result, and advance the pointer. This correctly handles strings containing '#' or digits since we always know the exact length. Time complexity is O(n) for both encode and decode where n is the total character count; space complexity is O(n).

title: Sliding Window Maximum
problem_statement_markdown: Given an array nums and a sliding window of size k, return the maximum value in each window as the window slides from left to right.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a monotonic deque storing indices in decreasing order of their corresponding values. For each element at index i: first remove from the front any indices that have fallen outside the current window (index < i - k + 1). Then remove from the back any indices whose values are less than or equal to the current element (they can never be the maximum of any future window). Append the current index. Once i >= k-1, the front of the deque holds the index of the maximum element in the current window. This processes each element at most twice (once added, once removed), giving O(n) time and O(k) space.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problem_statement_markdown: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(s: str) -> int:
    char_set = set()
    left = 0
    max_len = 0
    for right in range(len(s)):
        while s[right] in char_set:
            char_set.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        char_set.add(s[right])
        max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)
    return max_len

metadata.reference_approach: Use a sliding window with two pointers (left, right) and a hash set to track characters in the current window. Expand the window by advancing the right pointer and adding s[right] to the set. When a duplicate is encountered (s[right] already in the set), shrink the window from the left by removing s[left] and advancing left until the duplicate is gone. Track the maximum window size throughout. Time: O(n), Space: O(min(n, k)) where k is the charset size.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problem_statement_markdown: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. Must run in O(n).

metadata.reference_approach: Add all numbers to a hash set for O(1) lookups. Iterate through each number in the set; only begin counting a sequence when (num - 1) is NOT in the set (indicating the current number is the start of a new sequence). From that start, incrementally check if (current + 1) exists in the set, extending the streak. Track the maximum streak found. Since each number is visited at most twice overall (once as a start candidate, once during a streak extension), the total time is O(n) with O(n) space for the set.

title: Longest Palindrome (Frequency Map)

If any character has an odd frequency, we can place one such character in the center of the palindrome, adding 1 to the length. This gives the maximum palindrome length in O(n) time and O(1) space (since the alphabet size is bounded).

title: Two Sum (HashMap)
problem_statement_markdown: Given an array of integers and a target, return indices of two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one solution exists.

If so, return [map[complement], i] immediately. This single-pass approach runs in O(n) time and O(n) space, avoiding the O(n²) cost of checking every pair.

title: Isomorphic Strings

For each pair of characters (cs, ct) at the same position, check if cs already maps to something other than ct, or if ct already maps to something other than cs. If either inconsistency is found, return False. Otherwise record both mappings and continue. This enforces the bijection requirement.
