title: Word Search
problem_statement_markdown: Given a 2D board and a word, return true if the word exists in the board following adjacent cells (horizontally/vertically). Each cell may be used only once.

metadata.reference_approach: Use DFS backtracking starting from every cell in the board. For each starting cell, recursively attempt to match successive characters of the word by exploring all four adjacent directions. To prevent reuse of a cell in a single path, temporarily mark the cell as visited (e.g., replace with '#') before recursing, then restore it afterward. Return true as soon as a complete match is found, false if all starting positions fail. Time complexity is O(m·n·4^L) where L is the word length, and space is O(L) for the recursion stack.

title: Number of Connected Components
problem_statement_markdown: Given n nodes (0 to n-1) and a list of undirected edges, return the number of connected components.

metadata.reference_approach: Use Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) with path compression and union by rank. Initialize each of the n nodes as its own component. For each edge, attempt to union the two endpoints; if they belong to different components, merge them and decrement the component count by 1. The final component count is the answer. Time complexity is O(n * α(n)) ≈ O(n) where α is the inverse Ackermann function, and space is O(n).

title: Course Schedule II (Topological Sort)
problem_statement_markdown: Return one valid ordering of courses given prerequisites. If no valid ordering exists, return empty array.

reference_solution.python:
from collections import deque

def solution(numCourses, prerequisites):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
    in_degree = [0] * numCourses

    for course, prereq in prerequisites:
        adj[prereq].append(course)
        in_degree[course] += 1

    queue = deque([i for i in range(numCourses) if in_degree[i] == 0])
    order = []

    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for neighbor in adj[node]:
            in_degree[neighbor] -= 1
            if in_degree[neighbor] == 0:
                queue.append(neighbor)

    return order if len(order) == numCourses else []

metadata.reference_approach: Use Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based topological sort). Build an adjacency list and compute in-degrees for all nodes. Initialize a queue with all nodes that have in-degree 0. Process nodes from the queue: append each to the result, then decrement the in-degree of its neighbors, enqueuing any that reach 0. If the result contains all numCourses nodes, a valid topological ordering exists; otherwise a cycle was detected and return an empty array. Time: O(V+E), Space: O(V+E).

title: Course Schedule (Cycle Detection)
problem_statement_markdown: There are n courses. Given prerequisites as [course, prereq] pairs, determine if it's possible to finish all courses (detect if cycle exists in directed graph).

metadata.reference_approach: Build a directed adjacency list from the prerequisites pairs. Use DFS with 3-state node coloring: unvisited (0), currently visiting (1), and fully processed (2). For each unvisited node, mark it as visiting and recurse on its neighbors. If a neighbor is already in the visiting state, a back edge (cycle) is found. Once all neighbors are processed, mark the node as fully visited. If any DFS call detects a cycle, return false; otherwise return true. Time complexity: O(V+E) where V=numCourses and E=len(prerequisites). Space complexity: O(V+E) for the adjacency list and recursion stack.

title: Graph Valid Tree
problem_statement_markdown: Given n nodes and edges for an undirected graph, determine if the graph is a valid tree (connected + no cycle; equivalently: n-1 edges, all nodes reachable).

metadata.reference_approach: Use Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) with path compression and union by rank. First, check if the number of edges equals n-1; if not, it cannot be a valid tree. Then, attempt to union each edge's endpoints. If any union finds both endpoints already in the same component (cycle detected), return false. If all edges are processed without detecting a cycle and the edge count is exactly n-1, the graph is a valid tree. Time complexity: O(n * alpha(n)) where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function (nearly constant). Space complexity: O(n).

title: Minimum Height Trees
problem_statement_markdown: For an undirected tree with n nodes, find all roots that minimize tree height. Return all such root nodes.

metadata.reference_approach: Use iterative leaf-trimming (similar to topological sort from outside in). Build an adjacency list, identify all leaves (degree 1 nodes), then repeatedly remove them layer by layer while tracking remaining node count. Stop when 2 or fewer nodes remain — those are the answer (the centroid(s) of the tree). Since each node/edge is processed once, time complexity is O(n) and space is O(n).

title: Number of Islands
problem_statement_markdown: Given a 2D binary grid of '1's (land) and '0's (water), count the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.

metadata.reference_approach: Use DFS (or BFS) flood fill: iterate over every cell; when a '1' is found, increment the island count and recursively sink all connected land cells by marking them '0'. Each cell is visited at most once, giving O(m*n) time and O(m*n) space for the recursion stack in the worst case.

title: Critical Connections (Bridges)
problem_statement_markdown: A critical connection is an edge that, if removed, disconnects the network. Find all critical connections (bridges) using Tarjan's algorithm.

metadata.reference_approach: Use Tarjan's bridge-finding DFS: assign each node a discovery time (disc) and a low-link value (low) representing the earliest discovered node reachable via DFS subtree edges. Traverse the graph; for each tree edge (node→neighbor), after recursing, update low[node] = min(low[node], low[neighbor]). If low[neighbor] > disc[node], then (node, neighbor) is a bridge since neighbor cannot reach node or its ancestors without this edge. For back edges, update low[node] = min(low[node], disc[neighbor]). Time: O(V+E), Space: O(V+E).

title: Accounts Merge
problem_statement_markdown: Given accounts where each account is [name, email1, email2, ...], merge accounts sharing any email. Return merged accounts sorted.

metadata.reference_approach: Use Union-Find (disjoint set) on email addresses. For each account, union all emails together using the first email as the representative. Maintain an email-to-name mapping. After processing all accounts, group emails by their root representative, then construct result arrays with the name prepended to sorted emails. Time complexity O(NK·α(NK)) where N is number of accounts and K is average emails per account; α is the inverse Ackermann function from path compression. Space complexity O(NK).

title: Coin Change II (Number of Combinations)
problem_statement_markdown: Count the number of combinations of coins that make up a given amount (order does not matter — this is a combination, not permutation problem).

metadata.reference_approach: Use 1D dynamic programming (unbounded knapsack). Initialize dp[0]=1 (one way to make amount 0: use no coins). For each coin, iterate from that coin value up to the target amount, updating dp[j] += dp[j - coin]. Iterating coins in the outer loop ensures each combination (not permutation) is counted exactly once, because each coin denomination is processed in a fixed order. Time complexity O(n * amount) where n is the number of coins, space complexity O(amount).

title: Edit Distance
problem_statement_markdown: Find the minimum number of operations (insert, delete, replace) required to convert word1 to word2 (Levenshtein distance).

starter_code.python:
def solution(word1: str, word2: str) -> int:
    pass

metadata.reference_approach: Use 2D dynamic programming where dp[i][j] represents the edit distance between the first i characters of word1 and first j characters of word2. Initialize dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j (base cases: converting to/from empty string). For each pair (i, j), if characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j] (delete), dp[i][j-1] (insert), dp[i-1][j-1] (replace)). Time complexity O(m*n), space O(m*n) reducible to O(min(m,n)) with a rolling array.

title: Unique Paths
problem_statement_markdown: A robot starts at the top-left corner of an m x n grid. It can only move right or down. How many unique paths are there to reach the bottom-right corner?

metadata.reference_approach: Use a 1D DP array of length n, initialized to all 1s (represents the first row where there is exactly one path to each cell). For each subsequent row i from 1 to m-1, update dp[j] += dp[j-1] for each column j from 1 to n-1. dp[j] accumulates paths from the cell above (previous dp[j]) and the cell to the left (dp[j-1]). Return dp[n-1]. This runs in O(m*n) time and O(n) space.

title: Regular Expression Matching
problem_statement_markdown: Implement regex matching with '.' (matches any single character) and '*' (matches zero or more of the preceding element). The entire string must match the pattern.

Initialize dp[0][0] = True and handle patterns like 'a*', 'a*b*' that can match empty strings. For each cell, if the pattern character is '*', we can either use zero occurrences (dp[i][j-2]) or one or more occurrences if the preceding pattern character matches the current string character (dp[i-1][j]). If the pattern character is '.' or matches the string character exactly, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]. Time complexity O(mn), Space complexity O(mn) where m and n are lengths of s and p.

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
problem_statement_markdown: Find the length of the longest palindromic subsequence in a string.

metadata.reference_approach: Use 2D dynamic programming where dp[i][j] represents the length of the longest palindromic subsequence in s[i..j]. Initialize dp[i][i] = 1 for all i. For substrings of increasing length, if s[i] == s[j], dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]). The answer is dp[0][n-1]. Time complexity O(n²), space O(n²) reducible to O(n) with a rolling array.

title: Jump Game II (Min Jumps)
problem_statement_markdown: Given an array where each element represents the maximum jump length at that position, find the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a greedy approach: track the current reachable boundary (cur_end) and the farthest index reachable from any position seen so far (farthest). Iterate through all indices except the last; at each step, update farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]). When i reaches cur_end, we must use a jump — increment the jump counter and set cur_end = farthest. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Climbing Stairs
problem_statement_markdown: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. In how many distinct ways can you climb n stairs?

metadata.reference_approach: Use bottom-up dynamic programming with two variables. The number of ways to climb n stairs follows the Fibonacci recurrence: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], because at step i you either came from i-1 (took 1 step) or i-2 (took 2 steps). Base cases are dp[1]=1, dp[2]=2. We iterate from 3 to n updating two rolling variables, achieving O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
problem_statement_markdown: Return the values visible from the right side of a binary tree (rightmost node at each level).

metadata.reference_approach: Use BFS (level-order traversal) with a queue. For each level, process all nodes and record only the last node's value as it is the rightmost visible node from the right side. This runs in O(n) time and O(n) space since every node is visited once and the queue holds at most O(n) nodes at a time (widest level).

title: Find Eventual Safe States
problem_statement_markdown: A node is 'safe' if every path starting from it eventually reaches a terminal node (no outgoing edges) without entering a cycle. Find all safe nodes.

metadata.reference_approach: Use DFS with 3-state coloring: 0=unvisited, 1=currently visiting (on DFS stack), 2=confirmed safe. For each node, mark it as 'visiting' before exploring neighbors. If we encounter a 'visiting' node, a cycle exists and the current path is unsafe. If all neighbors lead to safe nodes, mark the current node as safe (state=2). This avoids recomputation via memoization in state. The result is all nodes where dfs returns True. Time complexity O(V+E), space O(V) for the state array and recursion stack.

title: Happy Number
problem_statement_markdown: A happy number: repeatedly replace number by sum of squares of digits. If reaches 1 → happy. If enters cycle → not happy. Detect which.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a HashSet to track numbers seen during the transformation sequence. At each step, compute the sum of squares of digits. If we reach 1, the number is happy. If we encounter a number we've seen before, we've entered a cycle and the number is not happy. Time complexity is O(log n) per step (digit extraction) with O(log n) distinct values before a cycle is detected, and space is O(log n) for the set. Alternatively, Floyd's cycle detection can be used for O(1) space.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
problem_statement_markdown: Find the k closest points to the origin (0,0) from a list of points. Distance = sqrt(x^2+y^2) but no need to sqrt.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a max-heap of size k to maintain the k closest points seen so far. For each point, compute its squared distance (no sqrt needed). If the heap has fewer than k elements, push it. Otherwise, if the current point is closer than the farthest point in the heap (i.e., its negated distance is greater than the heap's root), replace the root. This runs in O(n log k) time and O(k) space.

title: IPO (Maximize Capital)

reference_solution.python:
import heapq

def solution(k, w, profits, capital):
    min_cap_heap = sorted(zip(capital, profits))
    max_profit_heap = []
    idx = 0
    n = len(profits)
    
    for _ in range(k):
        while idx < n and min_cap_heap[idx][0] <= w:
            heapq.heappush(max_profit_heap, -min_cap_heap[idx][1])
            idx += 1
        if not max_profit_heap:
            break
        w += -heapq.heappop(max_profit_heap)
    
    return w

test_cases.label: all three rounds affordable step by step

metadata.reference_approach: Sort projects by capital requirement into a min-heap. Maintain a max-heap of profits for currently affordable projects. For each of k rounds, push all projects with capital ≤ w into the max-heap, then greedily pick the highest profit project. Stop early if no projects are affordable. Time O(n log n) for sorting + O(k log n) for heap operations = O(n log n). Space O(n).

title: Largest Number
problem_statement_markdown: Given a list of non-negative integers, arrange them to form the largest number. Return the result as a string.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a custom comparator: for any two numbers a and b (as strings), place a before b if the concatenation a+b is lexicographically greater than b+a. Apply this comparator via functools.cmp_to_key (Python) or Array.sort (JS). After sorting, join all strings. Handle the edge case where all numbers are zero by checking if the first character of the result is '0'. Time complexity O(n log n) due to sorting, space O(n) for the string array.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problem_statement_markdown: Find the median of two sorted arrays in O(log(m+n)) time. This is the classic hard binary search problem.

metadata.reference_approach: Binary search on the partition index of the smaller array. For each candidate partition i in nums1 and derived partition j in nums2 (so that left halves together have (m+n+1)//2 elements), check the cross-conditions max_left1 <= min_right2 and max_left2 <= min_right1. If satisfied, compute the median directly; otherwise adjust binary search bounds. Time complexity O(log(min(m,n))), Space O(1).

title: Missing Number
problem_statement_markdown: Given an array of n distinct numbers in range [0, n], find the missing number.

metadata.reference_approach: Use XOR: initialize result = n (length of array), then XOR every index i and every value nums[i] into result. Each number that is present cancels itself out (appears once as index and once as value), leaving only the missing number. Time O(n), Space O(1). Alternatively, use the math approach: expected sum n*(n+1)/2 minus actual sum gives the missing number in O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
problem_statement_markdown: Partition string s such that every substring in the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible partitions.

metadata.reference_approach: Precompute a 2D boolean DP table where dp[i][j] is True if s[i..j] is a palindrome, using the recurrence: s[i]==s[j] and (j-i<=2 or dp[i+1][j-1]). Then use backtracking: starting from index 'start', try every end index; if dp[start][end] is True, add the substring to the current path and recurse from end+1. When start reaches n, record the current path as a valid partition. Time complexity O(n * 2^n), space O(n) for the recursion stack plus O(n^2) for the DP table.

title: Permutations
problem_statement_markdown: Return all permutations of a distinct integer array.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(nums):
    result = []
    n = len(nums)
    used = [False] * n

    def backtrack(path):
        if len(path) == n:
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(n):
            if not used[i]:
                used[i] = True
                path.append(nums[i])
                backtrack(path)
                path.pop()
                used[i] = False

    backtrack([])
    return result

metadata.reference_approach: Use backtracking with a boolean `used` array. At each recursion level, iterate over all elements; if an element is not yet used, mark it used, append it to the current path, recurse, then unmark and remove it (backtrack). When the path length equals n, record a copy of the path as a complete permutation. This explores all n! permutations with O(n) work per permutation, giving Time O(n! * n) and Space O(n) for the recursion stack and path.

title: Rotting Oranges
problem_statement_markdown: Grid of 0 (empty), 1 (fresh orange), 2 (rotten). Each minute, rotten oranges infect adjacent fresh ones. Return minimum minutes until all oranges rot, or -1 if impossible.

metadata.reference_approach: Use multi-source BFS starting from all initially rotten oranges simultaneously. Enqueue all rotten oranges at time 0 while counting fresh oranges. Process the BFS queue: for each rotten orange, infect adjacent fresh oranges (mark them rotten, decrement fresh count, enqueue with time+1). Track the maximum time seen. After BFS, if fresh count is 0 return the max time elapsed, otherwise return -1 (some fresh oranges were unreachable). Time: O(m*n), Space: O(m*n).

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
problem_statement_markdown: Given an m x n integer matrix, if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. Do it in-place.

metadata.reference_approach: Use the first row and first column of the matrix as marker arrays to avoid extra space. First, record whether the first row or first column themselves contain any zeros. Then iterate through the rest of the matrix (rows 1..m-1, cols 1..n-1): if matrix[i][j]==0, set matrix[i][0]=0 and matrix[0][j]=0. Next, iterate again through the inner cells and zero out any cell whose row-marker or col-marker is 0. Finally, if the first row originally had a zero, zero it out entirely; same for the first column. This achieves O(m*n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag)
problem_statement_markdown: Sort an array of 0s, 1s, and 2s in-place in a single pass without using the sort function (Dutch National Flag problem).

metadata.reference_approach: Use three pointers: lo (next position for 0), mid (current element), hi (next position for 2 from end). Iterate while mid <= hi: if nums[mid]==0, swap with nums[lo] and advance both lo and mid; if nums[mid]==1, just advance mid; if nums[mid]==2, swap with nums[hi] and decrement hi (don't advance mid since swapped element is unprocessed). This achieves a single-pass O(n) time, O(1) space solution.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
problem_statement_markdown: Given roots of trees root and subRoot, return true if subRoot is a subtree of root (there exists a node in root whose subtree is identical to subRoot).

metadata.reference_approach: For each node in the main tree, check if the subtree rooted at that node is identical to subRoot using a recursive isSameTree helper. The isSameTree function compares two trees structurally and value-wise. The main isSubtree function recurses into left and right children if the current node doesn't match. Time complexity is O(m*n) where m and n are the sizes of the two trees; space complexity is O(h) where h is the height of the main tree due to recursion stack.

title: Binary Search
problem_statement_markdown: Implement binary search on a sorted array. Return the index of the target or -1 if not found.

test_cases.label: single element array target not found

metadata.reference_approach: Use iterative binary search with two pointers lo and hi initialized to 0 and len(nums)-1. At each step compute mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2 to avoid integer overflow, compare nums[mid] with target, and narrow the search window by updating lo or hi accordingly. Return mid when found, or -1 if the loop ends without a match. Time complexity O(log n), space complexity O(1).

title: Combination Sum
problem_statement_markdown: Find all unique combinations of candidates (reusable) that sum to target. Candidates are distinct positive integers.

metadata.reference_approach: Sort the candidates array first to enable early pruning. Use backtracking: at each step, iterate through candidates starting from the current index (to avoid duplicate combinations) and try adding each candidate to the current path. Since candidates can be reused, recurse with the same index i (not i+1). If the remaining sum reaches 0, record the path. If a candidate exceeds the remaining sum, break early (due to sorting). Time complexity O(n^(T/min)) where T is target and min is the smallest candidate; space O(T/min) for recursion depth.

title: Counting Bits
problem_statement_markdown: Given n, return an array where ans[i] = number of 1s in the binary representation of i, for 0 <= i <= n.

metadata.reference_approach: Use dynamic programming: dp[0] = 0, and for each i from 1 to n, dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1). Every number's popcount equals that of its right-shifted value (which removes the least significant bit) plus whether the last bit is set. This builds the answer in a single O(n) pass with O(n) space.

title: Daily Temperatures
problem_statement_markdown: Given daily temperatures, return array where answer[i] is the number of days until a warmer temperature. If no future warmer day, answer[i] = 0.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a monotonic decreasing stack of indices. Iterate through each temperature; while the stack is non-empty and the temperature at the stack's top index is less than the current temperature, pop that index and record the difference (current index minus popped index) as the number of days to wait. Then push the current index. Elements remaining in the stack at the end have no future warmer day (result stays 0). Time O(n), Space O(n).

title: Design Pub/Sub System

Implement: subscribe(topic, callback) — registers a callback for a topic; publish(topic, message) — sends message to all subscribers of topic; unsubscribe(topic, callback) — removes a callback. A threading.Lock guards all mutations to the subscriber map. On publish, we snapshot the subscriber list under the lock, then release before invoking callbacks — this avoids deadlocks if callbacks themselves call subscribe/publish. The solution function drives a sequence of operations and records results: subscribe/unsubscribe return None, publish returns the count of subscribers notified at the time of publishing. Time complexity: O(n) per publish where n is the number of subscribers on that topic; O(1) amortized for subscribe; O(n) for unsubscribe (list scan). Space: O(T × S) where T is number of topics and S is subscribers per topic.

title: Find K Closest Elements
problem_statement_markdown: Given a sorted array, find the k closest integers to x. Return them sorted. When equidistant, prefer the smaller element.

metadata.reference_approach: Use binary search to find the optimal left boundary of a k-element window in the sorted array. The search range for the left index is [0, n-k]. At each midpoint, compare the distance from x to arr[mid] vs arr[mid+k]. If x - arr[mid] > arr[mid+k] - x, the right element is closer so shift the window right (lo = mid+1); otherwise shift left (hi = mid). When ties occur, the condition keeps hi = mid which biases toward smaller elements. Return arr[lo:lo+k]. Time complexity O(log(n-k) + k), Space O(k).

title: Find Peak Element
problem_statement_markdown: Find any peak element (greater than its neighbors) in an array where nums[-1] = nums[n] = -inf. Must run in O(log n).

metadata.reference_approach: Binary search on the array: maintain lo and hi pointers. At each step, compute mid. If nums[mid] < nums[mid+1], a peak must exist in the right half (set lo = mid + 1). Otherwise, a peak exists at mid or in the left half (set hi = mid). The loop terminates when lo == hi, which is the index of a peak. Time complexity O(log n), space O(1).

title: Graph Clone (Deep Copy)
problem_statement_markdown: Clone a connected undirected graph where each node has a value and a list of neighbors. Return the deep copy of the given node.

metadata.reference_approach: Use DFS (or BFS) with a HashMap that maps each original node to its cloned counterpart. When visiting a node for the first time, create a new clone node with the same value, store it in the map, then recursively clone all neighbors and append them to the clone's neighbor list. If a node has already been cloned (found in the map), return the existing clone to handle cycles. This visits each node and edge exactly once, giving Time: O(V+E) and Space: O(V).

title: Insert Interval
problem_statement_markdown: Insert a new interval into a sorted non-overlapping interval list. Merge if necessary.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(intervals, new_interval):
    result = []
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    new_interval = list(new_interval)
    # Phase 1: add all non-overlapping before new_interval
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < new_interval[0]:
        result.append(list(intervals[i]))
        i += 1
    # Phase 2: merge overlapping intervals
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= new_interval[1]:
        new_interval[0] = min(new_interval[0], intervals[i][0])
        new_interval[1] = max(new_interval[1], intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    result.append(new_interval)
    # Phase 3: add remaining
    while i < n:
        result.append(list(intervals[i]))
        i += 1
    return result

metadata.reference_approach: Use three phases: (1) Append all intervals that end strictly before the new interval starts (no overlap). (2) Merge all intervals that overlap with the new interval by updating the new interval's start to the minimum and end to the maximum. (3) Append all remaining intervals after the merged region. This runs in O(n) time and O(n) space since each interval is visited at most once.

title: Kth Largest Element in Array
problem_statement_markdown: Find the kth largest element in an unsorted array in better than O(n log n).

metadata.reference_approach: Use Quickselect to find the kth largest in O(n) average time. Convert kth largest to (n-k)th smallest (0-indexed target). Partition around a pivot: place all elements ≤ pivot before it, then check if the pivot lands at the target index — if so return it; if pivot index < target recurse right; else recurse left. Shuffle first to guarantee O(n) average performance. Space is O(1) ignoring recursion stack (O(log n) average stack depth).

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problem_statement_markdown: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence in an array.

metadata.reference_approach: Use patience sorting with binary search: maintain a 'tails' array where tails[i] is the smallest possible tail element of all increasing subsequences of length i+1. For each number, binary search for its insertion position in tails; if it extends beyond the current tails array, append it (increasing LIS length by 1), otherwise replace the existing element at that position. The final length of tails is the answer. Time O(n log n), Space O(n).

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problem_statement_markdown: Find the maximum depth (number of nodes along the longest path from root to leaf) of a binary tree.

metadata.reference_approach: Use recursive DFS: the depth of an empty tree is 0, and for any node it is 1 plus the maximum depth of its left and right subtrees. This visits every node exactly once giving O(n) time and O(h) space on the call stack, where h is the tree height (O(log n) balanced, O(n) worst case).

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problem_statement_markdown: Given string s and integer k, find the length of the longest substring containing the same letter after replacing at most k characters.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a sliding window with two pointers (left, right). Maintain a frequency count of characters in the current window and track the maximum frequency character count seen so far (max_count). The window is valid if (window_size - max_count) <= k, meaning we need at most k replacements to make all characters the same. Expand right on each iteration; when the window becomes invalid, shrink from the left. The answer is the maximum valid window size encountered. Time O(n), Space O(1) since at most 26 distinct characters.

title: Meeting Rooms I
problem_statement_markdown: Given a list of meeting intervals, determine if a person can attend all meetings (i.e., no two meetings overlap).

metadata.reference_approach: Sort intervals by start time in O(n log n). Then perform a single linear pass checking each consecutive pair: if the next meeting starts before the previous one ends (intervals[i][0] < intervals[i-1][1]), there is an overlap and we return False. If no such pair exists, return True. Overall complexity is O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problem_statement_markdown: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list. Return the head of the merged list.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a dummy head node and iterate through both lists simultaneously, always appending the smaller current node to the result list and advancing that pointer. When one list is exhausted, attach the remainder of the other. This runs in O(m+n) time and O(1) space (iterative), avoiding the O(m+n) stack space of the recursive approach.

title: Palindromic Substrings
problem_statement_markdown: Count all palindromic substrings in a string.

metadata.reference_approach: Use the expand-around-center technique: iterate over each index as a potential center for odd-length palindromes (center at index i) and even-length palindromes (center between i and i+1). For each center, expand outward as long as the characters match, incrementing the count for each valid palindrome found. This runs in O(n²) time and O(1) space, covering all 2n-1 possible centers.

title: Permutations II (With Duplicates)
problem_statement_markdown: Return all unique permutations of an integer array that may contain duplicates.

metadata.reference_approach: Sort the input array so duplicate values are adjacent. Use a boolean 'used' array to track which elements are in the current path. During backtracking, skip an element if it's already used, or if it equals the previous element and the previous element has NOT been used (this enforces a fixed relative order among duplicates, preventing duplicate permutations). When a path reaches the full length, record it. Time complexity O(n! * n), space O(n) for the recursion stack and used array.

title: Reverse Bits
problem_statement_markdown: Reverse the bits of a 32-bit unsigned integer.

metadata.reference_approach: Iterate exactly 32 times. In each iteration, shift the result left by 1 to make room, then OR in the least significant bit of n (extracted via n & 1), then right-shift n by 1. After 32 iterations the bits of n have been reversed into result. Time complexity is O(32) = O(1), space complexity is O(1).

title: Remove Invalid Parentheses
problem_statement_markdown: Remove the minimum number of invalid parentheses to make the input string valid. Return all unique valid strings.

metadata.reference_approach: BFS level-by-level: start with the original string in the queue. For each level, try removing each parenthesis character one at a time to generate candidates. If any valid string (balanced parentheses) is found at the current BFS level, collect all valid strings at that level and stop. A visited set prevents duplicate processing. This guarantees minimum removals because BFS explores by number of deletions. title: Single Number (XOR)

title: Same Tree

title: Spiral Matrix
problem_statement_markdown: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order.

metadata.reference_approach: Use four boundary pointers (top, bottom, left, right) initialized to the matrix edges. In each iteration, traverse the top row left-to-right, then the right column top-to-bottom, then (if top <= bottom) the bottom row right-to-left, then (if left <= right) the left column bottom-to-top. After each traversal, shrink the corresponding boundary inward. Continue while top <= bottom and left <= right. This visits every element exactly once in spiral order. Time complexity: O(m*n), Space complexity: O(1) extra (excluding the output array).

title: The Skyline Problem
problem_statement_markdown: Given buildings as [left, right, height], compute the skyline as a list of [x, height] key points.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a sweep line approach: convert each building [l,r,h] into two events — a start event (l, -h, r) and an end event (r, 0, 0). Sort all events by x-coordinate (breaking ties so starts before ends and taller buildings first via negative height). Maintain a max-heap of (-height, end_x) with a sentinel (0, inf). For each event, push start events onto the heap, then lazily remove any buildings whose end_x <= current x. The current skyline height is the negative of the heap's top. When this height changes from the previous recorded height, append [x, cur_max] to the result. Time complexity O(n log n) for sorting and heap operations; Space O(n) for events and heap.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal

metadata.reference_approach: Use BFS with a deque. Initialize the queue with the root. At each iteration, record the current queue size (= number of nodes at this level), then dequeue exactly that many nodes — collecting their values into a level list and enqueuing their non-null children. Append the level list to the result. This naturally separates levels without needing sentinel nodes. Time complexity O(n) since every node is enqueued and dequeued once; Space complexity O(n) for the queue which at most holds all nodes on the widest level.

title: Minimum Path Sum
problem_statement_markdown: Given an m x n grid filled with non-negative integers, find the path from top-left to bottom-right that minimizes the sum of numbers along the path. You can only move right or down.

metadata.reference_approach: Use dynamic programming in-place (on a deep copy to avoid mutating input). Set dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]), treating the first row (only come from left) and first column (only come from above) as base cases. The answer is dp[m-1][n-1]. Time complexity O(m*n), Space O(1) ignoring the copy (or O(m*n) with copy).

title: Non-overlapping Intervals

metadata.reference_approach: Sort intervals by end time. Greedily keep the interval with the earliest end time. For each subsequent interval, if it overlaps with the current end (start < end), increment removal count. Otherwise, update end to current interval's end. This greedy strategy maximizes the number of kept intervals. Time O(n log n) for sorting, Space O(1).

title: Number of Provinces

metadata.reference_approach: Use Union-Find (disjoint set union) with path compression. Initialize each city as its own root. Iterate over all pairs (i, j) in the upper triangle of the adjacency matrix; if isConnected[i][j] == 1, union the two cities. Finally, count the number of distinct roots among all cities. Time complexity O(n²·α(n)) ≈ O(n²) since we must scan all n² matrix entries; space O(n) for the parent array.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problem_statement_markdown: Determine if you can partition an array into two subsets such that the sum of elements in both subsets is equal.

metadata.reference_approach: Check if total sum is odd — if so, return False immediately. Otherwise, set target = total // 2 and use 0/1 knapsack DP where dp[j] represents whether sum j is achievable. Initialize dp[0] = True and iterate each number, updating dp in reverse order (from target down to num) to prevent reuse: dp[j] |= dp[j - num]. Return dp[target]. Time complexity O(n * sum), Space O(sum).

title: Product of Array Except Self
problem_statement_markdown: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all elements of nums except nums[i]. You must solve it in O(n) time without using the division operator.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    answer = [1] * n
    
    # Build prefix products
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):
        answer[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    
    # Multiply suffix products
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        answer[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    
    return answer

metadata.reference_approach: Use a two-pass prefix/suffix approach. First, build an output array where answer[i] is the product of all elements to the left of i (prefix product). Then traverse right-to-left, maintaining a running suffix product and multiplying it into answer[i]. This correctly computes the product of all elements except nums[i] for each position. Time complexity is O(n) and space complexity is O(1) extra (not counting the output array).

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

    fast = dummy
    slow = dummy
    for _ in range(n + 1):
        fast = fast.next
    while fast:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next
    return dummy.next

Then move both pointers one step at a time until 'fast' is null. At this point, 'slow' points to the node just before the one to be removed. Set slow.next = slow.next.next to remove the target node and return dummy.next. This achieves the removal in a single O(L) pass with O(1) extra space.

title: Reverse Linked List

def solution(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    return prev

When curr becomes None, prev holds the new head. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. A recursive approach is also valid but uses O(n) stack space.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K

Then increment the map entry for the current running_sum. This runs in O(n) time and O(n) space.

title: Kth Smallest Element in BST
problem_statement_markdown: Find the kth smallest element in a BST (1-indexed).

reference_solution.python:
def solution(root, k):
    stack = []
    current = root
    count = 0

    while stack or current:
        while current:
            stack.append(current)
            current = current.left

        current = stack.pop()
        count += 1
        if count == k:
            return current.val

        current = current.right

    return -1

metadata.reference_approach: Use iterative in-order traversal with an explicit stack. Go as far left as possible, then pop nodes one by one while incrementing a counter. When the counter equals k, return the current node's value. In-order traversal of a BST visits nodes in ascending sorted order, so the kth visited node is the kth smallest. Time complexity is O(H + k) where H is the tree height (O(log n) for balanced, O(n) for skewed), and space complexity is O(H) for the stack.

If both left and right subtrees return non-null results, the current node is the LCA (p and q are in different subtrees). If only one subtree returns non-null, propagate that result upward. The solution returns the integer value of the LCA node. Time complexity: O(n) where n is the number of nodes. Space complexity: O(h) where h is the height of the tree due to recursion stack.

title: Min Stack
problem_statement_markdown: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and getMin — all in O(1) time.

metadata.reference_approach: Use two stacks: a main stack for all values and a parallel min_stack where each position tracks the minimum value seen so far up to that depth. On push, append to both stacks — the min_stack gets min(new_val, current_min). On pop, remove from both. top() returns main stack's top, getMin() returns min_stack's top. All operations are O(1) time, O(n) space.

title: Number of 1 Bits (Hamming Weight)
problem_statement_markdown: Count the number of set bits (1s) in the binary representation of an unsigned integer.

test_cases.label: large number 2147483647 all 31 lower bits set

metadata.reference_approach: Brian Kernighan's trick: repeatedly clear the lowest set bit with n &= (n-1) and increment a counter each iteration until n becomes 0. Each iteration removes exactly one set bit, so the loop runs exactly k times where k is the number of set bits (Hamming weight). Time complexity O(k), space O(1).

title: Path Sum II (All Root-to-Leaf Paths)
problem_statement_markdown: Find all root-to-leaf paths where the path sum equals a target. Return all such paths.

test_cases.label: classic example with two valid paths
target not met with two leaves

metadata.reference_approach: Use DFS backtracking: maintain a current path list and remaining sum. At each node, append the node's value and subtract it from remaining. When a leaf is reached and remaining equals 0, snapshot the path into results. After recursing into both children, pop the node from the path (backtrack). This explores all root-to-leaf paths in O(n) node visits, but copying paths at leaves costs O(n) each time, giving O(n²) worst-case time and O(n) space for the recursion stack and path.

title: Redundant Connection
problem_statement_markdown: Given a tree with one extra edge added, find the redundant edge that creates a cycle. Return the edge that appears last in the input.

metadata.reference_approach: Use Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) with path compression and union by rank. For each edge, find the roots of both endpoints. If they share the same root, the edge creates a cycle and is redundant — return it immediately. Otherwise, union the two components. Since we process edges in order and return as soon as we find the cycle-creating edge, we naturally return the last such edge in input order. Time complexity is O(n·α(n)) ≈ O(n) where α is the inverse Ackermann function; space is O(n).

title: Rotate Image (Matrix)
problem_statement_markdown: Given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image, rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise in-place.

metadata.reference_approach: To rotate an n×n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in-place, use a two-step process: (1) Transpose the matrix by swapping matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for all i < j — this reflects elements across the main diagonal. (2) Reverse each row — this completes the 90-degree clockwise rotation. Time complexity is O(n²) since every element is visited a constant number of times, and space complexity is O(1) as the rotation is performed in-place with no auxiliary data structures.

title: Reorder List
problem_statement_markdown: Reorder list L0→L1→...→Ln to L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1→... in-place without modifying node values.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    # Phase 1: find middle
    slow, fast = head, head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    # Phase 2: reverse second half
    prev, curr = None, slow.next
    slow.next = None
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    # Phase 3: merge two halves
    first, second = head, prev
    while second:
        tmp1, tmp2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = tmp1
        first = tmp1
        second = tmp2
    return head

metadata.reference_approach: Three-phase algorithm: (1) Find the middle node using slow/fast pointers in O(n). (2) Reverse the second half of the list in O(n). (3) Interleave the first half and reversed second half by alternating next pointers. Overall Time O(n) | Space O(1).

title: Subsets
problem_statement_markdown: Return all possible subsets (power set) of distinct integers. No duplicate subsets.

metadata.reference_approach: Use backtracking: start with an empty path and at each recursive call, add a copy of the current path to the result (capturing all prefixes/subsets). Then iterate from the current start index to the end of nums, appending each element and recursing with start+1 to avoid reuse of earlier elements, then popping to backtrack. This generates all 2^n subsets. Time complexity O(2^n * n) due to copying each subset; space O(n) for the recursion stack.

title: Surrounded Regions
problem_statement_markdown: Given a board of 'X' and 'O', capture all 'O' regions surrounded by 'X' on all four sides. 'O' connected to any border 'O' is not captured.

test_cases.label: standard 4x4 with surrounded and border O
O connected to border not captured

metadata.reference_approach: Perform DFS/BFS from every 'O' cell on the four borders of the board, marking all reachable 'O' cells as 'S' (safe). After the traversal, iterate over the entire board: any remaining 'O' is surrounded and flipped to 'X', while any 'S' is restored back to 'O'. This ensures only 'O' regions connected to the border survive. Time complexity is O(m×n) and space complexity is O(m×n) due to the recursion stack.

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT d.driver_id, d.name, COUNT(r.ride_id) AS completed_rides
FROM drivers d
JOIN rides r ON d.driver_id = r.driver_id AND r.status = 'completed'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM promotions p
  JOIN rides r2 ON p.ride_id = r2.ride_id
  WHERE r2.driver_id = d.driver_id AND p.discount_amt > 2
)
GROUP BY d.driver_id, d.name
HAVING COUNT(r.ride_id) >= 3
ORDER BY completed_rides DESC;

Verify NOT EXISTS excludes drivers with any tip > 2
Edge case: driver with exactly 3 rides and all tips <= 2

This anti-join pattern is safer than NOT IN because it properly handles NULL values and short-circuits evaluation, making it the preferred technique for exclusion queries in SQL.

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT j.company,
       COUNT(a.app_id) AS total_applications,
       SUM(CASE WHEN a.status IN ('interview', 'offer', 'hired') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS interviews,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN a.status IN ('interview', 'offer', 'hired') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(a.app_id), 2) AS interview_rate_pct
FROM jobs j
JOIN applications a ON j.job_id = a.job_id
GROUP BY j.company
HAVING COUNT(a.app_id) >= 3
ORDER BY interview_rate_pct DESC;

-- Find stores with more than 100 orders in their first 30 days after creation

reference_solution.sql:
SELECT s.store_id, s.name, s.plan, COUNT(o.order_id) AS first_month_orders
FROM stores s
JOIN orders o ON s.store_id = o.store_id
  AND o.order_date BETWEEN s.created_at AND date(s.created_at, '+30 days')
  AND o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY s.store_id, s.name, s.plan
HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) > 9
ORDER BY first_month_orders DESC;

metadata.reference_approach: Join the stores table with the orders table using a multi-condition join: match on store_id AND filter orders where order_date falls between each store's created_at and created_at + 30 days (using SQLite's date() function), AND only include completed orders. Group by store_id, name, and plan, then filter using HAVING to only show stores with more than 9 completed orders in their first 30 days. This per-row date threshold cannot be applied in a WHERE clause because each store has its own created_at date; instead it must be part of the JOIN condition so each row's threshold is evaluated independently. Finally, order by the order count descending to show the fastest-growing stores first.

title: Instacart: Shopper Efficiency Rank
problem_statement_markdown: Rank shoppers by their on-time delivery rate (within 60 minutes) for last month.

starter_code.sql:
-- Rank shoppers by their on-time delivery rate (within 60 minutes) for last month.
-- Require at least 10 deliveries per shopper.
-- Write your SQL query here

reference_solution.sql:
WITH stats AS (
  SELECT 
    shopper_id, 
    COUNT(*) AS total, 
    SUM(CASE WHEN (CAST((julianday(delivery_time) - julianday(order_time)) * 24 * 60 AS INTEGER)) <= 60 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS on_time
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'delivered'
    AND order_time >= datetime('2024-12-01')
    AND order_time < datetime('2025-01-01')
  GROUP BY shopper_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10
)
SELECT 
  shopper_id, 
  total, 
  ROUND(100.0 * on_time / total, 2) AS on_time_rate,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY 100.0 * on_time / total DESC) AS rnk
FROM stats
ORDER BY rnk;

test_cases.label: Verify at least 3 shoppers ranked with on-time delivery rate >= 0%
Verify shopper with highest on-time rate is ranked 1
Verify only shoppers with at least 10 deliveries are included

metadata.reference_approach: The solution uses a CTE to compute per-shopper delivery statistics for orders in December 2024 with 'delivered' status. For each shopper, it counts total deliveries and counts how many were completed within 60 minutes (calculated using SQLite's datetime functions). The HAVING clause filters to only shoppers with at least 10 deliveries, ensuring statistical significance. Finally, RANK() OVER assigns rankings ordered by descending on-time rate, allowing ties. The final SELECT presents shopper_id, delivery counts, on-time percentage rate, and ranking position.

  p.category,
  COUNT(oi.item_id) AS times_ordered,
  SUM(CASE WHEN oi.found = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS not_found,

ORDER BY oos_pct DESC;

WITH hourly AS (
  SELECT
    w.size,
    datetime(strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:00:00', q.executed_at)) AS hour,
    SUM(q.credits_used) AS credits
  FROM queries q
  JOIN warehouses w ON q.account_id = w.account_id
  WHERE q.executed_at >= datetime('2023-12-19') AND q.executed_at < datetime('2023-12-20')
  GROUP BY w.size, datetime(strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:00:00', q.executed_at))
)
SELECT
  size,
  hour,
  credits,
  ROUND(
    AVG(credits) OVER (
      PARTITION BY size
      ORDER BY hour
      ROWS BETWEEN 23 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ),
    4
  ) AS rolling_24h_avg
FROM hourly
ORDER BY size, hour;

title: Two Sum
problem_statement_markdown: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. You may assume exactly one solution exists, and you may not use the same element twice.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a hash map to store each number's index as you iterate. For each element, compute the complement (target - num) and check if it already exists in the map. If it does, return [map[complement], current_index]. This gives O(n) time and O(n) space, compared to the O(n²) brute-force nested-loop approach.

title: Word Break
problem_statement_markdown: Given a string and a dictionary of words, determine if the string can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.

metadata.reference_approach: Build a boolean DP array dp of length n+1 where dp[i] means s[:i] can be segmented using words from the dictionary. Initialize dp[0]=True (empty string). For each end index i from 1 to n, try every split point j from 0 to i-1: if dp[j] is True and s[j:i] is in the word set, set dp[i]=True and break. Return dp[n]. Time O(n^2), space O(n).

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problem_statement_markdown: Given a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST). Each node's value must be strictly greater than all values in its left subtree and strictly less than all values in its right subtree. This constraint must hold for every node, not just immediate children.

test_cases.label: subtree violation [10,5,15,null,null,6,20] - 6 in right subtree but 6 < 10

metadata.reference_approach: Pass min/max bounds during DFS traversal. The naive approach of checking left.val < root.val < right.val fails for subtree violations (e.g. a node deep in the right subtree that is less than the root). Instead, each recursive call carries a valid range [min_val, max_val] and rejects any node whose value falls outside it. The bounds tighten as we go deeper: going left sets a new upper bound (node.val), going right sets a new lower bound. Time O(n), space O(h).

title: Design LFU Cache
problem_statement_markdown:
Implement a Least Frequently Used (LFU) Cache with O(1) get and put operations. The cache has a fixed capacity. When eviction is needed, remove the key with the lowest access frequency. If multiple keys have the same minimum frequency, evict the least recently used among them.

The solution function receives two arrays: operations (strings) and args (arrays of arguments). Return an array of results — use null for void operations (constructor, put) and the integer result for get.

test_cases.label: update existing key value without eviction
tie in min-freq evicts LRU: get(1) raises freq, put(3) evicts key 2 (LRU at min-freq)

metadata.reference_approach: Use two hash maps and a min_freq tracker for O(1) all operations. key_map maps each key to its [value, freq]. freq_map maps each frequency to an OrderedDict (Python) or insertion-order Map (JS) of keys at that frequency — the insertion order gives LRU semantics within a frequency bucket. On get: update frequency, shift key from freq_map[f] to freq_map[f+1]; if freq_map[f] empties and f == min_freq, increment min_freq. On put with eviction: pop the leftmost (least recently used) key from freq_map[min_freq], then insert the new key at freq 1 and reset min_freq to 1. Updating an existing key also calls _update but does not reset min_freq. Time O(1) per op, space O(capacity).

title: Car Fleet
problem_statement_markdown: N cars head to the same destination. Given positions and speeds, cars that catch up form a fleet. Return number of fleets that arrive.

test_cases.label: all cars caught by slowest front car

metadata.reference_approach: Sort cars by starting position in descending order (closest to target first). Compute the time each car needs to reach the target. Use a monotonic stack: iterate through cars from closest to farthest. If the current car's time-to-destination is greater than the top of the stack, it forms a new fleet (it cannot catch up to the car ahead). Otherwise, it joins the fleet of the car ahead (stack top remains). The final stack size is the number of fleets. Time O(n log n) due to sorting, Space O(n) for the stack.

title: Coin Change
problem_statement_markdown: Given coins of different denominations and a target amount, find the minimum number of coins needed to make up that amount. Return -1 if it is impossible to make up the amount.

metadata.reference_approach: Use bottom-up dynamic programming where dp[i] represents the minimum number of coins needed to make amount i. Initialize dp[0] = 0 (base case) and all other values to infinity. For each amount from 1 to the target, iterate over all coin denominations and update dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - c] + 1) whenever coin c <= i. The answer is dp[amount] if it's not infinity, otherwise -1. Time complexity: O(amount * len(coins)), Space complexity: O(amount).

title: Container With Most Water
problem_statement_markdown: Given n non-negative integers representing heights of vertical lines, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container that holds the most water.

test_cases.label: Two tall spikes at ends of interior

metadata.reference_approach: Use two pointers starting at both ends of the array. At each step, compute the area as min(h[left], h[right]) * (right - left) and update the maximum. Move the pointer pointing to the shorter line inward, since keeping the taller line gives the best chance of finding a larger area with a smaller width. This greedy strategy is provably optimal. Time complexity: O(n), Space complexity: O(1).

title: House Robber
problem_statement_markdown: Rob houses in a row; you cannot rob two adjacent houses. Find the maximum amount of money you can rob.

test_cases.label: nine-house array with large middle value

metadata.reference_approach: Use dynamic programming with two variables tracking the best outcome up to the previous house (prev1) and two houses back (prev2). For each house, the new best is max(skip current = prev1, rob current = prev2 + nums[i]). Update both variables in a single pass. Time O(n), Space O(1).

title: House Robber II (Circular)
problem_statement_markdown: Houses are arranged in a circle, meaning the first and last houses are adjacent. Find the maximum amount of money you can rob without robbing adjacent houses.

metadata.reference_approach: Reduce the circular house robber problem to two instances of the linear House Robber I problem. Since the first and last houses are adjacent, in any optimal solution we cannot include both. So we solve two subproblems: rob houses 0..n-2 (exclude last) and rob houses 1..n-1 (exclude first), then take the maximum. Each subproblem is solved with a simple DP using two variables tracking the best rob amount up to the current and previous house. Time complexity O(n), Space complexity O(1).

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
problem_statement_markdown: Given an array of bar heights in a histogram, find the largest rectangle that can be formed.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(heights):
    stack = []  # monotonic increasing
    max_area = 0
    heights = heights + [0]  # sentinel, don't mutate input
    for i, h in enumerate(heights):
        start = i
        while stack and stack[-1][1] >= h:
            idx, height = stack.pop()
            max_area = max(max_area, height * (i - idx))
            start = idx
        stack.append((start, h))
    return max_area

metadata.reference_approach: Use a monotonic increasing stack storing (start_index, height) pairs. Iterate through the heights with a sentinel 0 appended at the end. For each bar, if it is shorter than the stack top, pop bars and compute their rectangle area using the current index as the right boundary and the popped bar's stored start as the left boundary. Track the earliest start index that can extend to the current position. This runs in O(n) time and O(n) space since each bar is pushed and popped at most once.

title: Generate Parentheses
problem_statement_markdown: Generate all combinations of n pairs of well-formed (valid) parentheses.

metadata.reference_approach: Use backtracking with two counters tracking open and close parentheses used so far. At each step, add '(' if open_count < n (we still have opening parens to place), and add ')' if close_count < open_count (we can close a previously opened paren). When the string reaches length 2*n, it's a valid combination. This generates all valid combinations without ever producing invalid ones. Time complexity is O(4^n / sqrt(n)) — the nth Catalan number — and space complexity is O(n) for the recursion stack.

title: Minimum Cost to Connect Ropes
problem_statement_markdown: Given rope lengths, connect all ropes into one. Cost = sum of two ropes being connected. Minimize total cost.

reference_solution.python:
import heapq

def solution(ropes):
    if not ropes:
        return 0
    if len(ropes) == 1:
        return 0
    heap = ropes[:]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    total_cost = 0
    
    while len(heap) > 1:
        a = heapq.heappop(heap)
        b = heapq.heappop(heap)
        cost = a + b
        total_cost += cost
        heapq.heappush(heap, cost)
    
    return total_cost

metadata.reference_approach: Use a min-heap (priority queue) to always combine the two shortest ropes first. Pop the two smallest values, add them together to get the connection cost, accumulate that cost into the total, then push the combined rope back into the heap. Repeat until only one rope remains. This greedy approach (equivalent to Huffman coding) ensures the minimum total cost because shorter ropes are combined earlier and thus contribute less to subsequent sums. Time complexity: O(n log n) for n heap operations; Space complexity: O(n) for the heap.

title: Minimum Window Substring
problem_statement_markdown: Given strings s and t, return the minimum window substring of s that contains all characters of t. If none exists, return empty string.

starter_code.python:
def solution(s: str, t: str) -> str:
    pass

reference_solution.python:
def solution(s: str, t: str) -> str:
    if not t or not s:
        return ""
    
    from collections import Counter
    
    need = Counter(t)
    have = {}
    
    have_count = 0
    need_count = len(need)
    
    left = 0
    min_len = float('inf')
    min_left = 0
    
    for right in range(len(s)):
        char = s[right]
        have[char] = have.get(char, 0) + 1
        
        if char in need and have[char] == need[char]:
            have_count += 1
        
        while have_count == need_count:
            # Update minimum window
            window_len = right - left + 1
            if window_len < min_len:
                min_len = window_len
                min_left = left
            
            # Shrink from left
            left_char = s[left]
            have[left_char] -= 1
            if left_char in need and have[left_char] < need[left_char]:
                have_count -= 1
            left += 1
    
    if min_len == float('inf'):
        return ""
    return s[min_left:min_left + min_len]

metadata.reference_approach: Use a sliding window with two frequency maps (need for t, have for current window). Expand the right pointer adding characters to the window. Track have_count (number of unique chars in t satisfied by window). When have_count equals need_count (all chars covered), record the window if it's the smallest so far, then shrink from the left by incrementing left pointer and updating have counts. This runs in O(|s| + |t|) time since each character is added and removed at most once, and O(|s| + |t|) space for the frequency maps.

title: Reorganize String
problem_statement_markdown: Rearrange characters so no two adjacent characters are the same. Return empty string if impossible.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a max-heap (by frequency) of (negative_count, character) pairs. Repeatedly pop the two most frequent characters, append both to the result, decrement their counts, and re-push if count > 0. If only one character remains in the heap with count > 1, return empty string (impossible). Otherwise append the last character. Time O(n log 26) = O(n), Space O(n).

A 32-bit mask (0xFFFFFFFF) is applied at each step to handle Python's arbitrary-precision integers — after the loop, check the sign bit (bit 31) of a; if set the result is negative and we sign-extend with `a | ~mask`. Time complexity is O(1) since integers are bounded to 32 bits; space complexity is O(1).

metadata.reference_approach: Use Python's Counter to tally element frequencies in O(n), then use heapq.nlargest to extract the top k keys by frequency in O(n log k). This combines to O(n log k) time and O(n) space. An alternative is bucket sort: create buckets indexed by frequency (1 to n), place each element in its bucket, then scan from highest to lowest frequency collecting k elements in O(n) time.

title: Inorder Traversal (Iterative)
problem_statement_markdown: Implement binary tree inorder traversal iteratively (without recursion).

reference_solution.python:
def solution(root):
    result = []
    stack = []
    current = root

    while stack or current:
        while current:
            stack.append(current)
            current = current.left
        current = stack.pop()
        result.append(current.val)
        current = current.right

    return result

metadata.reference_approach: Use an explicit stack to simulate the call stack of recursive inorder traversal. Maintain a 'current' pointer starting at root. In a loop, push all left-spine nodes onto the stack (going as far left as possible), then pop a node, record its value, and move current to its right child. Repeat until both stack and current are empty. This visits nodes in left-root-right order. Time complexity is O(n) since each node is pushed and popped exactly once. Space complexity is O(h) where h is the tree height (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed).

title: Invert Binary Tree
problem_statement_markdown: Invert (mirror) a binary tree. Every left child becomes right child and vice versa.

metadata.reference_approach: Use a recursive post-order traversal: for each node, recursively invert the left and right subtrees, then swap them. Base case is a null node. This visits every node exactly once giving O(n) time complexity and O(h) space complexity where h is the tree height (call stack depth), which is O(log n) for balanced trees and O(n) worst case for skewed trees.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
problem_statement_markdown: Design algorithms to serialize a binary tree to a string and deserialize it back. Your serialization format is your choice.

reference_solution.python:
from collections import deque

def solution(root):
    # Serialize
    tokens = []
    def dfs(node):
        if not node:
            tokens.append('null')
            return
        tokens.append(str(node.val))
        dfs(node.left)
        dfs(node.right)
    dfs(root)
    data = ','.join(tokens)
    
    # Deserialize
    queue = deque(data.split(','))
    def build():
        val = queue.popleft()
        if val == 'null':
            return None
        node = TreeNode(int(val))
        node.left = build()
        node.right = build()
        return node
    return build()

test_cases.label: tree with null in middle level

metadata.reference_approach: Use pre-order DFS (NLR) traversal to serialize: visit each node and append its value, or 'null' for missing children, joined by commas. To deserialize, split the string into a token queue and recursively consume tokens — if the token is 'null' return None, otherwise create a TreeNode and recursively build its left then right subtrees. Both operations run in O(n) time and O(n) space where n is the number of nodes.

title: N-Queens
problem_statement_markdown: Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so no two queens attack each other. Return all distinct board solutions.

reference_solution.python:
def solution(n):
    result = []
    cols = set()
    diag1 = set()  # row - col
    diag2 = set()  # row + col
    board = [['.' ] * n for _ in range(n)]

    def backtrack(row):
        if row == n:
            result.append([''.join(r) for r in board])
            return
        for col in range(n):
            if col in cols or (row - col) in diag1 or (row + col) in diag2:
                continue
            board[row][col] = 'Q'
            cols.add(col)
            diag1.add(row - col)
            diag2.add(row + col)
            backtrack(row + 1)
            board[row][col] = '.'
            cols.remove(col)
            diag1.remove(row - col)
            diag2.remove(row + col)

    backtrack(0)
    return result

metadata.reference_approach: Backtrack row by row, placing exactly one queen per row. Track occupied columns and both diagonals using sets: the column index, the (row - col) value for the anti-diagonal, and the (row + col) value for the main diagonal. For each row try every column; if no conflict exists on any of the three sets, place the queen, recurse to the next row, then remove it. When all n rows are filled, record the board state. This yields all valid placements in O(n!) time with O(n) space for the recursion stack and the three sets.

title: Sudoku Solver
problem_statement_markdown: Solve a 9x9 Sudoku puzzle in-place. Fill '.' cells with digits 1-9 satisfying row, column, and 3x3 box constraints.

metadata.reference_approach: Scan the board for the first empty cell ('.'). Try placing each digit '1' through '9' in that cell, validating against the row, column, and 3x3 box using a single loop of nine checks. If placement is valid, recurse; if recursion succeeds, return the board. If no digit works, reset the cell to '.' and return False, triggering backtracking. When no empty cell remains, the board is fully solved. The solution returns the modified board for harness compatibility. Time complexity is O(9^m) where m is the number of empty cells; practical performance is much faster due to early pruning.

Implement two methods: hit(timestamp) — records a hit at the given timestamp (in seconds); getHits(timestamp) — returns the number of hits in the past 300 seconds from the given timestamp. For hit(t): if times[t%300] == t, increment hits[t%300]; else reset times[t%300]=t and hits[t%300]=1. For getHits(t): sum hits[i] for all i where t - times[i] < 300 (i.e., within the 300-second window). Time: O(1) for hit, O(300)=O(1) for getHits; Space: O(300)=O(1).

title: Design Search Autocomplete (Trie)
problem_statement_markdown: Design a search autocomplete system. Users type a character at a time and the system returns the top 3 most frequent historical sentences matching the current prefix. metadata.reference_approach: Build a Trie where each node stores a frequency map of all complete sentences passing through it. On initialization, insert all historical sentences with their frequencies by traversing each character and updating freq_map at every node along the path. On input(c): if c is '#', insert the accumulated input as a new sentence (freq +1) and reset state; otherwise, walk one step down the trie. If the node exists, return the top-3 sentences from its freq_map sorted by (-frequency, lexicographic). If no node exists, return []. Time: O(m) per character for trie traversal + O(k log k) for top-3 extraction where k=distinct sentences; Space: O(N*M) where N=sentences, M=avg length.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
problem_statement_markdown: Given a height matrix, find all cells that can flow to both the Pacific Ocean (top/left) and Atlantic Ocean (bottom/right). Water flows to equal-height or lower cells.

reference_solution.python:
from collections import deque

def solution(heights):
    if not heights:
        return []
    rows, cols = len(heights), len(heights[0])
    directions = [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)]

    def bfs(starts):
        visited = set(starts)
        queue = deque(starts)
        while queue:
            r, c = queue.popleft()
            for dr, dc in directions:
                nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                if (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols
                        and (nr, nc) not in visited
                        and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]):
                    visited.add((nr, nc))
                    queue.append((nr, nc))
        return visited

    pacific_starts = [(0, c) for c in range(cols)] + [(r, 0) for r in range(rows)]
    atlantic_starts = [(rows-1, c) for c in range(cols)] + [(r, cols-1) for r in range(rows)]

    pacific = bfs(pacific_starts)
    atlantic = bfs(atlantic_starts)

    return [list(cell) for cell in pacific & atlantic]

test_cases.label: Strictly decreasing grid — only Pacific-border cells reach both oceans

metadata.reference_approach: Perform reverse BFS from each ocean's border cells (Pacific: top row + left column; Atlantic: bottom row + right column), climbing uphill (visiting neighbors with height >= current). This finds all cells that can reach each ocean. The answer is the intersection of both reachable sets. Time: O(m*n) since each cell is visited at most twice. Space: O(m*n) for the visited sets and BFS queues.

title: Smallest Range Covering K Lists
problem_statement_markdown: Given k sorted lists, find the smallest range [a,b] that includes at least one element from each list.

reference_solution.python:
import heapq

def solution(nums):
    heap = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(nums)]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    cur_max = max(lst[0] for lst in nums)
    best = [heap[0][0], cur_max]
    
    while True:
        cur_min, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if j + 1 >= len(nums[i]):
            break
        next_val = nums[i][j + 1]
        heapq.heappush(heap, (next_val, i, j + 1))
        cur_max = max(cur_max, next_val)
        cur_min = heap[0][0]
        if cur_max - cur_min < best[1] - best[0]:
            best = [cur_min, cur_max]
    
    return best

test_cases.label: three interleaved lists — initial window is already optimal

metadata.reference_approach: Use a min-heap initialized with the first element from each of the k lists, tracking the current maximum value across all heap entries. At each step, extract the minimum element, compute the current range [min, max], and update the best answer if the range is smaller. Then advance that list's pointer and push the next element into the heap, updating the global max. Stop when any list is exhausted (no valid range can cover all lists from that point). Time complexity O(n log k) where n is total elements, space O(k) for the heap.

Edge: small repo with 100% rate but <10 PRs excluded

       COUNT(*) AS total_prs,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'merged' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS merged,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'merged' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS merge_rate_pct

  SELECT 7 AS workspace_id, 700 + ((n-1) % 5) + 1 AS user_id FROM (WITH RECURSIVE c(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM c WHERE n<7) SELECT n FROM c)
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 8 AS workspace_id, 800 + ((n-1) % 4) + 1 AS user_id FROM (WITH RECURSIVE c(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM c WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM c)
) AS ws;

WITH daily AS (
  SELECT w.plan,
         date(m.sent_at) AS day,
         COUNT(DISTINCT m.user_id) AS dau
  FROM messages m
  JOIN workspaces w ON m.workspace_id = w.workspace_id
  WHERE m.sent_at >= date('now', '-30 days')
  GROUP BY w.plan, date(m.sent_at)
)
SELECT plan, day, dau,
       ROUND(AVG(dau) OVER (
         PARTITION BY plan
         ORDER BY day
         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ), 0) AS rolling_7d
FROM daily
ORDER BY plan, day;
