The search path queries an Elasticsearch cluster kept in sync from the events database through a change stream. The browse path serves event detail pages from a CDN and Redis cache, falling back to the events service and PostgreSQL on a miss, with a real-time channel pushing seat-availability deltas to open seat maps. The booking path routes fans through a virtual waiting queue that admits them in batches; admitted requests place seat holds as Redis TTL keys, then a checkout service uses Optimistic Concurrency Control against versioned seat rows in PostgreSQL and only commits the booking after the payment service authorizes the charge, while expired holds release back to the available pool.

title: Design Youtube
problem_statement_markdown:
A video-sharing platform lets creators upload long-form video and lets viewers watch it on any device and network. The two hard problems sit at opposite ends of the pipeline. On upload, a creator pushes a large file, sometimes many gigabytes, over a connection that may drop midway, and the raw file is useless for streaming until it is transcoded into multiple resolutions and packaged into segments. On playback, a viewer expects the video to start in a second or two and to keep playing smoothly when their bandwidth fluctuates, whether they are on fiber or a weak mobile signal. The design has to move large blobs reliably and then serve them globally with low startup latency.

## Functional Requirements
- A creator can upload a video file along with its title and description.
- An interrupted upload can resume from where it stopped instead of restarting.
- An uploaded video is transcoded into several resolutions and packaged for adaptive streaming.
- A viewer can play a video that starts quickly and adapts quality to current bandwidth.
- A viewer can seek to any point in the video without downloading the whole file.

## Non-Functional Requirements
- The system favors availability over strict consistency; a newly uploaded video appearing after a short processing delay is acceptable.
- Playback stays low latency and smooth even on poor networks through adaptive bitrate switching.
- The platform scales to hundreds of millions of viewers and a continuous high volume of uploads.
- Uploads are resilient: a failed chunk or worker does not force the creator to start over.
- The system supports very large source files without holding them entirely in application memory.

## Out of Scope
- Recommendation and ranking of videos.
- Comments, likes, subscriptions, and other engagement features.
- Monetization, ads, and creator payouts.
- Live streaming and real-time broadcast.
- Content moderation and copyright matching.

requirements: Upload a video file with title and description metadata
Resume an interrupted upload from the last successful chunk
Transcode each upload into multiple resolutions (for example 360p, 720p, 1080p)
Package transcoded output into HLS or DASH segments with a manifest
Start playback within a second or two and switch bitrate as bandwidth changes
Seek to arbitrary timestamps by requesting only the needed segments
required_components: Client-driven chunked, resumable upload (multipart upload to object storage via pre-signed URLs)
Object storage (S3 or GCS) as the durable store for raw uploads and transcoded segments
Message queue (SQS or Kafka) that decouples upload completion from the transcoding pipeline
Transcoding worker fleet that produces multiple resolutions and codecs (H.264, VP9, AV1)
Packaging step that emits HLS (.m3u8) or DASH (.mpd) manifests and time-aligned segments
Metadata service backed by a database storing title, description, status, and segment references
CDN that caches segments at edge locations close to viewers
Adaptive bitrate player that reads the manifest and requests segments per current bandwidth
Read cache for hot video metadata to absorb popular-video traffic
scalability_signals: Source files are huge and connections are unreliable, so chunked resumable upload straight to object storage means a dropped connection retries one part rather than the whole file.
Transcoding is CPU-heavy and bursty, so a message queue between upload and processing lets a worker fleet scale horizontally and absorb upload spikes without blocking creators.
Reads dominate and a small set of videos goes viral, so a CDN caching segments at the edge keeps origin and object-storage egress flat while serving most playback from the edge.
Networks vary widely across viewers, so packaging into multiple bitrates with a manifest lets the player adapt per segment instead of the server guessing one quality.
Metadata is read far more than written, so a read cache in front of the metadata store shields the database when a video trends.
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A creator's client splits the source file into chunks and uploads them with pre-signed URLs directly to object storage, bypassing the application servers; an upload service tracks chunk progress so the transfer can resume. When the upload completes, a message lands on a queue that a transcoding worker fleet consumes, reading the raw file from object storage, producing several resolutions and codecs, packaging them into HLS or DASH segments and a manifest, and writing both back to object storage while updating the metadata service. On the read side, a viewer's adaptive bitrate player fetches the manifest and video metadata (served through a read cache) and then pulls segments from a CDN, which caches them at the edge and falls back to object storage on a miss, switching bitrate as the viewer's bandwidth changes.

title: Design a Photo-Sharing Service Like Instagram
problem_statement_markdown:
A photo-sharing app lets people post images, follow others, and scroll a home feed of recent posts from accounts they follow. The product starts small but the design has to hold up when a single popular account has tens of millions of followers and a feed read happens on every app open. Media is large and immutable once uploaded, while the feed itself changes constantly as new posts arrive.

## Functional Requirements

- Upload a photo with a caption and store it durably
- Follow and unfollow other accounts
- Read a reverse-chronological home feed of posts from followed accounts
- View any user's profile grid of their own posts
- Like a post and see an aggregate like count

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Feed reads return in under 200ms at p99
- Media survives a full region outage with no data loss
- The system handles celebrity accounts with tens of millions of followers without a write storm
- Read traffic dwarfs writes by roughly 100 to 1

## Out of Scope

- Direct messaging, stories, comments threading, and video transcoding
- Content moderation and ranking by engagement (assume reverse-chronological)

requirements: Post a photo and have it appear durably in the author's profile grid
Open the app and see a fresh home feed within a fraction of a second
Follow an account and start seeing its new posts
See accurate like counts that converge quickly
Handle a post from an account with millions of followers without stalling
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The client uploads a photo to an API server, which writes the blob to S3 and a metadata row to the sharded post database, then emits an event to Kafka. A fan-out worker reads the event and pushes the post ID into each follower's Redis timeline, while celebrity posts are skipped and merged at read time. On feed read, the client hits the API server, which assembles post IDs from the Redis timeline cache, hydrates metadata from the database, and returns image URLs served through the CDN.
required_components: Object store such as S3 for immutable image blobs
CDN for image read fan-out close to users
Metadata database (sharded relational store) for posts, users, and the follow graph
Redis or Memcached feed cache holding precomputed timelines per user
Fan-out-on-write worker pool pushing new post IDs into follower timelines
Hybrid fan-out path that falls back to fan-out-on-read for celebrity accounts
Message queue such as Kafka decoupling upload from feed fan-out
Like counter backed by Redis with periodic flush to the database
scalability_signals: Reads outnumber writes about 100 to 1, so the feed should be precomputed and cached rather than assembled on every read
A celebrity post would write to tens of millions of timelines at once, so very-high-follower accounts pull on read instead of pushing on write
Images are immutable and large, so they belong in an object store fronted by a CDN, never in the relational database
The follow graph and post metadata grow unbounded, so the metadata store is sharded by user ID

title: Design a Lowest-Price Book Order Aggregator
problem_statement_markdown:
A buyer submits an ISBN, a maximum bid price, and a payment method. The service queries hundreds of independent downstream bookstores, each with its own latency and reliability, to find the lowest available price. If the lowest price is at or below the bid, the service places the order through that store and charges the buyer. Otherwise it returns the lowest price found or reports that no store has the book. The downstream calls are slow, numerous, and prone to partial failure, so the design lives or dies on how it handles timeouts and stragglers.

## Functional Requirements

- Accept an order request with ISBN, bid price, and payment method
- Query hundreds of downstream bookstores in parallel for price and availability
- Place an order with the lowest-price store when its price is at or below the bid
- Return the lowest price found when no store meets the bid
- Report no inventory when no store has the book
- Charge the buyer only once even if the request is retried

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A single slow bookstore must not block the whole aggregation
- Partial failures of downstream stores are expected and tolerated
- Order placement is exactly-once from the buyer's point of view
- The system sustains high external call volume without exhausting connections

## Out of Scope

- Bookstore onboarding UI and contract negotiation
- Shipping logistics and returns

requirements: Submit one ISBN and bid and get back either a confirmed order or the best price available
See a result even when a third of downstream stores time out
Never get double-charged when the client retries the same request
Get a clear no-inventory answer when the book is unavailable everywhere
Have repeated lookups of the same ISBN return quickly from a recent quote
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The buyer sends an order request to the API gateway, which checks the idempotency store to reject duplicate retries. The aggregator scatters parallel price queries to hundreds of bookstore adapters, each guarded by a circuit breaker and a timeout, and gathers whatever quotes return before the deadline. If the lowest quote is at or below the bid, the order service reserves stock at that store and the payment service charges the buyer, recording the result back in the idempotency store; otherwise the lowest price or a no-inventory result is returned.
required_components: API gateway accepting buyer order requests
Scatter-gather aggregator that queries downstream stores in parallel with per-call timeouts
Circuit breaker per downstream store to shed failing dependencies
Bounded thread pool or async I/O layer for hundreds of concurrent outbound calls
Idempotency store (Redis) keyed by request ID to dedupe retries
Price-quote cache with short TTL to absorb repeated ISBN lookups
Order and payment service with a two-phase reserve-then-charge flow
Dead-letter queue for orders that fail mid-placement
scalability_signals: Hundreds of downstream calls per request means the aggregator must run them in parallel with a hard deadline and return partial results when stragglers miss it
Downstream stores fail independently and often, so each gets a circuit breaker so one bad store does not drag down the request
The buyer may retry on a timeout, so an idempotency key guards against double charges
Repeated lookups of the same ISBN are common, so a short-TTL quote cache cuts external traffic

title: Design a Financial Ledger Service
problem_statement_markdown:
A payments company needs a ledger that records every transaction and answers balance queries per merchant. Money correctness is non-negotiable: balances must always reflect the sum of recorded transactions, double-entry must stay balanced, and the same transaction must never be recorded twice. On top of the core ledger sit invoice and payment matching and reconciliation, all driven by API calls.

## Functional Requirements

- Record a transaction (debit and credit legs) via API
- Query a merchant's current balance
- Return a transaction history for a merchant
- Match incoming payments against open invoices
- Reconcile invoices and flag mismatches

## Non-Functional Requirements

- The ledger is append-only and never edited in place
- Balances are always consistent with the sum of legs
- A transaction is recorded exactly once even under retries
- Balance queries stay fast as transaction volume grows

## Out of Scope

- Card-network and bank connectivity
- Tax computation and reporting filings
- Merchant onboarding

requirements: Record a transaction and have it reflected in the balance
Read a merchant's balance and trust it is exact
Pull a merchant's full transaction history
Match a payment to the invoice it settles
Catch and surface a reconciliation discrepancy
metadata.reference_diagram_description: An API call to record a transaction writes balanced debit and credit legs into the append-only ledger inside one database transaction, guarded by an idempotency key. A running per-merchant balance is updated as a materialized aggregate so balance queries hit a replica or cache rather than scanning history. The matching service links incoming payments to open invoices, and a reconciliation job periodically compares stored balances against the summed legs and flags any mismatch.
required_components: Append-only ledger table with double-entry debit and credit legs
Idempotency key per transaction to prevent double recording
Per-merchant balance maintained as a running aggregate or materialized view
Database transactions guaranteeing both legs commit together
Invoice store and a matching service linking payments to invoices
Reconciliation job comparing recorded balances against expected sums
Read replicas or a balance cache for fast balance queries
scalability_signals: Money state must be auditable and immutable, so the ledger is append-only with double-entry legs that always balance
Retries can resend a transaction, so an idempotency key makes recording exactly-once
Balance reads are frequent, so a per-merchant running balance or materialized view avoids summing the whole history each time
Discrepancies are inevitable at scale, so a reconciliation job continuously checks recorded balances against the sum of legs

title: Design a News Aggregation Feed with Event Clustering
problem_statement_markdown:
A news aggregator pulls raw articles from many publishers, RSS feeds, and crawlers and presents a timeline of stories. The hard part is that dozens of outlets report the same event, so the system has to cluster those articles into a single story and dedupe near-identical coverage, then rank stories for the feed. Articles arrive continuously and the same event keeps gaining new coverage over time.

## Functional Requirements

- Ingest raw articles from publishers, RSS, and crawlers
- Cluster articles that cover the same event into one story
- Deduplicate near-identical articles within a cluster
- Present a ranked timeline of stories
- Attach new incoming articles to existing event clusters

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Clustering keeps up with a continuous article stream
- Near-duplicate detection is accurate across outlets
- The timeline reflects new coverage within minutes
- The system scales to many sources and high article volume

## Out of Scope

- Original reporting and content creation
- Publisher contracts and paywall handling
- Personalized per-user ranking (assume a global timeline)

requirements: See a timeline of distinct news stories, not duplicate articles
Have many outlets' versions of one event collapse into a single story
Get fresh stories appearing within minutes of publication
See a growing story accumulate new coverage under one cluster
Read a clean feed free of near-identical repeats
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Connectors ingest articles from publishers, RSS, and crawlers into the article store and onto a Kafka stream. A consumer embeds each article and queries a vector index or LSH for the nearest existing event cluster, attaching it or creating a new cluster, while near-duplicate detection collapses repeated wire copies. The ranking service orders the resulting clusters into a timeline that the feed API serves and refreshes within minutes.
required_components: Ingestion layer with connectors for publishers, RSS, and crawlers
Article store (object store plus a metadata index)
Text embedding or shingling stage producing comparable representations
Near-duplicate detection (MinHash or cosine similarity) for dedup
Online clustering service grouping articles into event clusters
Vector index or LSH for fast nearest-cluster lookup
Ranking service ordering clusters for the timeline
Stream processor (Kafka plus a consumer) driving continuous updates
scalability_signals: Many outlets cover one event, so articles are embedded and grouped by similarity into event clusters rather than shown one by one
New coverage keeps arriving, so clustering is online and attaches fresh articles to existing clusters via a nearest-cluster lookup
Near-duplicate wire copies are common, so MinHash or cosine similarity dedups within a cluster
Freshness matters, so a stream processor updates clusters and the timeline within minutes of ingestion

title: Design a Competitive Coding Judge with Leaderboards
problem_statement_markdown:
A LeetCode-style platform runs coding competitions where users submit solutions that are compiled and run against test cases inside sandboxed containers, then scored and reflected on a live leaderboard. Submissions surge when a contest starts, the judge must run untrusted code safely, and the leaderboard has to update in near real time for thousands of contestants. Scaling the judge fleet and keeping the leaderboard fast are the core challenges.

## Functional Requirements

- Accept a code submission for a problem in a chosen language
- Run the submission against test cases in an isolated sandbox
- Score the result (accepted, wrong answer, time limit, runtime error)
- Track submission status so users can poll progress
- Update a live contest leaderboard ranked by score and time

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Untrusted code runs in a hardened sandbox with resource limits
- The judge fleet scales out for contest-start submission surges
- Leaderboard reads are fast for thousands of concurrent viewers
- Submission status is available within seconds

## Out of Scope

- Problem authoring and test-case creation tooling
- Discussion forums and editorials
- Payment for premium tiers

requirements: Submit a solution and get a verdict back
See submission status move from queued to running to judged
Run multiple languages safely
Watch a live leaderboard update during a contest
Trust that one user's code cannot affect another's run
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A user submits code to the submission API, which enqueues a judge job and returns a pending status. An autoscaling fleet of judge workers pulls jobs from the queue, fetches test cases from the object store, and runs the code in a sandboxed container with strict resource limits, writing the verdict to the result database. Each accepted result updates a Redis sorted set powering the live leaderboard, while a status cache lets the user poll progress without hitting the database.
required_components: Submission API queuing jobs into a message broker (Kafka or SQS)
Autoscaling judge worker fleet pulling jobs from the queue
Sandboxed execution in Docker or gVisor with CPU, memory, and time limits
Test-case store (object store) read by judge workers
Result database recording verdicts and timings
Redis sorted set for the live leaderboard ranked by score
Status cache so users poll submission state cheaply
scalability_signals: Contest starts cause submission spikes, so submissions go onto a queue and an autoscaling judge fleet drains them rather than running inline
The judge runs untrusted code, so each submission executes in a resource-limited sandbox isolated from the host and other runs
Thousands watch the leaderboard, so ranking lives in a Redis sorted set that returns top-N in logarithmic time
Users poll for verdicts, so submission status is served from a cache to spare the result database

title: Design a Polling News Aggregator
problem_statement_markdown:
A news aggregator periodically polls many third-party sources, RSS feeds and publisher APIs, to collect new articles and assemble them into a feed. Sources update at different rates and impose rate limits, so the poller has to schedule fetches without hammering any one source, detect what is new since the last poll, and aggregate the results into a timeline. The system has to stay polite to sources while keeping the feed fresh.

## Functional Requirements

- Register sources to poll with their feed URLs
- Poll each source on a schedule respecting its rate limits
- Detect new articles since the last fetch
- Normalize and store articles into a common schema
- Assemble a fresh aggregated timeline feed

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Polling respects per-source rate limits and avoids duplicate fetches
- The feed reflects new articles within the polling interval
- Adding sources does not overload the scheduler
- A slow or failing source does not stall the others

## Out of Scope

- Event clustering and cross-outlet deduplication
- Personalized ranking
- Content rights and licensing

requirements: Add a source and have it polled automatically
Get new articles picked up each polling cycle
Avoid refetching articles already seen
See a unified feed across all sources
Keep a flaky source from blocking the rest
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A source registry holds each feed's URL and poll interval, and a scheduler dispatches poll jobs to a worker pool that fetches feeds in parallel with per-source rate limiting. Workers use ETag and Last-Modified headers to skip unchanged sources and content hashing to detect new articles, which are normalized and written to the article store through a queue. A feed assembly service merges the deduplicated articles from all sources into a single fresh timeline.
required_components: Source registry holding feed URLs and per-source poll intervals
Scheduler (cron or a distributed scheduler) dispatching poll jobs
Worker pool fetching feeds in parallel with per-source rate limiting
Change detection via ETag, Last-Modified, or content hashing
Article store with a normalized schema and a dedup index
Message queue decoupling fetch from processing
Feed assembly service merging sources into a timeline
scalability_signals: Sources update at different rates and rate-limit callers, so each source carries its own poll interval and the worker pool throttles per source
Most polls return nothing new, so ETag and Last-Modified checks avoid refetching and reprocessing unchanged feeds
A failing source must not block others, so fetches run in parallel through a queue and isolate failures
Freshness is bounded by the poll interval, so hot sources get shorter intervals than slow ones

title: Design a Real-Time Auction System
problem_statement_markdown:
An auction feature lets users bid on an item and see the current highest price update in real time as bids arrive. Many users may bid on the same item at once, so the system must accept bids correctly under contention, keep a single source of truth for the highest bid, and push live price updates to every viewer with low latency. Correctness under concurrent bids and fast fan-out of the new high price are the central concerns.

## Functional Requirements

- Place a bid on an item for a given amount
- Accept a bid only if it exceeds the current highest bid
- Track the single authoritative highest bid per item
- Push the updated highest price to all viewers in real time
- Close the auction at its end time and declare a winner

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Concurrent bids on one item are serialized correctly with no lost updates
- Viewers see the new high price within a second of a bid
- The system handles many simultaneous bidders per popular item
- The final winner is unambiguous and consistent

## Out of Scope

- Payment capture and settlement after winning
- Item listing and catalog management
- Fraud and shill-bidding detection

requirements: Place a bid and learn immediately if it is now the highest
See the current highest price update live without refreshing
Have my bid rejected cleanly if someone outbid me first
Watch a popular item with thousands of others smoothly
See a clear winner when the auction ends
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A bidder sends a bid to the bid service, which performs a conditional compare-and-set against the per-item highest-bid record in Redis, accepting it only if it beats the current high and appending it to the Kafka bid log. On acceptance, the new high price is published to the item's pub/sub channel and pushed through the WebSocket gateway to every viewer within a second. A scheduler closes the auction at its end time and reads the append-only bid log to declare the winner.
required_components: Bid service applying a conditional compare-and-set on the highest bid
Per-item highest-bid record in Redis or a row with optimistic locking
Message broker (Kafka) recording the ordered bid log per item
WebSocket or SSE gateway pushing price updates to viewers
Pub/sub channel per item fanning out the new high price
Append-only bid history for audit and winner determination
Scheduler closing auctions at their end time
scalability_signals: Concurrent bids race for the same item, so a conditional compare-and-set on the highest bid serializes them and rejects stale ones
Viewers need live updates, so a WebSocket gateway with a per-item pub/sub channel fans out the new price rather than polling
A popular item concentrates load, so the highest bid is held in a fast in-memory record with optimistic locking
The winner must be unambiguous, so an append-only bid log is the source of truth at close time

title: Design an Image Feed Front-End with Offline Support
problem_statement_markdown:
This is a front-end system design for an image feed (no likes or comments) that loads endlessly as the user scrolls and keeps working when the network drops. Given a paginated image API, the design covers how to fetch and cache pages, render a smooth infinite scroll without janking the main thread, serve already-seen images offline, and stay testable. The focus is client architecture: data fetching, caching, rendering, and offline behavior.

## Functional Requirements

- Load an initial page of images and render them in a scrollable feed
- Fetch the next page automatically as the user nears the bottom
- Cache fetched images and metadata for offline viewing
- Show previously loaded images when the network is unavailable
- Recover gracefully and resume fetching when the network returns

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Scrolling stays smooth with no main-thread jank
- Already-seen images load instantly from cache
- The feed works offline for cached content
- The architecture is unit and integration testable

## Out of Scope

- Backend feed-ranking and image storage
- Likes, comments, and social actions
- Authentication flows

requirements: Scroll an endless feed that loads more as I go
See images I already viewed even with no connection
Avoid stutter while new images load in
Get a clear state when offline and fresh content is unavailable
Resume loading without interruption once back online
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The client's data-fetching layer requests image pages by cursor, deduping in-flight requests and writing results into a normalized in-memory cache. A virtualized list renders only the images in or near the viewport, and an Intersection Observer near the bottom triggers the next page. A service worker intercepts image requests and reads from IndexedDB or Cache Storage so previously loaded content renders offline, with network-status detection switching the UI between online fetching and offline cached views.
required_components: Paginated data-fetching layer with a cursor and request dedup
In-memory store plus a normalized cache for feed pages
IndexedDB or Cache Storage for offline image and metadata persistence
Service worker intercepting image requests for offline serving
Intersection Observer triggering next-page prefetch near the viewport edge
Windowed or virtualized list rendering only visible items
Network-status detection driving online and offline UI states
scalability_signals: The feed is unbounded, so an Intersection Observer prefetches the next page before the user reaches the bottom instead of loading everything
Rendering thousands of images would jank, so a virtualized list keeps only visible items in the DOM
Offline support is required, so a service worker plus IndexedDB persists images and metadata for cached viewing
Re-viewing scrolled content is common, so a normalized cache serves seen images instantly without a refetch

title: Design a Fitness App Exercise History Feed
problem_statement_markdown:
A fitness app lets users log workouts and view their exercise history: a chronological feed of past sessions with sets, reps, and times. History is per-user and append-mostly, read often when the user opens their log, and grows steadily over years of use. The design covers how to store workout entries, serve a fast paginated history feed, and keep recent history snappy as the dataset grows.

## Functional Requirements

- Log a workout session with exercises, sets, reps, and a timestamp
- View a paginated chronological history of past sessions
- Filter history by exercise type or date range
- Show summary stats over a chosen period
- Load older history on demand as the user scrolls back

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Recent history loads fast on app open
- History reads scale as a user accumulates years of sessions
- Writes are durable and never lost once confirmed
- Pagination stays efficient deep into the history

## Out of Scope

- Social sharing and friend feeds
- Workout-plan recommendation
- Wearable-device raw signal processing

requirements: Log a workout and see it appear in my history
Open my log and see recent sessions immediately
Filter to a specific exercise or date range
See totals and trends over a week or month
Scroll back through older sessions smoothly
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A logged workout is written durably to the entry store, partitioned by user ID and indexed on user plus timestamp, and the user's recent-session cache and period aggregates are updated. On history read, the app requests a page by timestamp cursor; the service serves recent pages from the Redis cache and older pages from the indexed store, applying any exercise or date filters. Summary stats come from the precomputed aggregates, and attached media is served from the object store.
required_components: Workout entry store (relational or wide-column) keyed by user and time
Time-ordered index on user ID plus timestamp for chronological reads
Cursor-based pagination using the timestamp as the cursor
Read cache (Redis) for a user's most recent sessions
Precomputed summary aggregates per user per period
Object store for any attached media (photos, form videos)
Write path appending entries durably before acknowledging
scalability_signals: History is read on every app open, so the most recent sessions are cached and the store is indexed by user plus timestamp for fast chronological reads
Offset pagination degrades deep in a long history, so reads use a timestamp cursor that stays efficient at any depth
Summary stats would be costly to compute on every read, so per-period aggregates are precomputed and updated on write
History grows for years per user, so the entry store is partitioned by user ID to keep each user's reads local

title: Design Instagram with a Media Consistency Deep Dive
problem_statement_markdown:
This is an end-to-end design of a photo-sharing service like Instagram, with a deep dive on keeping blob storage consistent. A post couples a metadata row with an image in object storage, and the two writes can diverge: the image upload may succeed while the metadata write fails, or vice versa, leaving an orphaned blob or a post that points at nothing. The design covers feed, storage, and scaling, then drills into how the metadata database and S3 stay consistent.

## Functional Requirements

- Upload a photo and create a post that references the stored image
- Read a home feed of posts from followed accounts
- View a user's profile grid
- Guarantee a visible post always has a valid image behind it
- Clean up orphaned blobs whose metadata write never landed

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A post is never shown without its image being durably present
- No orphaned blobs accumulate from failed metadata writes
- Feed reads are fast under heavy read traffic
- Uploads survive partial failures between S3 and the database

## Out of Scope

- Stories, reels, and direct messaging
- Engagement-based feed ranking
- Comment threads

requirements: Post a photo and trust it shows with its image intact
Never see a broken post that points at a missing image
Open a fast home feed of followed accounts
See my own posts in a profile grid
Have failed uploads cleaned up rather than lingering
metadata.reference_diagram_description: On upload the client writes the image to S3 and the API server records a pending post; only after the metadata row committing the S3 reference lands does the post become visible, which guarantees a shown post always has a durable image. A garbage-collection job periodically sweeps S3 for blobs whose metadata never committed and deletes them. Reads assemble timelines from a Redis feed cache fed by Kafka fan-out workers, and images are served through a CDN from S3.
required_components: Object store (S3) for immutable image blobs with a CDN for reads
Metadata database (sharded) for posts, users, and the follow graph
Two-phase upload: write blob first, then commit metadata referencing it
Pending-upload marker so a post is only visible after metadata commits
Garbage-collection job sweeping blobs with no committed metadata
Feed cache (Redis) with fan-out workers for timeline assembly
Message queue (Kafka) decoupling upload from fan-out
scalability_signals: The image and its metadata are two separate writes that can diverge, so the blob is written first and the post becomes visible only after the metadata commit references it
Failed metadata writes leave orphan blobs, so a garbage-collection job sweeps any blob lacking committed metadata
Showing a post without its image is unacceptable, so visibility is gated on the metadata commit, never on the blob upload alone
Reads dominate, so images go through a CDN and timelines are precomputed in a feed cache

title: Design a Game Recommendation System
problem_statement_markdown:
A platform recommends games to users, pulling from a catalog that includes both blockbuster titles with rich signal and a long tail of niche games with almost none. The system generates candidates, ranks them with a model, and has to define a loss function that does not let the popular head drown out the long tail. Handling sparse features for niche games and choosing the right training objective are the heart of the problem.

## Functional Requirements

- Generate game candidates relevant to a user
- Rank candidates by predicted engagement
- Use user, game, and contextual features in ranking
- Represent long-tail games with sparse signal effectively
- Train the ranker against a loss that balances head and tail

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Recommendations return in interactive time
- Long-tail games get fair exposure, not only blockbusters
- The model retrains regularly on fresh interaction data
- Ranking quality is measurable offline and online

## Out of Scope

- Game hosting and download delivery
- Pricing and store checkout
- Anti-cheat and matchmaking

requirements: See game suggestions that fit my taste
Discover niche games, not just the top sellers
Get suggestions quickly when browsing
Have new and obscure titles surface once they gain a little signal
Have recommendations improve as I play more
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A request hits the serving layer, which generates candidates from collaborative-filtering and content-embedding lookups in the embedding store, covering both head and long-tail games. The ranking model pulls user, game, and contextual features from the feature store and scores the candidates, returning a ranked list in interactive time. An offline pipeline retrains the neural ranker on logged plays using a popularity-debiased, negatively sampled loss so long-tail titles get fair exposure.
required_components: Candidate generation via collaborative filtering and content embeddings
Embedding store for user and game vectors, including sparse long-tail items
Feature store with user, game, and contextual features
Ranking model (a neural ranker) scoring candidates
Loss function with negative sampling or popularity debiasing for the long tail
Offline training pipeline on logged plays and clicks
Serving layer with a candidate-then-rank two-stage pipeline
scalability_signals: The catalog has a long tail of sparse-signal games, so content embeddings supplement collaborative filtering to represent items with few interactions
Popularity bias would bury niche titles, so the loss uses negative sampling and popularity debiasing to give the tail fair gradient
Ranking the whole catalog is too costly, so a candidate stage narrows it before the neural ranker scores
Tastes shift, so the ranker retrains regularly on logged plays and is evaluated both offline and online

title: Design a Distributed Job Scheduler
problem_statement_markdown:
A job scheduler runs user-defined jobs at specified times or on recurring schedules, across a fleet of workers. Jobs must fire close to their scheduled time, run exactly once despite worker crashes, retry on failure, and scale to large numbers of scheduled jobs. The design covers how jobs are stored, how due jobs are picked up without two workers grabbing the same one, and how failures are handled.

## Functional Requirements

- Register a job with a run-at time or a recurring schedule
- Trigger due jobs close to their scheduled time
- Run each due job exactly once across the worker fleet
- Retry failed jobs with a backoff policy
- Track job status and execution history

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Jobs fire within a small delay of their scheduled time
- No job runs twice even if a worker crashes mid-execution
- The scheduler scales to millions of registered jobs
- A worker failure does not drop or duplicate jobs

## Out of Scope

- The business logic inside each job
- A workflow DAG engine for job dependencies
- Per-job resource autoscaling

requirements: Schedule a one-off or recurring job
Have jobs run on time without manual triggering
Trust a job runs once even when a worker dies
See failed jobs retried automatically
Look up whether a job ran and what happened
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Jobs are registered in a job store indexed by next-run time. A dispatcher polls for jobs due now and claims each with an atomic lease, then hands it to a worker via the message queue. Workers execute leased jobs, send heartbeats, and on success record status and compute the next run for recurring jobs; on failure the retry policy reschedules with backoff. If a worker crashes, its lease expires and the dispatcher reclaims the job, with an idempotency marker preventing a double run.
required_components: Job store (database) holding schedules, next-run times, and status
Time-indexed query or a timer wheel to find jobs due now
Dispatcher claiming due jobs with an atomic lease to prevent double pickup
Worker fleet pulling leased jobs and executing them
Message queue handing jobs from dispatcher to workers
Retry and backoff policy with a dead-letter path for poison jobs
Heartbeat and lease-expiry so a crashed worker's job is reclaimed
scalability_signals: Two workers could grab the same due job, so the dispatcher claims each job with an atomic lease that only one worker can win
A worker can crash mid-run, so leases expire on missed heartbeats and the job is safely reclaimed and retried
Exactly-once is the goal, so a lease plus an idempotent execution marker prevents a reclaimed job from running twice
Millions of jobs make a full scan too slow, so the store is indexed by next-run time and only imminent jobs are polled

title: Design an Online Bookstore Platform
problem_statement_markdown:
An online bookstore lets shoppers browse a catalog, search for titles, add books to a cart, and check out against live inventory. Inventory is finite per title, so two shoppers racing for the last copy cannot both succeed. The catalog is read constantly while inventory and orders are written far less often, which shapes where caching and consistency belong.

## Functional Requirements

- Browse and search the book catalog by title, author, and category
- View a book detail page with price and stock status
- Add books to a cart and adjust quantities
- Check out and place an order against current inventory
- Prevent overselling the last copy of a title
- View order history for an account

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Catalog and search pages load fast under heavy read traffic
- Inventory decrements are correct under concurrent checkout
- Orders are never lost once confirmed
- The platform stays available during catalog read spikes

## Out of Scope

- Payment gateway internals and fraud checks
- Warehouse fulfillment and shipping tracking
- Recommendations and reviews

requirements: Search the catalog and get relevant results quickly
See accurate stock status on a book page
Add to cart and check out in one flow
Get a clear out-of-stock message when a title sells out mid-checkout
Look up past orders
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The shopper hits a CDN-fronted web tier that serves catalog and search pages from a search index and read replicas. Adding to cart writes to a Redis cart store keyed by session. At checkout, the order service calls the inventory service to atomically decrement stock for each title, and on success writes a confirmed order row to the relational database and emits a fulfillment event to the queue.
required_components: Catalog database (relational) for books, authors, and categories
Search index such as Elasticsearch for title and author queries
CDN and read replicas serving cached catalog pages
Inventory service with row-level locking or atomic decrement on stock
Cart service backed by Redis keyed by session
Order service writing confirmed orders transactionally
Message queue decoupling order placement from fulfillment
scalability_signals: Catalog reads vastly outnumber writes, so search and detail pages are served from a search index and cached replicas rather than the primary
The last-copy race is a correctness problem, so inventory uses an atomic conditional decrement to prevent overselling
Carts are ephemeral and high churn, so they live in Redis rather than the relational store
Order confirmation must be durable, so it is written transactionally before any fulfillment event fires

title: Design an Object Storage Service Like S3
problem_statement_markdown:
A blob storage service stores and serves arbitrary objects organized into buckets, addressed by key. Objects range from kilobytes to gigabytes, must be highly durable, and are read far more than they are written. The design covers the metadata layer mapping keys to physical data, how large objects are chunked and replicated, and how the system achieves very high durability and availability at scale.

## Functional Requirements

- Create buckets and store objects under a key
- Retrieve an object by bucket and key
- Delete an object
- Support large objects via multipart upload
- List objects in a bucket by prefix

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Objects are extremely durable, surviving disk and node failures
- Reads scale to very high throughput
- Storage scales horizontally to petabytes and beyond
- Writes are acknowledged only after durable replication

## Out of Scope

- Access-control policy language and IAM internals
- Lifecycle tiering to cold storage
- Cross-region replication configuration UI

requirements: Put an object and get it back intact by key
Trust stored objects are not lost to hardware failure
Upload very large files in parts
List the contents of a bucket by prefix
Delete objects I no longer need
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A client PUT hits the API layer, which the chunking layer splits into fixed-size blocks; the placement service uses consistent hashing to spread each block across storage nodes in different failure domains, replicating or erasure-coding it, and the metadata service records the key-to-chunk mapping only after durable acknowledgment. A GET looks up chunk locations in the metadata service and reads blocks in parallel from the storage nodes to reassemble the object, while a background scrubber continuously re-replicates any chunks lost to node failures.
required_components: Request router and API layer handling PUT, GET, DELETE, and LIST
Metadata service mapping bucket and key to object chunk locations
Chunking layer splitting large objects into fixed-size blocks
Distributed storage nodes holding replicated or erasure-coded chunks
Replication or erasure coding across failure domains for durability
Consistent hashing or a placement service distributing chunks
Background repair and scrubber detecting and re-replicating lost chunks
scalability_signals: Durability is the headline requirement, so each chunk is replicated or erasure-coded across independent failure domains and a write is acknowledged only after enough copies land
Objects span kilobytes to gigabytes, so large ones are chunked and uploaded in parts and reassembled on read
Reads dominate, so the metadata lookup is cheap and chunks are spread across many nodes for parallel throughput
Disks fail constantly at scale, so a background scrubber detects lost chunks and re-replicates to hold the durability target

title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store
problem_statement_markdown:
A key-value store provides get and put on opaque values, distributed across many nodes so it scales beyond one machine and survives node failures. The design covers how keys are partitioned across nodes, how data is replicated for durability and availability, what consistency model is offered, and how the cluster handles a node joining or leaving. An in-process LRU cache fronts hot keys to cut read latency.

## Functional Requirements

- Put a value under a key
- Get the value for a key
- Delete a key
- Distribute keys across many nodes by partition
- Replicate each key to multiple nodes for durability

## Non-Functional Requirements

- The store scales horizontally by adding nodes
- Data survives the loss of a node without loss
- Reads and writes stay fast under load
- The cluster rebalances when nodes join or leave

## Out of Scope

- Range scans and secondary indexes
- SQL query support and joins
- Multi-key transactions

requirements: Put and get values by key reliably
Keep serving when a node goes down
Add nodes to grow capacity without downtime
Read hot keys with very low latency
Have the cluster rebalance automatically as it changes
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A client request reaches a coordinator node, which uses the consistent-hashing ring to find the partition and its N replica nodes. The coordinator fans the put or get to the replicas and waits for a write or read quorum, checking each node's LRU cache before disk on reads. Gossip keeps every node's view of ring membership current so that when a node joins or leaves only the affected key range rebalances, and hinted handoff plus read repair reconcile replicas after failures.
required_components: Consistent-hashing ring partitioning keys across nodes
Replication to N successor nodes on the ring for durability
Coordinator node routing each request to the right partition
Quorum reads and writes (R plus W greater than N) for tunable consistency
Per-node LRU cache fronting hot keys to cut read latency
Hinted handoff and read repair for failure recovery
Gossip protocol propagating cluster membership and ring changes
scalability_signals: The dataset outgrows one machine, so consistent hashing partitions keys across nodes and adding a node moves only a slice of keys
Nodes fail, so each key is replicated to N successors and quorum reads and writes keep the store available with tunable consistency
Hot keys dominate reads, so a per-node LRU cache serves them without touching disk
Membership changes constantly at scale, so a gossip protocol spreads ring updates and hinted handoff heals writes during outages

title: Design a Per-Model Usage Limit API for an AI Chat App
problem_statement_markdown:
A consumer AI chat product offers several models on a free tier. Each model has its own access budget, for example a small model allows 50 messages per day while a frontier model allows 10 messages per rolling 5 hours. When a free user exhausts a model's budget, the client shows a toast that states how long until the next free access and offers an upgrade link to the paid tier. Paid users have higher or unlimited budgets.

The job is to design the API and the server-side counting layer that enforces these limits, and to describe the mobile client architecture that consumes it. The system has tens of millions of daily users sending bursts of requests, so the limit check sits on the hot path of every message send and must add only a few milliseconds.

## Functional Requirements
- Enforce a separate usage budget per user, per model, over a configured window
- Return the remaining count and the precise reset time on every check
- Block a request once the budget is exhausted and return a structured reason the client can render as a toast
- Support different limits for free and paid tiers, and let limits change without a deploy
- Let the client read current usage so it can show counters before the user hits the wall

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Limit check adds under 10ms at the median on the send path
- Counting is correct under concurrent sends from the same account on multiple devices
- Window resets are accurate to the second so the toast countdown does not lie
- Limits are configurable per model and per tier from a control plane

## Out of Scope
- The model inference and token streaming itself
- Billing and payment capture for the upgrade flow
- Abuse detection beyond simple per-user counting

requirements: User sends a message to a chosen model and the request is allowed only if budget remains
When budget is exhausted, the user sees a toast with the exact time until the next free access
The toast includes an upgrade link that routes the user to the paid tier
A user on two devices sees one shared budget, not two separate counts
Switching from a small model to a frontier model applies that model's own separate budget
The client can display remaining count and reset time before the limit is reached
Limits for a model can be raised or lowered by an operator and take effect quickly
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The mobile client holds a UsageRepository that talks through an API Gateway to a Usage Service. On each message send, the Usage Service runs an atomic Lua script against a Redis cluster keyed by user id and model id, decrementing a counter whose TTL equals the window. If the counter is above zero the request proceeds to the chat backend; if it is zero the service returns a 429 with the reset timestamp and tier, which the client renders as a countdown toast plus upgrade link. A Limit Config store supplies per-model, per-tier budgets that the Usage Service caches locally, and every consumption event is published to an async stream for analytics and reconciliation.
required_components: Mobile client using MVVM or MVI with a UsageRepository that caches limit state
API Gateway terminating TLS and routing /v1/chat and /v1/usage
Usage Service that owns the check-and-decrement logic
Redis with per-user-per-model counter keys and TTL set to the window length
Lua script or INCR with conditional expiry for atomic check-and-decrement
Limit Config store (Postgres or a feature-flag service) for per-model per-tier budgets
Auth Service issuing tokens that carry the user's tier
Async event stream to durably log consumption for analytics and reconciliation
scalability_signals: Every send triggers a limit check, so the counter store must serve 100k+ ops/sec, which points to in-memory Redis with sharding by user id rather than a relational row lock
The same account sends from several devices at once, so the decrement must be a single atomic Redis operation, implying a Lua script rather than a read-then-write round trip
The toast countdown must match the real reset, so the window reset should derive from the key TTL and server clock, not a client timer that can drift
Limits change per model without a deploy, so budgets live in a config store read by the Usage Service with a short local cache, not hardcoded constants

title: Design a Video Upload Event Pipeline and Analytics Warehouse
problem_statement_markdown:
A short-video platform records an event for every meaningful action in the upload lifecycle: a creator starts an upload, a chunk lands, transcoding begins, a rendition finishes, the video goes live. At peak the platform emits millions of these events per second across regions. Product and growth teams need both a streaming view, for example a near-real-time count of uploads stuck in transcoding, and a warehouse view that answers questions like daily completed uploads by country and device over the last 90 days.

The job is to design the ingestion and processing pipeline for these events, and the warehouse schema that serves low-latency analytical queries on top of it. The interview emphasized a Kafka plus Flink streaming core, partitioning strategy, and a star schema with columnar storage.

## Functional Requirements
- Ingest upload-lifecycle events from clients and backend services at very high volume
- Process events in a streaming layer to compute live aggregates such as in-flight uploads by stage
- Land cleaned, conformed events in a warehouse for historical analytical queries
- Expose fact and dimension tables that analysts can slice by creator, country, device, and time
- Support reprocessing a day of data if a transform bug is found

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Sustain millions of events per second with bounded end-to-end lag in the streaming path
- Streaming aggregates are available within seconds of the event
- Warehouse queries over 90 days return in single-digit seconds
- The pipeline tolerates a broker or worker failure without losing events

## Out of Scope
- The video transcoding system itself
- Player-side playback analytics
- Machine learning feature stores built on top of the warehouse

requirements: Every upload-lifecycle event is captured exactly once into the pipeline
An operator can watch a live count of uploads currently stuck in each stage
An analyst can query completed uploads by country and device for any day in the last 90 days
Late-arriving events still land in the correct day's partition
A bad transform can be fixed and a single day reprocessed without touching other days
Streaming and batch views agree on totals after reconciliation
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Clients and backend services publish upload-lifecycle events to Kafka topics partitioned by video id, with a Schema Registry validating each event. Two consumers read the log in parallel: a Flink streaming layer computes event-time windowed aggregates such as in-flight uploads per stage and writes them to a fast serving store for live dashboards, while a batch path persists raw events as Parquet in object storage. A Spark or dbt job conforms the raw events into a star schema in a columnar warehouse, building a fact_upload_event table partitioned by date alongside dim_creator, dim_device, dim_geo, and dim_date. Airflow orchestrates daily loads and any single-day backfills, and a reconciliation step compares streaming and batch totals.
required_components: Apache Kafka as the durable event log, partitioned by creator id or video id
Schema Registry enforcing event schemas and compatible evolution
Apache Flink jobs for windowed streaming aggregates with event-time watermarks
Object storage landing zone (S3 or GCS) holding raw events in Parquet
Columnar warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, or ClickHouse) for analytical queries
Star schema with a fact_upload_event table and dim_creator, dim_device, dim_geo, dim_date
Batch ETL (Spark or dbt) building conformed dimensions and daily fact partitions
Orchestrator (Airflow) scheduling daily loads and backfills
scalability_signals: Millions of events per second exceed any single broker, so Kafka topics are partitioned by video id to spread load and keep per-video ordering for stage transitions
Live in-flight counts need event-time correctness despite out-of-order arrival, so Flink uses watermarks and windowing rather than naive wall-clock counting
90-day queries scan billions of rows, so the warehouse stores facts in columnar format partitioned by date, letting the planner prune to the requested window
A transform bug should not force a full rebuild, so daily fact partitions are idempotent and independently reprocessable from the raw Parquet landing zone

title: Design a One-to-One Chat System
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a direct-message system that supports only one-to-one conversations, with no groups or channels. Two users exchange text messages. When the recipient is online the message should arrive within a fraction of a second. When the recipient is offline the message must be stored and delivered on reconnect, and a push notification should fire. The sender sees delivery and read states.

The design centers on real-time delivery, offline storage, presence detection, and durable session state. The interview discussion compared a message broker such as Kafka for the durable write path against Redis for presence and fast fan-out to connected sockets.

## Functional Requirements
- A user sends a text message to exactly one other user
- An online recipient receives the message in near real time over a persistent connection
- An offline recipient receives stored messages on reconnect and gets a push notification
- The sender sees sent, delivered, and read receipts
- Conversation history persists and is paginated on open
- The system tracks and exposes each user's online presence

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Online delivery latency under 300ms at the median
- No message is lost even if a chat server crashes mid-delivery
- Messages are delivered in order within a conversation
- Presence reflects reality within a few seconds of a user going offline

## Out of Scope
- Group chats, channels, and broadcast
- Voice, video, and file attachments
- End-to-end encryption key exchange

requirements: Sending a message to an online user delivers it within a fraction of a second
Sending to an offline user stores the message and pushes a notification
On reconnect, a user receives every message queued while they were away, in order
The sender sees the message move through sent, delivered, and read states
Opening a conversation loads recent history and pages backward on scroll
A user's contacts see them flip to offline within a few seconds of disconnect
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Clients hold a persistent WebSocket to a gateway node, and a Redis connection registry records which node owns each user's socket. When user A sends to user B, the Chat Service first appends the message to a Kafka topic for durability, then persists it to a Cassandra store partitioned by conversation id, then looks up B in the registry. If B is online, the message is pushed to B's gateway node and over the socket; if B is offline, it lands in B's offline queue and a push notification fires through APNs or FCM. Delivery and read receipts flow back over the same sockets, and a Presence Service tracks online state through socket heartbeats with TTLs in Redis.
required_components: WebSocket gateway holding persistent connections from online clients
Connection registry in Redis mapping user id to the gateway node holding their socket
Chat Service that persists each message and routes it to the recipient's gateway
Kafka topic as the durable write-ahead path so no message is lost on a crash
Message store (Cassandra) keyed by conversation id with a time-ordered clustering key
Offline queue per user for messages awaiting reconnect
Push notification service (APNs or FCM) for offline recipients
Presence Service updating online state via socket heartbeats
scalability_signals: A recipient may sit on any of many gateway nodes, so a Redis registry maps user id to node, letting the sender's server route the message to the exact socket instead of broadcasting
A chat server can crash between accept and deliver, so the message is written to Kafka before acknowledgment, making delivery a replayable consumer rather than a best-effort in-memory hop
History reads are always scoped to one conversation in time order, so Cassandra partitioned by conversation id with a timestamp clustering key serves pagination cheaply at scale
Presence changes constantly for millions of users, so it lives in Redis with heartbeat TTLs rather than the durable message store, keeping the hot path light

title: Design an Ad Frequency Capping System
problem_statement_markdown:
An ad platform must stop showing the same ad to a user too many times. A campaign sets a cap, for example show this ad to any one user at most three times per day and at most ten times per week. On each ad request the serving system asks whether a candidate ad is still under cap for that user, and after an ad is actually shown the platform records the impression. The platform serves a very high request rate across many edge regions.

The twist that makes this harder than a plain rate limiter is that the read path and the write path are separate. Checking the cap during candidate selection does not mean the ad wins the auction and gets served, so the count must only increment on a confirmed impression event, not on the read. The design must keep the counter strictly correct so a campaign with a cap of one is never over-served.

## Functional Requirements
- Check whether a candidate ad is under its per-user cap for the relevant windows
- Increment a user's impression count only when an impression is confirmed in the event path
- Support multiple simultaneous windows per campaign, for example daily and weekly caps
- Strictly enforce small caps so a cap of one is never exceeded
- Let advertisers configure cap values per campaign

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Cap check adds no more than a few milliseconds to ad selection
- Counting is correct under concurrent impressions for the same user and ad
- Counters expire on their own at the end of each window
- The system sustains very high read QPS during selection and high write QPS on impressions

## Out of Scope
- The auction and bidding logic that picks the winning ad
- Creative rendering and click tracking
- Advertiser billing and budget pacing

requirements: During selection, the platform learns whether an ad is still under cap for a user
An impression count rises only after the ad is confirmed served, not when it is merely considered
A campaign with a daily and a weekly cap has both checked on every request
A cap of one results in the ad being shown exactly once to a given user
Counts reset automatically at the end of each window without a cleanup job
An advertiser can set or change the cap for a campaign
metadata.reference_diagram_description: On each ad request, edge serving nodes call the Ad Serving Service, which performs a read-only cap check against a sharded Redis cluster holding per-user, per-campaign counters whose TTLs match each window. Candidate ads still under cap proceed to the auction, which is outside this design. Separately, confirmed impressions flow as events into a Kafka stream; a Frequency Counter consumer reads that stream and runs an atomic Lua increment against the same Redis keys, so a count only rises on a real impression. Campaign cap values come from a Config store, and because counters carry TTLs they reset automatically at window end.
required_components: Ad Serving Service that performs the read-side cap check during candidate selection
Redis cluster holding per-user-per-campaign counters with TTLs matching each window
Atomic Lua script for the increment so concurrent impressions cannot double-count or skip
Impression event stream (Kafka) carrying confirmed served impressions
Frequency Counter consumer that reads the impression stream and increments Redis
Campaign Config store for cap values per campaign and window
Edge serving nodes that call the cap check on each ad request
scalability_signals: Reads happen on every ad request but writes only on confirmed impressions, so the count lives in the event-tracking consumer, not the selection path, keeping selection a pure read against Redis
A cap of one demands strict correctness under concurrency, so the increment is a single atomic Lua operation rather than a get-then-set that two impressions could interleave
Windows expire constantly across billions of user-campaign pairs, so counters carry TTLs and disappear on their own instead of needing a sweep job
Read QPS dwarfs the durable store's capacity, so per-user counters sit in a sharded Redis cluster keyed by user and campaign rather than in a relational table

title: Design a Generalized Multiplayer Tic-Tac-Toe
problem_statement_markdown:
Design the game engine for a generalized Tic-Tac-Toe that supports k players on an n by n board. Players take turns placing their mark in an empty cell. A player wins by filling a full row, a full column, or one of the two main diagonals with their own mark. The engine models the board state, validates and applies moves, and detects a win the moment it happens.

The core challenge is win detection cost. A naive check scans the affected row, column, and diagonals after every move, which is linear in n per move. The interview pushed for win detection better than that by tracking running counts per line so a placement only updates a few counters and compares them against n. The board can be large and many games run at once.

## Functional Requirements
- Start a game with a chosen board size n and player count k
- Apply a move for the current player into an empty cell, rejecting out-of-turn or illegal moves
- Detect a win immediately when a player completes a row, column, or main diagonal
- Detect a draw when the board fills with no winner
- Report the winner and end the game

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Win detection runs in constant time per move, independent of n
- The engine supports many concurrent independent games
- Move application is correct under the turn order even with k players
- Memory per game scales linearly with the number of lines, not the square of n

## Out of Scope
- Networking, matchmaking, and lobby management
- Rendering and client UI
- AI opponents or move suggestion

requirements: A game can be created for arbitrary n and k within sane limits
A player can place a mark only on their turn and only in an empty cell
The instant a player completes any row, column, or main diagonal, they are declared the winner
A full board with no line completed ends as a draw
An illegal move returns a clear rejection without mutating state
Many games run at once without interfering with each other
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Each Game instance owns the board dimension n, the player count k, a turn pointer, and a compact set of line counters: one entry per row, one per column, and two for the diagonals. A counter records the player currently owning that line and how many of their marks sit on it; if a second player marks the same line, that counter is flagged dead. On a move, the validator checks turn order, bounds, and emptiness, then the placement updates at most one row counter, one column counter, and the relevant diagonal counters. The win detector compares each touched counter against n and declares a win on a match, or a draw when the filled-cell count reaches n squared. A game registry maps game ids to instances so many games run independently.
required_components: Game class holding board size n, player count k, and current turn pointer
Per-row counter array tracking, for each row, which player owns it and how many cells
Per-column counter array with the same per-line ownership tracking
Two diagonal counters for the main and anti-diagonal
Move validator checking turn order, bounds, and cell emptiness
Win detector comparing a touched line's count against n after each placement
Game registry mapping game id to Game instance for concurrent games
scalability_signals: A naive scan costs O(n) per move, so the engine keeps a count per row, per column, and per diagonal, turning win detection into a constant-time compare against n
A line is only a winning line if every cell belongs to one player, so each counter also records the owning player and resets to invalid the moment a second player marks that line
Memory must not blow up on large boards, so state is 2n+2 line counters rather than an n by n grid of per-cell win checks
Many games run together, so each Game owns its own counter arrays behind a game-id registry, avoiding shared mutable state across games

title: Design a Find My Device Location System
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a system that lets a person locate a lost device on a map. A device periodically reports its location while it has connectivity. The owner opens an app and sees the device's last known position, and can ask it to play a sound or mark it lost. The hard part is that the device may be offline, stolen, or in someone else's hands, so the design must protect location data from anyone but the owner while still being efficient at a fleet of hundreds of millions of devices.

The interview emphasized privacy, security, and efficiency: how a lost device reports its position, how an owner queries it, and how to keep location history from leaking. A strong answer treats location reports as encrypted payloads the server cannot read, and authorizes every owner query against device ownership.

## Functional Requirements
- A device reports its current location on a schedule and on demand
- An owner views the last known location of each device they own
- An owner can trigger play-sound or mark-as-lost on a device
- The server stores recent location reports for owner retrieval
- Only the verified owner of a device can read its location

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Location payloads are unreadable to the server and to anyone but the owner
- An owner query returns the latest position in under a second
- The system handles hundreds of millions of devices reporting periodically
- A stolen device's reports do not reveal the owner's identity to an attacker who seizes the server data

## Out of Scope
- The crowd-sourced offline finding network where nearby devices relay a lost device's beacon
- Hardware and radio details of the device itself
- Account recovery and identity proofing for new owners

requirements: A device uploads its location on a fixed interval and when explicitly pinged
An owner opens the app and sees each owned device's last known position on a map
An owner can mark a device lost and request it to play a sound
A person who is not the owner cannot read a device's location, even with a valid login
The latest location loads quickly when the owner opens the map
Even with full access to stored reports, an attacker cannot read raw locations
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A device agent encrypts each location report with a key that only the owner's devices hold, then uploads the opaque payload through an authenticated Ingestion API into a Location store keyed by device id with time-ordered recent reports. When the owner opens the app, the Query API first checks the Ownership Service that device id belongs to the requesting account, then returns the encrypted blobs, which the owner's client decrypts locally to plot on a map. Play-sound and mark-as-lost requests go out over a push command channel to the device. A key management scheme distributes the decryption key across the owner's own devices so the server never learns it, keeping stored data unreadable on its own.
required_components: Device agent that encrypts each location report with a key only the owner holds
Ingestion API authenticating the device and accepting opaque encrypted reports
Location store (a key-value or time-series DB) keyed by device id holding recent encrypted reports
Ownership Service mapping device id to owner account for authorization
Query API that checks ownership then returns the encrypted blobs for the client to decrypt
Command channel (push to device) for play-sound and mark-as-lost
Key management so the owner's devices share the decryption key without the server learning it
scalability_signals: The server must never see plaintext locations, so reports are end-to-end encrypted with an owner-held key and the store holds opaque blobs, meaning a server breach leaks ciphertext only
Owner queries always fetch one device's most recent points, so the store is keyed by device id with time-ordered reports, making the read a single fast lookup rather than a scan
Hundreds of millions of devices report periodically, so ingestion is a thin authenticated append that shards by device id, keeping write load flat and horizontal
Authorization is per query and per device, so every read passes through an Ownership check rather than trusting a logged-in session to imply access to a given device

title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a distributed key-value store that exposes a simple get and put API over a large dataset spread across many nodes. A single machine cannot hold the data or serve the request rate, so keys are partitioned across nodes and each partition is replicated for durability and availability. The design must reason explicitly about the consistency and availability tradeoff under network partitions.

The interview centered on partitioning, replication, and CAP-theorem tradeoffs. A strong answer picks consistent hashing for placement, replicates each key to a few nodes, and states clearly what the system gives up when a partition cuts replicas off from each other.

## Functional Requirements
- get(key) returns the latest value or not-found
- put(key, value) stores or overwrites a value
- Keys are distributed across many nodes so the dataset exceeds one machine
- Each key is replicated to several nodes so a node loss does not lose data
- Nodes can be added or removed with bounded data movement

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Reads and writes complete in single-digit milliseconds in the common case
- The system stays available for writes during a node failure
- The chosen consistency level is explicit and configurable per request
- Adding a node moves only a small fraction of keys, not the whole dataset

## Out of Scope
- Range queries, secondary indexes, and transactions across keys
- A SQL query layer on top
- Cross-datacenter geo-replication tuning

requirements: A client can put a value under a key and later get it back
Data is split across nodes so the store holds more than one machine can
Losing a single node loses no data because replicas exist elsewhere
Adding a node rebalances only a slice of keys rather than everything
During a network partition the operator's chosen tradeoff (stay available or stay strongly consistent) is honored
A client can request stronger or weaker consistency per operation
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Keys are placed on a consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes, and each key is replicated to its N successor nodes. A client request lands on any node acting as coordinator, which forwards it to the key's replica set and applies quorum logic: a write succeeds when W replicas acknowledge and a read returns once R replicas respond, with R plus W versus N setting the consistency-availability tradeoff. Concurrent writes are versioned with vector clocks so divergent values can be reconciled rather than lost. Nodes track membership and failures through gossip, and a background anti-entropy process using Merkle trees repairs replicas that drifted apart during a partition.
required_components: Consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes for key-to-node placement
Coordinator logic on each node that routes a request to the key's replica set
Replication of each key to N successor nodes on the ring
Quorum read and write logic (R and W tunable against N)
Vector clocks or last-write-wins versioning to resolve concurrent writes
Gossip-based membership and failure detection
Anti-entropy repair (Merkle trees) to reconcile divergent replicas
scalability_signals: The dataset exceeds one machine, so keys map onto a consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes, spreading load evenly and capping data movement when membership changes

A network partition forces a choice, so the system uses tunable quorums where R plus W greater than N gives strong consistency and lower values favor availability, making the CAP tradeoff a per-request knob
Concurrent writes to the same key can diverge across replicas, so versioning with vector clocks or last-write-wins reconciles them rather than silently dropping data
Replicas drift after partitions heal, so anti-entropy with Merkle trees repairs them in the background instead of comparing full datasets

title: Design a Cloud File Storage and Sync Service
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a cloud file storage and sync service in the spirit of Google Drive. A user uploads and downloads files, organizes them in folders, shares them with others, and sees the same contents across all their devices. A change made on a laptop appears on the phone soon after. The hard parts are syncing efficiently without re-uploading whole files, and resolving conflicts when two devices edit the same file while offline.

The interview pushed on file upload and download, storage and metadata separation, sharing, and multi-device synchronization with conflict handling. A strong answer chunks files, deduplicates chunks, syncs only changed chunks, and uses versioning to handle conflicting edits.

## Functional Requirements
- Upload, download, rename, move, and delete files and folders
- Sync a user's files across all their devices
- Share a file or folder with another user with read or edit access
- Detect and handle conflicting edits made on different devices
- Show file version history

## Non-Functional Requirements
