- Editing a small part of a large file syncs only the changed chunks, not the whole file
- A change propagates to other online devices within seconds
- Durability is high so an uploaded file is not lost
- The system supports large files up to several gigabytes

## Out of Scope
- In-document collaborative editing like a shared text cursor
- Full-text search inside file contents
- Billing and storage-quota enforcement details

requirements: A user uploads a file and later downloads it intact from any device
Editing a file on one device causes the change to appear on the user's other devices shortly after
Editing a few bytes of a large file transfers only the affected chunks
A user shares a folder and the recipient sees it with the granted permission
Two offline edits to the same file produce a detectable conflict with both versions kept
A user can view and restore previous versions of a file
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A client sync agent watches the local folder, splits files into content-addressed chunks, and uploads only chunks whose hashes are not already stored. Chunks land in object storage as deduplicated blocks, while a relational Metadata Service records the file tree, each file's ordered chunk list, versions, and sharing ACLs. When a file changes, the Metadata Service records a new version and a Notification Service pushes a change event to the user's other online devices, which then pull only the new chunks. Sharing grants other users access through the ACL model, and conflicting offline edits are detected via per-device clocks and preserved as separate versions for the user to reconcile.
required_components: Client sync agent that watches the local folder and computes per-chunk hashes
Chunking and content-addressed dedup layer (fixed or content-defined chunks)
Block storage in object storage (S3 or GCS) holding deduplicated chunks
Metadata Service (relational DB) tracking files, folders, versions, and chunk lists
Notification Service pushing change events to a user's online devices
Sharing and permission model mapping users to file and folder ACLs
Versioning and conflict resolution keeping divergent versions with vector or device clocks
scalability_signals: Re-uploading a whole large file on every edit is wasteful, so files are split into content-addressed chunks and only changed chunks transfer, cutting bandwidth to the size of the edit
The same chunk often appears across files and users, so content-addressed storage deduplicates blocks, shrinking the object store and speeding uploads of known content
Metadata and bytes have different access patterns, so file trees and version lists live in a relational Metadata Service while raw chunks live in object storage, each scaled on its own
Two offline devices can edit the same file, so versions are tracked with per-device clocks and conflicting edits are kept side by side rather than one silently overwriting the other

title: Design a Payment Processing System
problem_statement_markdown:
A payment system records charges and transactions on behalf of merchants and moves money between a buyer's funding source and a merchant's account. The same charge request may arrive more than once because of network retries, so the system must apply it exactly once. Money state must stay consistent even when downstream banks or card networks are slow or fail mid-flight.

## Functional Requirements

- Accept a charge request for an amount, currency, buyer source, and merchant
- Apply each charge exactly once even under client retries
- Record every state transition of a transaction (created, authorized, captured, failed, refunded)
- Query the current status of any transaction
- Issue refunds against a prior charge

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A charge is never applied twice for the same idempotency key
- Transaction state is consistent even if the processor crashes mid-flight
- Failed external calls are retried safely without duplicating money movement
- The transaction history is an immutable audit trail

## Out of Scope

- Card-network protocol details and PCI vault internals
- Merchant onboarding and payout scheduling
- Currency exchange-rate sourcing

requirements: Submit a charge and get a definitive authorized or failed result
Retry a charge safely and have it count once
Look up where any transaction sits in its lifecycle
Refund a charge and see the reversal recorded
Recover cleanly when a downstream bank call times out
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The merchant calls the API with an idempotency key, which is checked against the idempotency store to short-circuit duplicates. The state machine service creates a transaction in the append-only ledger and writes an outbox row; a worker drains the outbox, calls the bank or card network with retry-and-backoff through the queue, and records the authorized or failed transition back to the ledger. A reconciliation job later compares the ledger against external settlement files to catch any drift.
required_components: API layer accepting charge requests with a client idempotency key
Idempotency store (Redis or a unique DB constraint) keyed on the idempotency key
Transaction ledger (append-only) recording every state transition
State machine service driving created to authorized to captured transitions
Outbox table plus a worker for reliable downstream bank or card-network calls
Message queue for retrying external calls with backoff
Reconciliation job comparing internal ledger against external settlement reports
scalability_signals: Network retries are routine, so an idempotency key makes a repeated charge a no-op rather than a second debit
A crash mid-charge cannot lose money, so the transactional outbox pattern ties the ledger write and the external call into one recoverable unit
Money state must be auditable, so the ledger is append-only and never mutated in place
External settlement can drift, so a reconciliation job catches mismatches against bank reports

title: Design an In-Memory Key-Value Store with TTL
problem_statement_markdown:
Design an in-memory key-value store that holds short-lived data with high throughput. Clients put values under keys, read them back, and entries expire after a retention period. The first version keeps values for a short window, then a follow-up extends retention to 24 hours, which changes the memory math. The store must serve a high query rate, so a first step is estimating the QPS and the memory footprint that retention implies.

The interview walked from a basic in-memory store to follow-ups on saving space, extending the retention window to 24 hours, and handling concurrent access from many clients. A strong answer sizes the working set, picks an eviction and expiry strategy, and protects the map under concurrency.

## Functional Requirements
- put(key, value) stores a value with a time-to-live
- get(key) returns the value if present and not expired, else not-found
- Entries expire automatically once past their retention window
- The retention window is configurable, from a short window up to 24 hours
- Concurrent clients can read and write safely

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Reads and writes complete in microseconds in the common case
- Memory stays bounded even as retention extends to 24 hours
- Expired entries are reclaimed without a manual sweep blocking reads
- The store survives concurrent access without corruption or lost updates

## Out of Scope
- Durability to disk and crash recovery
- Distribution and replication across machines
- Range scans and secondary indexes

requirements: A client puts a value under a key and reads it back within the retention window
Reading an expired key returns not-found
Extending retention to 24 hours keeps entries available for a full day
The operator can estimate memory from QPS, average entry size, and retention
Many clients read and write at once without corrupting the store
Memory is reclaimed as entries expire rather than growing without bound
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The store is a hash map from key to an entry carrying the value and an expiry timestamp. A get checks the timestamp and treats an expired entry as absent, removing it lazily, while a background sampler periodically scans a random batch and evicts expired keys so memory is reclaimed without blocking reads. The map is sharded into stripes each with its own lock, so concurrent clients writing different keys do not contend. A capacity estimator multiplies QPS by retention seconds by average entry size to size the memory budget, and when retention to 24 hours would exceed that budget an LRU eviction policy caps the footprint.
required_components: Hash map from key to an entry holding value and expiry timestamp
Lazy expiry that checks the timestamp on read and treats stale entries as absent
Active expiry sampler that periodically evicts a batch of expired keys
Sharded locks or a concurrent map so writes do not serialize on one lock
Capacity estimator deriving memory from QPS times retention times entry size
Eviction policy (LRU or size cap) for when memory pressure exceeds the budget
scalability_signals: Extending retention from a short window to 24 hours multiplies the live set, so the working-set estimate is QPS times retention seconds times entry size, which drives the memory budget and whether one machine suffices
Checking every key for expiry on a timer would stall the store, so expiry is lazy on read plus a background sampler that evicts a batch, keeping reads off the critical path
A single global lock serializes all writers, so the map is sharded into stripes with independent locks, letting concurrent clients write different keys in parallel
If retention growth pushes memory past budget, an LRU eviction caps the footprint so the store degrades gracefully rather than running out of memory

title: Design a RAG Retrieval System for an Internal Coding Agent
problem_statement_markdown:
An internal coding agent answers data questions for engineers, for example which table holds active subscriptions or how a revenue notebook computes its metric. To answer well, the agent must ground itself in the right table or notebook before generating a response. Design the retrieval system that, given a natural-language data question, returns the most relevant tables and notebooks so the agent can cite real schemas and code instead of guessing.

The interview centered on indexing and embedding tables and notebooks, retrieval, ranking, and relevance metrics. A strong answer treats schemas, column descriptions, and notebook cells as documents, embeds them, retrieves candidates by vector similarity, then re-ranks with signals like table popularity and recency.

## Functional Requirements
- Index tables (names, columns, descriptions, sample lineage) and notebooks (titles, markdown, code cells)
- Given a question, retrieve the top candidate tables and notebooks
- Rank candidates so the most relevant ground the agent's answer
- Keep the index fresh as schemas change and notebooks are edited
- Expose a relevance metric so retrieval quality can be measured and improved

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Retrieval returns candidates in a few hundred milliseconds
- The index covers tens of thousands of tables and notebooks
- Updated schemas and notebooks become retrievable within minutes
- Ranking quality is measurable against a labeled set of question-to-asset pairs

## Out of Scope
- The language model that writes the final answer
- Access-control enforcement on which assets a user may see
- The agent's tool-calling and code-execution loop

requirements: An engineer asks a data question in plain language and gets back relevant tables and notebooks
The most relevant asset for the question ranks at or near the top
A renamed column or edited notebook becomes findable shortly after the change
Both structured tables and prose-and-code notebooks are searchable in one query
Retrieval quality can be scored against a labeled question-to-asset set
Popular and recently used assets are favored when relevance is otherwise close
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Asset extractors pull table schemas from the data catalog and cells from notebooks, then a chunker turns each into focused documents such as a column group or a single notebook cell. An embedding model vectorizes the chunks into a vector index for similarity search, while the same text is indexed in a BM25 keyword store for exact identifier matches. At query time a hybrid retriever runs both, fuses the candidate sets, and a re-ranker scores them by combining vector similarity with table popularity, recency, and lineage signals, returning the top tables and notebooks for the agent to ground on. Extractors run incrementally so changed assets are re-embedded within minutes, and an offline evaluation harness scores retrieval against labeled question-to-asset pairs to drive tuning.
required_components: Asset extractors pulling schemas from the catalog and cells from notebooks
Chunking that turns a table or notebook into embeddable documents (per column group, per cell)
Embedding model producing dense vectors for each chunk
Vector index (HNSW or IVF in a store like pgvector or a dedicated vector DB) for similarity search
Keyword index (BM25) for exact name and identifier matches
Hybrid retriever fusing vector and keyword candidates
Re-ranker combining similarity with popularity, recency, and lineage signals
Offline evaluation harness scoring retrieval against labeled relevance pairs
scalability_signals: Tables and notebooks differ from prose, so each is chunked into focused documents, for example a column group or a single cell, so a question matches the precise part rather than a whole sprawling asset
Pure vector search misses exact identifiers like a table name, so the retriever fuses BM25 keyword hits with embedding similarity, catching both semantic and literal matches
Schemas and notebooks change constantly, so extractors run incrementally and re-embed only changed chunks, keeping the index fresh within minutes rather than rebuilding nightly
Top-k similarity alone is noisy, so a re-ranker layers in table popularity, recency, and lineage, and an offline harness scores it against labeled pairs to guide tuning

title: Design a Video Sharing Platform
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a video sharing platform in the spirit of YouTube. A creator uploads a video, the platform transcodes it into several resolutions, stores it durably, and serves smooth playback to viewers worldwide. Viewers browse, watch, and the platform tracks view counts and basic metadata. Reads vastly outnumber writes, and playback must start fast and adapt to the viewer's bandwidth.

The design covers upload, transcoding and storage, streaming and delivery through a CDN, metadata, and view counting. A strong answer separates the heavy upload-and-transcode write path from the read-heavy delivery path and pushes bytes to the edge.

## Functional Requirements
- A creator uploads a video file
- The platform transcodes the video into multiple resolutions and formats
- Viewers stream videos with adaptive quality based on bandwidth
- The platform stores and serves video metadata (title, description, thumbnail)
- The platform counts and displays view counts

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Playback starts within a couple of seconds for most viewers
- The system serves far more reads than writes and scales the read path independently
- Uploaded videos are stored durably with no loss
- Streaming adapts smoothly to changing network conditions

## Out of Scope
- Recommendation and ranking of the home feed
- Comments, likes, and subscriptions
- Monetization and ad insertion

requirements: A creator uploads a video and it becomes playable after processing
The same video is available in several resolutions for different devices and networks
Playback starts quickly and shifts quality as bandwidth changes
A viewer sees the video's title, thumbnail, and description
View counts increase as people watch and are displayed on the video
Popular videos play smoothly for viewers far from the origin
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A creator uploads through an Upload service that hands back a pre-signed URL, so the raw file goes straight to object storage. A transcoding pipeline of workers pulls jobs off a queue, produces multiple resolutions as HLS or DASH segments, and writes them back to object storage, while the Metadata Service records titles, thumbnails, and rendition manifests in a relational DB. Viewers fetch the manifest and segments through a CDN that caches them at the edge, and the player adapts bitrate to bandwidth using the manifest. View events flow into a write-buffered counter that aggregates asynchronously, avoiding a hot row on viral videos, and the count is read back from the Metadata Service for display.
required_components: Upload service issuing pre-signed URLs for direct-to-object-storage uploads
Object storage (S3 or GCS) for raw uploads and transcoded renditions
Transcoding pipeline (worker fleet on a queue) producing multiple resolutions and HLS or DASH segments
Metadata Service (relational DB) for titles, descriptions, and rendition manifests
CDN caching video segments and thumbnails at edge locations
Adaptive bitrate manifests (HLS or DASH) the player uses to switch quality
View counter using a write-buffered async path to avoid hot-row contention
scalability_signals: Uploads are large and bursty while playback is constant and global, so the write path is an async transcode pipeline and the read path is CDN-fronted segments, scaled separately
Viewers span many devices and networks, so transcoding produces several renditions and the player uses an HLS or DASH manifest to adapt bitrate, trading a little storage for smooth playback
Bytes served from a single origin would be slow and costly, so video segments and thumbnails are cached at CDN edges, keeping origin load low and start times short
A naive per-view database increment on a viral video creates a hot row, so views are buffered and aggregated asynchronously rather than updated synchronously per play

title: Design a Robot Obstacle Avoidance System
problem_statement_markdown:
Design the perception-and-control system that lets a mobile robot move through a shared space without colliding with people. The robot has a goal position and a planned path, but humans move unpredictably across that path. The system must sense nearby people, represent the surrounding space and obstacles, and decide on each control cycle how to steer or stop so it never runs into anyone, while still making progress toward its goal.

The interview asked for the approach in architecture and pseudocode: which sensors to use, what data structures represent the environment and obstacles, and the logic that detects people and steers around them. A strong answer fuses sensor input into an occupancy representation and runs a fast local planner inside a safety envelope.

## Functional Requirements
- Sense people and obstacles around the robot in real time
- Maintain a representation of the local environment with occupied and free space
- Plan a collision-free local motion toward the goal each control cycle
- Stop or yield when a person blocks the only safe path
- Resume progress toward the goal once the path clears

## Non-Functional Requirements
- The sense-plan-act loop runs within the robot's control cycle, on the order of tens of milliseconds
- The robot never collides with a detected person, preferring to stop over to risk
- Detection works in varied lighting and partial occlusion
- The system degrades to a safe stop if a sensor fails

## Out of Scope
- Global route planning across a building
- Mechanical actuation and motor control internals
- Multi-robot coordination and traffic rules

requirements: The robot detects a person stepping into its path
The robot steers around the person if a safe path exists, otherwise stops
The robot keeps moving toward its goal when the way is clear
A person standing still is treated as an obstacle to route around
If a sensor drops out, the robot falls back to a safe stop
The robot resumes once the blocking person moves away
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Each control cycle, a fused sensor suite of LiDAR, an RGB-D camera, and ultrasonic sensors feeds detections into a common coordinate frame, which updates a rolling occupancy grid of free and occupied cells around the robot. A person detector identifies humans and a short-horizon predictor projects their near-future motion, marking soon-to-be-occupied cells. A local planner, such as a dynamic-window or potential-field method, searches for a velocity command that reaches toward the goal while staying in free space, and outputs the steer command. Below it, a safety-envelope monitor checks for imminent collision and overrides with an emergency stop when no safe motion exists or a sensor fails, and the robot resumes planning once the grid clears.
required_components: Sensor suite (LiDAR for range, RGB-D camera for people detection, ultrasonic for close range)
Sensor fusion combining detections into one coordinate frame
Occupancy grid representing local free and occupied cells around the robot
Person detector and short-horizon motion predictor for moving humans
Local planner (dynamic window or potential field) producing a safe velocity command
Safety envelope and emergency-stop monitor that overrides on imminent collision
Control loop executing sense, fuse, plan, act each cycle
scalability_signals: No single sensor is reliable alone, so LiDAR, depth camera, and ultrasonic are fused into one frame, covering range, people detection, and close-range gaps that any one sensor misses
The environment changes every cycle, so it is held as a rolling occupancy grid around the robot rather than a static map, letting the planner reason over current free space
People move while the robot plans, so a short-horizon motion predictor projects their path, and the local planner steers into space that will still be free, not just space free now
Planning can fail or a sensor can drop out, so a safety envelope monitor sits below the planner and forces an emergency stop, making the default behavior safe rather than optimistic

title: Design a Food Delivery Shopping Cart
problem_statement_markdown:
Design the shopping cart for a food delivery app in the spirit of Uber Eats. A customer browses one restaurant, adds dishes with options and quantities, edits the cart, and proceeds to checkout. The cart must reflect live pricing and availability, survive across devices and sessions, and stay consistent when an item sells out or a price changes between adding it and checking out. At peak, millions of carts are active at once.

The round focused on the cart service: data model, keeping the cart in sync across the customer's devices, handling item availability and price changes, and the handoff to checkout. A strong answer keeps a fast cart store, validates against the live catalog at checkout, and is explicit about what happens when an item becomes unavailable.

## Functional Requirements
- Add, update quantity, and remove items with their selected options in a cart scoped to one restaurant
- Show the running subtotal as the cart changes
- Persist the cart so it is the same across the customer's phone and web
- Validate item availability and price at checkout and surface any changes
- Hand the validated cart to the order and payment flow

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Cart reads and writes feel instant, under 100ms at the median
- The cart survives app restarts and device switches
- At checkout the cart total matches live catalog prices, not stale ones
- The system supports millions of concurrently active carts

## Out of Scope
- Restaurant menu and catalog management
- Delivery dispatch and driver routing
- Payment authorization and capture internals

requirements: A customer adds a dish with options and sees the subtotal update immediately
Changing quantity or removing an item updates the cart and total
The cart shows the same contents whether opened on phone or web
If an item sold out since it was added, checkout flags it before charging
If a price changed since adding, the customer sees the new total before paying
A cart from one restaurant does not mix items from another
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The Cart Service exposes add, update, remove, and get-cart operations backed by a Redis cart store keyed by user id and restaurant, so every device reads one shared cart and operations stay under 100ms. Cart entries reference catalog items rather than copying prices, and a durable database backs up carts so an evicted cache entry can be rehydrated. While shopping, the service shows a running subtotal; at checkout a validator re-prices the entire cart against the Catalog Service, the source of truth for availability and price, and surfaces any sold-out item or price change before creating the order. Cart mutations carry idempotency keys to dedupe retried requests, and the validated cart is handed to the order and payment flow.
required_components: Cart Service exposing add, update, remove, and get-cart APIs
Cart store in Redis keyed by user id plus restaurant for fast reads and writes
Catalog Service as the source of truth for item availability and price
Checkout validator that re-prices the cart against the live catalog before order creation
Sync via the cart store so all devices read one shared cart state
Durable backup of carts (a database) so an evicted cache entry is not lost
Idempotency keys on cart mutations to dedupe retried client requests
scalability_signals: Carts are read and mutated constantly while shopping, so they live in Redis keyed by user and restaurant, giving sub-100ms operations rather than hitting a relational row per tap
Prices and stock drift between adding and paying, so the cart stores item references and the checkout validator re-prices against the live Catalog, so the customer never pays a stale total
The same customer shops across devices, so a single shared cart record is the source of truth and every device reads it, rather than each device holding a local cart that diverges
Mobile clients retry on flaky networks, so cart mutations carry idempotency keys, preventing a double-add when a request is sent twice

title: Design a Daily Puzzle Service
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a service that publishes one puzzle per day to every user. A user opens the app, plays the day's puzzle, submits an answer, and immediately sees their score and how they did. Everyone gets the same puzzle on the same calendar day, results are recorded, and a user can view past scores. Traffic is spiky, with a large surge right after the day's puzzle goes live across time zones.

The interview framed it as a deceptively simple design: publish a daily puzzle, accept submissions, score them, and let users check results. A strong answer handles the daily rollover cleanly, prevents one user from submitting twice, and absorbs the launch-time spike with caching.

## Functional Requirements
- Publish exactly one puzzle per calendar day to all users
- Let a user fetch today's puzzle
- Accept a user's answer submission and score it
- Show the user their score and result immediately after submitting
- Let a user view their past puzzle results

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Fetching the daily puzzle is fast even during the launch surge
- A user can submit only once per day's puzzle, enforced server-side
- Scoring is consistent so the same answer always yields the same score
- The daily rollover is correct across time zones per the chosen reference time

## Out of Scope
- Authoring and curating the puzzle content
- Social sharing of results
- Global leaderboards and rankings

requirements: Every user sees the same puzzle for a given calendar day
A user fetches today's puzzle quickly even when many open the app at once
Submitting an answer returns the score right away
A user cannot submit the same day's puzzle more than once
A user can browse their results from previous days
The puzzle changes over at the defined daily boundary
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A Puzzle Service serves the current day's puzzle by a date key, fronted by a CDN or edge cache so the launch-time surge of identical reads is absorbed at the edge rather than hitting the database. Puzzles and their answer keys live in a relational store keyed by date, and a scheduled publisher activates the next day's puzzle at the rollover time. When a user submits, the Submission Service scores the answer deterministically against the stored key and inserts a row into a submissions table that has a unique constraint on user id plus puzzle date, so a second submission for the same day is rejected at the database. Scores are recorded in a results store the user can page through to see past days.
required_components: Puzzle Service serving the current day's puzzle by date key
Puzzle store (relational DB) holding puzzles keyed by date and their answer keys
CDN or edge cache for the read-heavy today's-puzzle fetch
Submission Service that scores an answer and records the result
Submissions table with a unique constraint on (user id, puzzle date) to enforce one entry
Results store recording each user's score per day for history
Scheduled publisher that activates the next day's puzzle at the rollover time
scalability_signals: Everyone fetches the same puzzle the moment it goes live, so today's puzzle is served from a CDN or cache keyed by date, turning a surge of identical reads into cache hits instead of database load
A user must submit only once, so the submissions table carries a unique constraint on user id plus puzzle date, making the database reject a duplicate rather than relying on client checks
Scoring must be deterministic, so the answer key is stored with the puzzle and scoring is a pure function of answer and key, giving the same result on any retry
The puzzle rolls over on a fixed boundary, so a scheduled publisher flips the active date at the reference time, keeping all regions on the same day's puzzle

title: Design a Reporting and Log Generation System
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a reporting system that takes a set of inputs, runs them through processing, and produces report logs that users can view and download. A user configures a report, the system runs it against a data source, generates structured log output, and makes the result available. Some reports are quick and interactive; others scan large datasets and run for minutes. The design must cover the front-end request flow, the back-end processing, and the performance characteristics that keep long reports from blocking the system.

The interview asked for the design across front-end, back-end, and performance. A strong answer separates a fast interactive request path from an async job path for heavy reports, and streams or paginates large log output rather than building it all in memory.

## Functional Requirements
- A user submits report parameters and triggers a run
- The system processes the inputs and generates report log output
- The user sees report status: queued, running, ready, failed
- The user views and downloads the generated logs when ready
- The system keeps a history of past report runs

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Submitting a report and seeing it accepted feels instant
- A long-running report does not block other users or tie up a request thread
- Large report logs are delivered without loading the whole result into memory at once
- Failed reports surface a clear error and can be retried

## Out of Scope
- The business logic of any specific report type
- Access control on which data a user may report against
- Scheduled and recurring report automation

requirements: A user fills in report parameters and starts a run that is accepted immediately
The user watches the report move from queued to running to ready
When ready, the user views the report logs and downloads them
A long report runs in the background without freezing the user's session
A failed report shows why it failed and can be rerun
The user can revisit logs from earlier report runs
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The front-end submits report parameters to a Report API, which immediately returns a job id, records a run in a metadata store as queued, and enqueues the work on a job queue. A worker fleet pulls jobs, processes the inputs, generates report log output, writes the logs to object storage, and updates the run's status to ready or failed in the metadata store. The front-end polls or subscribes for status, and once a run is ready it fetches the logs through a streaming or paginated read path so large outputs are delivered in chunks rather than all at once. Past runs remain in the metadata store and their log files in object storage for later viewing and download, and failed runs surface an error and can be retried.
required_components: Front-end submitting report params and polling or subscribing for status
Report API that accepts a run, returns a job id, and enqueues the work
Job queue (SQS or a task broker) decoupling submission from execution
Worker fleet that processes inputs and generates report log output
Metadata store tracking each run's status, params, and result location
Object storage holding generated log files for download
Streaming or paginated read path so large logs are served in chunks
scalability_signals: Reports range from instant to minutes-long, so a heavy report returns a job id and runs async on a worker, keeping the request thread free instead of blocking until the report finishes
Many reports can be submitted at once, so a job queue buffers them and a worker fleet scales horizontally, smoothing bursts rather than overrunning the back-end
Report logs can be large, so output is written to object storage and served streamed or paginated, avoiding loading an entire result into memory for one response
Users need to track progress, so run status lives in a metadata store the front-end polls or subscribes to, decoupling status from the long-running job itself

title: Design a Corporate Card Expense Policy Engine
problem_statement_markdown:
A company issues credit cards to employees for business spending and sets policies that control how the cards may be used. Policies start simple, for example no restaurant charges over a limit, and grow into compound rules across a whole trip, for example total lodging on a trip may not exceed a cap. Design the architecture that evaluates each expense and each trip against the configured policies and flags violations for review.

The interview asked for the architecture to support configurable rules and to mark expenses and trips that violate them. A strong answer treats rules as data evaluated by a generic engine, so new policy types are added as configuration rather than code, and evaluates both at the single-expense level and across grouped trips.

## Functional Requirements
- Let an admin define spending policies as configurable rules
- Evaluate each incoming expense against the applicable rules
- Evaluate trip-level rules that span multiple expenses grouped into a trip
- Flag and record expenses and trips that violate a policy
- Let a reviewer see violations with the rule that was broken

## Non-Functional Requirements
- A new policy type can be added without a code deploy
- Single-expense evaluation completes within a second of the charge arriving
- Trip-level evaluation runs as expenses are grouped and re-runs if the trip changes
- Rule changes apply to future evaluations consistently

## Out of Scope
- The card network integration that captures the charge
- Employee reimbursement and payout flows
- Fraud detection beyond policy rule violations

requirements: An admin configures a rule such as no restaurant charge over a set amount
An incoming restaurant charge above that amount is flagged as a violation
A trip-level rule such as total lodging under a cap is checked across the trip's expenses
A reviewer sees each violation alongside the specific rule it broke
Adding a new kind of rule does not require changing the evaluation code
Editing an expense or trip re-evaluates the affected rules
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Admins define policies as structured rules, predicate plus scope plus threshold, in a rule definition store. An expense ingestion pipeline normalizes incoming charges, and a Rules Engine evaluates each expense against applicable single-expense rules within a second of arrival. A trip aggregator groups expenses into trips, and the engine runs trip-scoped rules across the grouped set. An evaluation event stream re-triggers the relevant rules whenever an expense or trip changes, so edits are re-checked without a full rescan. Violations are written to a violation store with the specific rule that was broken, and a reviewer API and UI surface those flagged expenses and trips for action.
required_components: Rule definition store holding policies as structured data (predicate, scope, threshold)
Rules Engine that evaluates expenses and trips against applicable rules generically
Expense ingestion pipeline receiving charges and normalizing them
Trip aggregator grouping expenses into trips for trip-scoped rules
Evaluation event stream triggering re-evaluation when an expense or trip changes
Violation store recording each flagged expense or trip with the broken rule
Reviewer API and UI surfacing violations for action
scalability_signals: Policies keep growing and changing, so rules are stored as data and run by a generic engine, letting a new policy be added as configuration rather than a code change and deploy
Some rules apply to one charge and others to a whole trip, so the engine evaluates at two scopes, single expense and aggregated trip, with a trip aggregator feeding the trip-level pass
Expenses and trips change after the fact, so an evaluation event stream re-runs only the affected rules when data changes, rather than rescanning everything on a schedule
Reviewers need to act on flags, so violations are recorded with the exact rule that broke, making the result auditable instead of a bare pass or fail

title: Design an End-to-End ML Pipeline for Customer Segmentation
problem_statement_markdown:
Design an end-to-end machine learning system that groups customers into segments from their behavior data, then serves those segments to downstream products. The flow runs from raw data through preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection and training, evaluation, and serving. The application here is unsupervised segmentation, so the modeling choice lands on a clustering method such as K-Means, and the design must handle the practical issues of cleaning messy input, choosing the number of clusters, and refreshing segments as behavior shifts.

The interview moved from data preprocessing through model selection and training, ending on implementing K-Means itself. A strong systems answer covers the data and feature path, why clustering fits, how to pick and validate the model, and how trained segments reach production.

## Functional Requirements
- Ingest raw customer behavior data and clean it for modeling
- Engineer and scale features suitable for distance-based clustering
- Train a clustering model that assigns each customer to a segment
- Evaluate cluster quality and pick the number of clusters
- Serve a customer's segment to downstream products and refresh it periodically

## Non-Functional Requirements
- The training pipeline runs reproducibly on a schedule
- Feature scaling is consistent between training and serving
- Segment lookups at serve time return in a few milliseconds
- The pipeline scales to millions of customers and many features

## Out of Scope
- The downstream campaigns that consume segments
- Deep neural architectures beyond the clustering baseline
- Real-time per-event streaming feature updates

requirements: Raw customer data is cleaned of missing and malformed values before modeling
Features are scaled so no single feature dominates the distance metric
Each customer is assigned to a segment by the trained model
The number of clusters is chosen using a quality metric, not guessed
A product can look up a customer's current segment quickly
Segments are recomputed on a schedule as behavior changes
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Raw customer behavior data is ingested and passed through a preprocessing stage that handles missing values and outliers, then a feature engineering step scales features with a standardizer fit on the training set. A scheduled training pipeline runs K-Means, selecting the number of clusters with the elbow method or silhouette score, and registers the trained model and centroids with a version. A batch scorer assigns every customer to a segment using the registered centroids and writes the result to a key-value serving store, so downstream products look up a customer's segment in a few milliseconds. The pipeline retrains and re-scores on a schedule as behavior shifts, with versioned models allowing rollback.
required_components: Data ingestion and a preprocessing stage handling missing values and outliers
Feature engineering and a scaler (standardization) fit on training data
K-Means clustering with k chosen via the elbow method or silhouette score
Training orchestration (a scheduled pipeline) for reproducible retraining
Model and centroid registry versioning each trained model
Batch scorer assigning every customer to a segment
Segment serving store (key-value) for fast per-customer lookups
scalability_signals: Distance-based clustering is dominated by unscaled features, so a scaler is fit on training data and reused at serving, keeping the feature distribution consistent across both paths
The number of segments is not known up front, so k is selected with the elbow method or silhouette score rather than hardcoded, making the model choice data-driven
Segmenting millions of customers is heavy, so assignment runs as a scheduled batch job and writes results to a key-value store, so serve-time lookups are a single fast read
Behavior drifts over time, so the pipeline retrains and re-scores on a schedule with versioned centroids, letting the team roll back if a new model degrades segments

title: Design a Ticket Booking System
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a ticket booking system in the spirit of Ticketmaster that sells reserved seats for high-demand events. When tickets for a popular concert go on sale, hundreds of thousands of users hit the system in the same minute, all trying to grab the same limited seats. The system must show seat availability, let a user hold seats briefly while they pay, and never sell the same seat twice. The booking path is the hard part because of the concurrency at sale time.

The interview asked to design ticket admissions handling high-demand sales and seat reservation. A strong answer separates browsing from booking, holds seats with a short expiry so abandoned carts release inventory, and uses a strong consistency boundary on the seat itself so no double-sell occurs.

## Functional Requirements
- Browse events and view seat availability for an event
- Reserve specific seats with a temporary hold while the user pays
- Confirm the booking on successful payment and release the hold on failure or timeout
- Prevent the same seat from being sold to two users
- Show a user their booked tickets

## Non-Functional Requirements
- The system absorbs a flash crowd of hundreds of thousands at sale open
- A seat is never double-sold under heavy concurrency
- Browsing availability stays responsive even during a sale surge
- Held seats are released automatically if the user does not complete checkout

## Out of Scope
- Dynamic pricing and resale marketplace
- Venue and seat-map authoring
- Payment provider integration internals

requirements: A user browses an event and sees which seats are available
A user selects seats and gets a short hold to complete payment
On successful payment the seats are confirmed as booked
If payment fails or times out, the held seats become available again
No two users can ever book the same seat
A user can view the tickets they have booked
metadata.reference_diagram_description: At sale open, a virtual waiting room throttles users into the booking path at a controlled rate so the seat inventory is shielded from the flash crowd. Browsing reads a cached availability view that tolerates slight staleness, keeping the surge off the transactional store. When a user reserves seats, the Inventory Service performs a transactional compare-and-set on each seat row in a relational DB, moving it from available to held only if no one else won, and sets a TTL so an abandoned hold auto-releases the seat. On successful payment the Order Service confirms the booking and the seat moves to booked; on failure or timeout the hold expires and the seat returns to available. Users read their confirmed tickets from the Order Service.
required_components: Inventory Service owning seat state (available, held, booked) per event
Relational DB with a row per seat and a transactional update for hold and booking
Distributed lock or conditional update (compare-and-set) on a seat to prevent double-sell
Hold mechanism with a TTL (Redis key or a hold expiry) that auto-releases abandoned seats
Virtual waiting room or queue throttling entry into the booking path at sale open
Read-cached availability view for browsing that tolerates slight staleness
Order Service confirming the booking after payment succeeds
scalability_signals: Hundreds of thousands arrive at the same instant, so a virtual waiting room admits users into the booking path at a controlled rate, protecting the seat inventory from a thundering herd
A seat must never sell twice, so the hold and booking use a transactional compare-and-set on the seat row, so only one concurrent request wins and the rest fail cleanly
Users abandon carts, so seats are held with a TTL that auto-releases them, returning inventory without a manual cleanup and preventing seats from being locked forever
Browsing must stay fast under load, so availability is served from a cache that tolerates slight staleness, while the booking path alone goes through the strongly consistent seat store

title: Design an Ad Frequency Capping System
problem_statement_markdown:
An ad-serving platform must limit how many times a given user sees a particular ad over a rolling window, for example no more than three impressions of one campaign per user per day. Every ad request checks the cap before serving and increments a count after serving. Traffic is enormous and the latency budget on the serving path is tight, so the cap check has to be fast and approximately correct rather than perfectly consistent.

## Functional Requirements

- Check whether a user is under the impression cap for an ad before serving it
- Record an impression after an ad is served
- Support per-user, per-campaign caps over a configurable rolling window
- Apply caps across multiple ad-serving hosts consistently enough to matter
- Let advertisers configure cap thresholds and window length

## Non-Functional Requirements

- The cap check adds only a few milliseconds to the serving path
- The system counts billions of impressions per day
- A small amount of over-delivery is acceptable under failure
- Counts expire automatically when the window rolls forward

## Out of Scope

- Ad ranking, auction, and bidding logic
- Billing and advertiser invoicing
- Creative storage and rendering

requirements: Get a fast yes or no on whether an ad can still be shown to a user
Have an impression counted right after it is served
Configure a cap of N impressions per user per day for a campaign
Stop seeing an ad once the daily cap is hit
Have yesterday's counts age out without manual cleanup
metadata.reference_diagram_description: An ad request reaches a serving host, which reads the user-plus-campaign counter from its local cache or from the central Redis counter store to decide if the cap is reached. If under the cap, the ad is served and an async increment is sent to Redis under a TTL-bucketed key, with the update replicated across regions. A configuration service supplies the threshold and window per campaign, and old window buckets expire automatically via TTL.
required_components: Distributed counter store (Redis) keyed by user plus campaign plus window bucket
Sliding-window or fixed-window bucket scheme with TTL for expiry
Local in-process cache on each ad server to absorb hot users
Async write path that increments counts off the serving critical path
Pub/sub or replication to share counts across serving regions
Cap-configuration service holding per-campaign thresholds and windows
Approximate counter (HyperLogLog or count-min sketch) for very high-volume campaigns
scalability_signals: The serving path has a few-millisecond budget, so the cap check reads a Redis counter or a local cache, never a relational database
Billions of impressions per day make exact cross-host counting too costly, so windowed buckets with TTL give approximate caps that self-expire
Some over-delivery is tolerable, so increments can be async and eventually consistent rather than blocking the serve
Hot users and campaigns concentrate load, so a local per-server cache shields the central counter store

title: Design a Video Generation Job Backend on a Fluctuating GPU Pool
problem_statement_markdown:
Design the backend that turns a video-generation request into a finished video. A client submits a prompt, the system schedules the work to a worker, and each worker produces exactly one video by calling an external GPU pool to run the model. The catch is that the GPU pool size fluctuates and any worker can be terminated at any moment, for example when capacity is reclaimed mid-job. The design must keep jobs from being lost, retry interrupted work, and report progress and the final result back to the client.

The interview centered on scheduling and worker flow with terminable workers calling a fluctuating external GPU pool, emphasizing failure handling. A strong answer makes job state durable and external to the worker, so a killed worker's job is simply picked up again rather than lost.

## Functional Requirements
- Accept a video generation request and return a job id immediately
- Schedule the job to an available worker that runs the model on the GPU pool
- Each worker produces one video per job
- Detect a terminated worker and reassign its in-flight job
- Report job status and deliver the finished video to the client

## Non-Functional Requirements
- A job is never lost even if its worker is killed mid-generation
- The system scales workers up and down with the fluctuating GPU pool
- Status updates reach the client within seconds of a state change
- Duplicate generation from a retried job is avoided or harmless

## Out of Scope
- The generative model architecture and weights
- Content safety filtering of prompts and outputs
- Billing per generation

requirements: A client submits a prompt and gets back a job id right away
The job is scheduled to a worker that calls the GPU pool to generate the video
If the worker is terminated mid-job, the job is retried on another worker
The client sees the job move through queued, running, and done
The finished video is delivered and retrievable by the client
A retried job does not bill or deliver two videos for one request
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A client submits a prompt to the Submission API, which records the job in a durable job state store as the source of truth and returns a job id immediately, enqueuing the work on a durable queue with visibility timeouts. Workers lease a job from the queue, call the external fluctuating GPU pool to generate one video, and heartbeat while running. If a worker is terminated mid-job, its lease expires and the job returns to the queue for another worker to retry, with an idempotency key ensuring the re-run resumes or replaces rather than producing a second video. Finished videos land in object storage, the job state store is updated to done, and status flows back to the client over a status channel.
required_components: Submission API returning a job id and recording the job durably
Durable job queue (SQS or a broker) holding pending and in-flight jobs with visibility timeouts
Job state store (database) tracking status, attempts, and result location as the source of truth
Worker fleet that leases a job, calls the external GPU pool, and produces one video
Heartbeat and visibility-timeout mechanism so a dead worker's job returns to the queue
Idempotency key per job so a re-run does not produce a duplicate deliverable
Object storage for finished videos and a status channel back to the client
scalability_signals: Any worker can be killed mid-job, so job state lives in a durable store and queue rather than in the worker, making a lost worker a non-event that another worker picks up
Reclaimed capacity should not strand a job, so jobs carry a visibility timeout and heartbeat, and a job whose worker stops heartbeating returns to the queue for reassignment
Retries can otherwise produce two videos, so each job carries an idempotency key so a re-run either resumes or replaces the prior attempt rather than billing and delivering twice
The GPU pool size fluctuates, so the worker fleet scales with available capacity and pulls work from the queue, decoupling intake rate from generation throughput

title: Design an Extensible Chat App with Pluggable Bots
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a chat application where human users and automated bots share channels. A user posts a message to a channel, and bots react to messages by appending their own output to the channel log. The system ships with several bots: AwayBot records a user as away when they type a command, TacoBot grants tacos to another user and tracks running totals, and MeetBot schedules a meeting and marks a user away. The defining requirement is extensibility: a new bot type must be addable without modifying existing bot or core logic.

The interview framed this as an object-oriented and event-driven design centered on a ChatApp that manages channels and processes messages. A strong answer makes message handling an event other components subscribe to, so adding a bot is registering a new handler rather than editing a switch statement.

## Functional Requirements
- A user posts a message to a channel and it is appended to the channel log
- Bots observe each message and append their own output when triggered
- Support AwayBot, TacoBot (tracking taco totals), and MeetBot out of the box
- Add a new bot type without changing existing bot or core code
- Each bot reacts only to messages matching its trigger

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Message processing preserves order within a channel
- Adding a bot requires no edit to existing classes (open for extension, closed for modification)
- One misbehaving bot does not break processing for the others
- State such as taco totals and away status is consistent across messages

## Out of Scope
- Network transport and persistence layer for messages
- Authentication and channel membership management
- Multi-server scaling and distribution

requirements: A user message posted to a channel appears in that channel's log
Typing /away marks the user away and AwayBot posts a confirmation
Typing /givetaco at a user with a count increments that user's taco total and TacoBot posts the result
Typing /meet schedules a meeting and MeetBot marks the user away
A brand new bot can be added by registering it, with no change to existing bots
Each bot ignores messages that do not match its trigger
metadata.reference_diagram_description: ChatApp manages channels, and when a user posts to a channel the message is appended to that channel's ordered log and published as a message event. Every bot implements a common Bot interface and is registered with a bot registry keyed by its trigger; the dispatcher hands each message to the bots whose triggers match. AwayBot, TacoBot, and MeetBot each react in isolation: AwayBot writes away status, TacoBot increments a per-user taco-totals store and posts the new total, and MeetBot schedules a meeting and sets away status. Because bots subscribe through the interface rather than being wired into core logic, a new bot is added by registering it, with no edit to existing classes, and a failing bot's error is contained so the rest keep processing.
required_components: ChatApp managing channels and dispatching each posted message
Channel holding an ordered message log
Message event published by ChatApp when a user posts
Bot interface (a handle(message, channel) contract) implemented by every bot
Bot registry mapping triggers to subscribed bot instances
Concrete bots: AwayBot, TacoBot with a taco-totals store, MeetBot with a scheduler
Shared state stores for away status and taco counts keyed by user
scalability_signals: New bots must not touch old code, so message handling is an event that bots subscribe to through a common Bot interface, making a new bot a registered handler rather than a new branch in a switch
Bots maintain running state, so taco totals and away status live in shared stores keyed by user, so TacoBot and MeetBot read and write consistent counts across messages
Order matters within a channel, so each channel processes its message log sequentially, so a bot's appended output lands after the message that triggered it
A faulty bot should not take down the channel, so each bot's handler runs in isolation and an error is contained, keeping the other bots processing normally

title: Design a CI System That Scales to Many Users
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a continuous integration system in the spirit of GitHub Actions. A developer pushes code or opens a pull request, the system reads a workflow definition from the repository, and runs the defined jobs on isolated runners. Results post back to the commit. The system serves many organizations whose pushes are bursty, so it must queue work fairly, isolate each job from others, and scale runner capacity up and down with demand.

The interview asked to design a GitHub Actions style CI system that supports many users and addresses scalability. A strong answer separates webhook intake from execution, runs each job in a fresh isolated environment, and scales an ephemeral runner pool against a job queue with fairness across tenants.

## Functional Requirements
- Trigger workflows on push and pull-request events from repositories
- Parse a workflow definition into a DAG of jobs with dependencies
- Run each job on an isolated runner and stream its logs
- Report job and workflow status back to the commit
- Support many organizations submitting jobs concurrently

## Non-Functional Requirements
- A pushed event starts running within seconds when capacity is free
- Jobs are isolated so one tenant's job cannot affect another's
- Runner capacity scales up under load and down when idle
- No single heavy tenant starves others of runners

## Out of Scope
- The source-control hosting itself
- The workflow definition language design
- Artifact registry and release distribution

requirements: A push or pull request triggers the repository's workflow
A workflow with dependent jobs runs them in the right order
Each job runs in a clean isolated environment and streams its logs live
The commit shows the pass or fail status of the workflow
Many organizations can run workflows at the same time
A burst from one heavy organization does not block other organizations' jobs
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A webhook ingestion service receives push and pull-request events and hands them to a workflow parser that builds a DAG of jobs from the repository's workflow file. A scheduler resolves dependencies and enqueues ready jobs onto a job queue that enforces per-tenant fairness so no organization monopolizes capacity. An ephemeral runner pool of containers or microVMs leases jobs, each running in a fresh isolated environment that is destroyed afterward, while an autoscaler grows and shrinks the pool against queue depth. Job logs stream through a logging pipeline, build outputs pass between jobs via an artifact and cache store, and a status reporter posts pass or fail results back to the commit.
required_components: Webhook ingestion service receiving push and pull-request events
Workflow parser building a job DAG from the repository's workflow file
Job scheduler resolving dependencies and enqueuing ready jobs
Job queue with per-tenant fairness so no org monopolizes runners
Ephemeral runner pool (containers or microVMs) providing isolated execution
Autoscaler sizing the runner pool against queue depth
Log streaming pipeline and a status reporter posting results back to the commit
Artifact and cache store for build outputs passed between jobs
scalability_signals: Pushes are bursty across many orgs, so webhook intake is decoupled from execution by a job queue, so a spike fills the queue rather than overwhelming the runners directly
One tenant's job must not affect another's, so each job runs in a fresh ephemeral container or microVM that is destroyed after, giving clean isolation per job
Demand swings widely, so an autoscaler grows and shrinks the runner pool against queue depth, paying for capacity only while jobs wait
A heavy org could hog all runners, so the queue applies per-tenant fairness, interleaving jobs so smaller tenants still get scheduled during a large org's burst

title: Design a Log Transmission and Central Storage System
problem_statement_markdown:
Design a system that ships logs from many distributed services to a central data-center store and lets users query them. Each service emits a stream of log lines. The system collects them reliably, transmits them to the central store without losing events when a network link drops, and supports two read patterns: a short-term tail for live debugging and historical queries over the last three months. Volume is high and write-heavy, while reads are comparatively rare but can scan large time ranges.

The interview described reliably transmitting logs to a central database and querying for short-term checks plus up to three months of history. A strong answer buffers at the edge so transient link failures do not drop logs, separates hot recent storage from cheap historical storage, and indexes by service and time for query.

## Functional Requirements
- Collect log lines from many services and forward them to the central store
- Transmit reliably so a network interruption does not lose logs
- Support a short-term live tail for recent logs
- Support historical queries over the last three months
- Filter logs by service, time range, and basic fields

## Non-Functional Requirements
- The pipeline absorbs high write volume without backpressure to the services
- No log is lost across a transient link failure between edge and center
- Recent-log queries return in under a second
- Historical queries over weeks of data complete in seconds, not minutes

## Out of Scope
- Log parsing rules and structured-field extraction policy
- Alerting and anomaly detection on log content
- Access control on which logs a user may read

requirements: Logs from every service reach the central store
A dropped network link does not cause logs to be lost once it recovers
A developer tails recent logs for a service to debug a live issue
An analyst queries logs from any point in the last three months
Logs can be filtered by service and time range
Services keep running smoothly even when log volume spikes
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Each host runs a log agent that tails files and buffers to local disk, spooling and replaying on recovery so a dropped link does not lose logs. Agents ship into a durable Kafka transport that carries logs into the central data center and absorbs write spikes without backpressuring the services. A consumer indexes recent logs into a hot store such as OpenSearch, keyed by service and time for fast live tail and search, while the full stream also lands in cold object storage as Parquet for the three-month history. A tiering job rolls aged logs from hot to cold past the retention threshold, and a query service routes recent queries to the hot store and historical queries to the cold store, filtering by service and time range.
required_components: Per-host log agent (Fluent Bit or Vector) tailing files and buffering to local disk
Edge buffer (local spool or a regional queue) absorbing transient link failures
Transport over a durable queue (Kafka) into the central data center
Hot store (Elasticsearch or OpenSearch) indexing recent logs by service and time for fast tail and search
Cold store (object storage in Parquet) holding the full three-month history cheaply
Tiering job rolling logs from hot to cold past a retention threshold
Query service routing recent queries to the hot store and historical queries to the cold store
scalability_signals: A network link between edge and center can drop, so the host agent spools to local disk and replays on recovery, so logs survive a transient outage instead of being lost
Write volume is high and bursty, so logs flow through a durable queue that buffers spikes, keeping backpressure off the services emitting them
Recent and historical reads differ sharply, so recent logs sit in an indexed hot store for sub-second tail while the three-month history lives in cheap columnar object storage
Keeping everything in the hot store would be expensive, so a tiering job rolls aged logs to the cold store, and the query service routes each query to the tier that holds its time range

title: Design a Real-Time Fraud Detection System
problem_statement_markdown:
A fraud system scores millions of transactions a day at over ten thousand requests per second and must return approve, flag, or block for each one inside a fifty-millisecond budget. The scoring uses machine-learning models that get retrained often, so operators need to swap a new model into production without taking the system down or restarting it. Speed and model agility matter as much as accuracy.

## Functional Requirements

- Score each incoming transaction as approve, flag, or block
- Return a decision within a 50ms latency budget
- Fetch the features a model needs at scoring time
- Hot-swap a new model version into production with no downtime
- Log every decision with the features and model version used

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Sustains 10,000-plus requests per second steadily
- p99 decision latency stays under 50ms
- Model rollout is zero-downtime and reversible
- Decisions are reproducible from the logged features and model version

## Out of Scope

- Offline model training pipelines and labeling
- Case-management UI for fraud analysts
- Chargeback and dispute workflows

requirements: Get an approve, flag, or block decision on every transaction in real time
Have decisions returned inside the latency budget under peak load
Deploy a retrained model and have it take effect without a restart
Roll a bad model back quickly
Audit any past decision with the exact features and model used
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A transaction enters through a load balancer to one of many scoring replicas. The replica reads precomputed features from the online feature store, loads the current model from the registry, and returns approve, flag, or block within the budget. A Kafka-plus-Flink stream continuously updates the feature store from live transactions, and every decision is written to an append-only log; new models are promoted in the registry only after passing a canary on live traffic.
required_components: Low-latency scoring service hosting model inference behind a thin API
Online feature store (Redis or a key-value store) for fast feature lookups
Model registry holding versioned models with a current-pointer for hot-swap
Streaming pipeline (Kafka plus Flink) computing fresh features from the transaction stream
Decision log (append-only) capturing features, score, and model version
Load balancer spreading 10k-plus RPS across scoring replicas
Shadow or canary path to validate a new model on live traffic before promotion
scalability_signals: The 50ms budget rules out computing features on the fly, so a precomputed online feature store serves them in single-digit milliseconds
Models change often, so a registry with a swappable current-pointer lets a new version go live without redeploying the service
Reproducibility matters for disputes, so every decision logs its exact features and model version
Peak load is 10k-plus RPS, so scoring is horizontally scaled behind a load balancer and a new model is canaried before full promotion

title: Design a Place Recommendation System for Maps
problem_statement_markdown:
A maps app recommends places to a user, for example a coffee shop or restaurant nearby that fits their habits. The system pulls from a huge catalog of places, narrows to a manageable candidate set, then ranks those candidates with a model that uses signals like distance, time of day, popularity, and the user's history. New users and brand-new places have little signal, so cold-start handling is part of the design.

## Functional Requirements

- Generate place candidates near a user's current location
- Rank candidates by predicted relevance to the user
- Use features from the user, the place, and the context (time, location)
- Handle cold-start for new users and newly added places
- Return a ranked short list fast enough for an interactive map

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Recommendations return in interactive time on a map screen
- The candidate stage keeps the ranking stage's work bounded
- Ranking quality improves as user history accumulates
- The pipeline retrains on fresh interaction data regularly

## Out of Scope

- Turn-by-turn navigation and routing
- Place metadata sourcing and moderation
- Ads and sponsored placement

requirements: See nearby place suggestions that fit the time of day
Get better suggestions as the app learns my habits
Get reasonable suggestions on my first session despite no history
See newly opened places surface once they have a little signal
Have suggestions appear without a noticeable wait
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The client sends location and context to a serving API, which queries a geospatial index for nearby places and forms a candidate set. The ranking service pulls user, place, and contextual features from the feature store and scores each candidate, applying cold-start priors when history is thin, then returns a ranked short list cached per location grid. An offline pipeline retrains the ranker on logged interactions and pushes updated models to serving.
required_components: Geospatial index (geohash or S2 cells) for fast nearby-candidate retrieval
Candidate generation stage narrowing the catalog to hundreds of nearby places
Feature store with user, place, and contextual features
Ranking model (gradient-boosted trees or a neural ranker) scoring candidates
Cold-start fallback using popularity and geographic priors
Offline training pipeline retraining on logged interactions
Serving cache for recently computed recommendations per location grid
scalability_signals: The place catalog is huge, so a geospatial index plus a candidate stage cuts it to hundreds before any expensive ranking runs
New users have no history, so cold-start falls back to popularity and location priors until signal accumulates
Context drives relevance, so time of day and current location are first-class ranking features, not afterthoughts
Interaction data ages, so the ranker retrains on a regular cadence from logged clicks and visits

title: Design a Data Lake for LLM Training Data
problem_statement_markdown:
Training a large language model needs an enormous, diverse corpus pulled from many internet sources: web crawls, public archives, code, and licensed datasets. The raw text is messy and uneven in quality, so the pipeline has to ingest at scale, clean and deduplicate, tokenize, and keep a catalog of what went into each training run. Storage, processing, and discoverability all have to scale to petabytes.

## Functional Requirements

- Ingest raw text from diverse sources (crawls, RSS, archives, code repos)
- Clean, filter, and deduplicate documents for quality and diversity
- Tokenize and shard data into training-ready formats
- Catalog datasets with lineage and version metadata
- Let training jobs read selected dataset versions efficiently

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Storage and processing scale to petabytes of text
- Pipelines are reproducible and versioned per training run
- Deduplication runs across the whole corpus, not just per source
- Data lineage is queryable for compliance and debugging

## Out of Scope

- Model architecture and the training loop itself
- Inference serving of the trained model
- Human labeling and RLHF data collection

requirements: Pull text from many source types into one place
Strip low-quality and duplicate documents before training
Get tokenized, sharded data ready for a training run
Look up exactly which dataset version a model was trained on
Read a chosen dataset version at high throughput during training
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Ingestion connectors land raw text from crawls, RSS, archives, and code into the raw tier of an object-store data lake. Spark jobs clean, quality-filter, and run global near-duplicate detection, then a tokenization stage writes sharded training files into the curated tier. An Iceberg catalog versions each dataset and records lineage, and Airflow orchestrates the whole pipeline so training jobs can read a specific, reproducible dataset version at high throughput.
required_components: Object store (S3 or GCS) as the raw and curated data lake tiers
Ingestion connectors for crawls, RSS, archives, and code sources
Distributed processing engine (Spark) for cleaning, filtering, and dedup
Near-duplicate detection (MinHash or SimHash) across the corpus
Tokenization stage writing sharded Parquet or WebDataset shards
Data catalog (Iceberg or a Hive metastore) tracking versions and lineage
Workflow orchestrator (Airflow) running the pipeline reproducibly
scalability_signals: The corpus is petabyte-scale, so raw and curated data live in an object store with a distributed engine like Spark doing the heavy transforms
Duplicate documents waste training compute and skew the model, so global near-duplicate detection runs across all sources, not within each one
Training runs must be reproducible, so a data catalog versions every dataset and records lineage
Training reads are throughput-bound, so curated data is written as sharded columnar files tuned for sequential scan

title: Design a CI/CD Test Failure and Notification System
problem_statement_markdown:
A CI/CD platform runs test suites on every code change, and tests fail for many reasons: a real regression, a flaky test, or broken infrastructure. The system has to detect failures, decide when a retry is worth attempting, distinguish flakes from genuine breaks, and notify the right people without drowning them in noise. Smart notification routing and flake handling are the heart of the problem.

## Functional Requirements

- Run test suites triggered by code changes and capture results
- Detect and classify test failures (regression, flake, infra error)
- Retry tests according to a configurable policy
- Notify the responsible owners through the right channel
- Suppress duplicate and known-flaky alerts to reduce noise

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Failure classification is accurate enough to be trusted
- Retries do not mask real regressions
- Notifications reach owners promptly without flooding them
- The system scales to many concurrent pipelines

## Out of Scope

- The build and compile toolchain itself
- Source-control hosting and code review
- Deployment rollout mechanics to production

requirements: Have failing tests detected and labeled automatically
Get flaky tests retried instead of blocking a merge outright
Get notified when a failure is a real regression I own
Avoid being paged for the same known flake repeatedly
See which test failed, on which change, and why
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A code change triggers the pipeline orchestrator to run test jobs, whose results land in the test result store. A classifier compares each failure against historical pass/fail data to label it flake, regression, or infra error, and the retry engine re-runs flaky or infra failures within a bounded policy. Confirmed failures flow through a queue to the notification router, which maps them to owners and channels while the suppression layer collapses duplicates and known flakes.
required_components: Pipeline orchestrator scheduling and running test jobs
Test result store recording pass/fail history per test
Failure classifier comparing against history to label flake vs regression
Retry policy engine deciding when and how often to re-run
Notification router mapping failures to owners and channels
Deduplication and suppression layer for known flakes
Message queue decoupling test execution from notification delivery
scalability_signals: Flaky tests are the dominant source of false alarms, so the classifier uses historical pass/fail patterns to tell a flake from a real regression before anyone is paged
Blind retries can hide regressions, so the retry policy is bounded and a persistent failure escalates instead of looping
Alert fatigue kills trust, so a suppression layer collapses duplicate and known-flake notifications
Many pipelines run at once, so notification delivery is decoupled from execution via a queue

title: Design an In-Memory Driver Billing Service
problem_statement_markdown:
A food-delivery app needs an in-memory service that tracks what it owes each driver. It supports adding drivers, recording deliveries with a cost, and reading a driver's running total in constant time. A later phase adds partial payments up to an amount and a constant-time unpaid balance, and finally a query for the maximum number of unique drivers working at the same time over the last 24 hours. The design centers on the right data structures so each operation stays fast as volume grows.

## Functional Requirements

- Add a driver to the system
- Record a delivery for a driver with a cost and timestamp
- Return a driver's total cost in O(1)
- Apply a payment up to a given amount against a driver's balance
- Return a driver's unpaid amount in O(1)
- Find the maximum count of unique drivers active simultaneously in the last 24 hours

## Non-Functional Requirements

- get_total_cost and get_unpaid_amount are constant time
- The peak-concurrency query runs in time linear in the relevant events
- Memory use stays bounded as old events age out of the 24-hour window
- Updates are correct under concurrent calls

## Out of Scope

- Persistence to a durable database and crash recovery
- Driver payout banking and tax handling
- A user-facing UI

requirements: Register a new driver
Log a delivery and its cost for a driver
Read a driver's running total instantly
Pay a driver partially and see the unpaid balance update instantly
Find the busiest overlap of drivers in the past day
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Calls land on the billing service, which keeps a hash map from driver ID to a running total and paid amount, updated atomically on each record_delivery and pay_up_to so get_total_cost and get_unpaid_amount are O(1).
