Snapshots copy the array in its current internal order, which the swap-on-remove mechanism makes fully deterministic.

title: Design a Video Sharing Platform Like YouTube
problem_statement_markdown:
A video platform lets creators upload long-form video, viewers stream it on demand across devices and network speeds, and everyone browses by title, channel, and recommendations. Uploaded files are large and arrive in many formats, so each one has to be transcoded into several resolutions before it can be served smoothly. Once published, a popular video is read millions of times while the original file is written once.

## Functional Requirements

- Upload a video file and have it become watchable after processing
- Stream a video at a resolution that matches the viewer's bandwidth
- Browse and search videos by title, channel, and metadata
- Track and display a view count per video
- Resume playback from where a viewer left off

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Playback starts within a couple of seconds anywhere in the world
- Uploaded originals survive a regional outage with no loss
- The system absorbs viral spikes where one video draws orders of magnitude more traffic than the rest
- Reads outweigh writes by a very wide margin

## Out of Scope

- Live streaming, monetization, and copyright matching
- Comment threads and creator analytics dashboards

requirements: Upload a raw video and have it transcoded into multiple resolutions before publishing
Stream adaptively so playback quality shifts with available bandwidth
Find a video quickly by searching title and channel
See a view count that reflects real traffic without slowing playback
Serve a trending video to millions without overloading origin storage
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A creator uploads a file to an API server, which stores the original in S3 and emits an event to Kafka. Transcoding workers pull the event, produce several bitrate renditions and segment manifests, write them back to S3, and mark the video ready in the sharded metadata database. A viewer requesting playback hits the API server, which returns a manifest whose segments are served through the CDN, while a search request is answered from Elasticsearch and view increments accumulate in Redis before flushing to the database.
required_components: Object store such as S3 for raw uploads and transcoded renditions
Transcoding worker pool that produces multiple bitrates and HLS or DASH segments
Message queue such as Kafka decoupling upload from the transcoding pipeline
CDN fronting segment delivery close to viewers
Metadata database (sharded relational store) for video records, channels, and view state
Search index such as Elasticsearch over title and channel metadata
View counter backed by Redis with periodic flush to the database
API gateway and stateless application servers for upload and playback requests
scalability_signals: Reads vastly outnumber writes, so segments are served from a CDN and never read straight from origin object storage
A raw upload is useless until transcoded, so the upload path returns fast and hands processing to an async worker pool through a queue
Exact view counts under heavy concurrency would hammer the database, so counts buffer in Redis and flush in batches
Video metadata and the catalog grow unbounded, so the metadata store is sharded by video or channel ID

title: Design an Offline Credit Card Payment Service with Holds and Nightly Settlement
problem_statement_markdown:
A payment service authorizes card transactions in real time but settles them in a nightly batch against a downstream card provider. When a merchant submits a charge, the service places a hold that reserves funds against the card immediately, then the real deduction happens later when a scheduled job sends all confirmed holds to the provider at a fixed time overnight. Holds can be released before settlement if an order is cancelled. The provider can be slow or briefly unavailable, so the design has to tolerate partial failure without double-charging or losing a transaction.

## Functional Requirements

- Place a hold that reserves an amount against a card and returns a reference
- Release a hold before settlement when an order is cancelled
- Run a nightly batch that converts confirmed holds into real deductions through the downstream provider
- Retry deductions the provider failed to process without duplicating a charge
- Report the status of any transaction (held, settled, released, failed)

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A hold response returns within a few hundred milliseconds
- No transaction is ever charged twice, even under retries or replays
- A provider outage during settlement delays charges but never loses or duplicates them
- The batch settles a full day of holds within its overnight window

## Out of Scope

- Fraud scoring and chargeback dispute handling
- Multi-currency conversion and tax computation

requirements: Place a hold that reserves funds and returns an idempotent reference
Release a hold cleanly so the amount is never settled later
Batch all confirmed holds into deductions at a fixed nightly time
Retry a failed deduction without charging the card a second time
Recover the exact transaction state after a crash mid-settlement
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A merchant calls the API service to place a hold, which writes a held row to the Postgres ledger keyed by an idempotency reference; a release flips that row to released. Overnight a scheduler triggers the settlement worker, which reads all confirmed holds, submits deductions to the downstream provider adapter with retries and backoff, and writes results through an outbox. A reconciliation job matches provider acknowledgements to ledger rows, moves matched holds to settled, and routes unresolved or failed deductions to a dead-letter queue for the next run.
required_components: API service exposing hold, release, and status endpoints
Transaction ledger in a relational database (Postgres) with hold and settlement state
Idempotency key store keyed by client reference to dedupe repeated requests
Scheduler such as a cron or workflow engine triggering the nightly batch
Batch settlement worker that submits deductions to the downstream provider
Outbox table plus reconciliation job to match provider responses against ledger rows
Dead-letter queue for deductions the provider rejected or failed to acknowledge
Downstream provider adapter with timeout, retry, and backoff
scalability_signals: Network calls to the provider can fail mid-flight, so every deduction carries an idempotency key and the provider response is reconciled rather than trusted blindly
Real charges are deferred to a fixed window, so authorization (the hold) and settlement (the deduction) are separate paths with separate durability guarantees
A crash during the batch must not replay charges, so settlement state transitions are recorded in the ledger before the external call and confirmed after
Settlement volume is bursty and concentrated overnight, so the batch worker pool scales for the window rather than for steady-state load

title: Design a Crash-Resilient File System
problem_statement_markdown:
A file system has to survive sudden power loss or a kernel crash without leaving files corrupted or half-written. The hard part is that a single logical operation, such as appending data and updating the file's metadata, touches several places on disk, and a crash can happen between any two writes. After a restart, the system must come back to a state where every file is either fully its old version or fully its new version, never a torn mix. Disk writes are slow relative to memory, so the design also has to keep performance reasonable while guaranteeing recovery.

## Functional Requirements

- Read and write file content and metadata (size, timestamps, block pointers)
- Survive a crash at any point and recover to a consistent state on remount
- Guarantee that a committed write is durable once acknowledged
- Reclaim space from deleted files without corrupting live ones
- Detect and repair partial writes left behind by a crash

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Recovery after a crash completes in bounded time, not a full disk scan
- A successful fsync means the data is on stable storage
- No committed file ends up in a torn or partially updated state
- Steady-state write throughput stays close to raw disk speed

## Out of Scope

- Distributed or networked file access
- Encryption at rest and access-control permissions

requirements: Persist file data and metadata so both reflect the same committed version
Recover to a clean, consistent state after a crash at any moment
Acknowledge a write only once it is durably recoverable
Bound recovery time so remount does not scan the whole disk
Reclaim freed blocks safely without losing live data
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A write enters the buffer cache, and before any final on-disk location is touched the change is appended to the write-ahead journal with a checksum and a commit record. Once the commit record is durable, a background writer applies the change to the inode table and data blocks, then a checkpoint advances the recovery pointer in the superblock and frees the consumed journal space. On remount the recovery routine reads the journal from the recovery pointer, replays every entry with a valid commit record and checksum, discards incomplete tail entries, and reconciles the block allocation bitmap before the file system is brought online.
required_components: Write-ahead journal (redo log) recording metadata and optionally data changes before applying them
Superblock holding the file system root, free-space map pointer, and journal head
Inode table mapping each file to its metadata and block pointers
Block allocation bitmap tracking free versus used disk blocks
Checkpoint mechanism that flushes applied journal entries and advances a recovery pointer
Recovery routine that replays committed journal entries and discards incomplete ones on remount
Buffer cache in memory with controlled flush ordering and fsync barriers
Checksums on journal records and blocks to detect torn writes
scalability_signals: A crash can land between any two disk writes, so changes go to a write-ahead journal first and are applied to their final location only after the journal commit record is durable
Scanning the entire disk to find damage would make recovery unbounded, so checkpoints advance a recovery pointer and replay starts from there
Disk writes are far slower than memory, so updates batch in a buffer cache and the journal absorbs ordering, trading a small write amplification for crash safety
Partial writes are physically possible, so checksums on journal records let recovery tell a committed entry from a torn one

title: Design a Resource Change Tracking and Notification System
problem_statement_markdown:
A cloud control plane manages resources like virtual machines, storage buckets, and network rules. Every change to a resource has to be applied to the source-of-truth database, recorded so the platform can notify anyone watching that resource, and made queryable so a caller can ask what changed between two points in time. The challenge is capturing changes reliably as they commit, fanning out notifications to many subscribers without slowing the write path, and answering diff queries efficiently over a resource's history.

## Functional Requirements

- Apply a change to a resource and persist its new state durably
- Emit a notification for every committed change to interested subscribers
- Query the difference between two states of a resource over a time range
- Let consumers subscribe to changes for specific resources or resource types
- Return the full change history for a resource in order

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A change notification reaches subscribers within a few seconds of commit
- No committed change is ever lost or notified twice in a way subscribers cannot dedupe
- Diff queries over history return without scanning the entire change log
- The write path stays fast even when many subscribers are attached

## Out of Scope

- Resource provisioning and the actual infrastructure actions behind a change
- Subscriber authorization policy and billing for notifications

requirements: Apply and persist a resource change as the new source of truth
Capture every committed change durably for downstream consumers
Deliver a notification per change to subscribers reliably and in order per resource
Answer a diff query between two resource states efficiently
Let a consumer replay missed changes after reconnecting
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A write hits the API service, which updates the resource state database; a change data capture pipeline tails the commit log and appends each change to a durable log in Kafka and to a versioned change-history table keyed by resource ID and sequence number. A notification dispatch service consumes the log, looks up matching subscribers in the subscription registry, and delivers ordered notifications, with each subscriber tracking an offset so it can replay after a disconnect. A diff request goes to the diff service, which loads the two requested versions from the history table and returns their differences without scanning the full log.
required_components: Resource state database (relational store) holding current resource records
Change data capture pipeline (Debezium-style) reading the database commit log
Append-only change log in a durable event store such as Kafka
Versioned change-history table keyed by resource ID and sequence number
Notification dispatch service consuming the change log and fanning out to subscribers
Subscription registry mapping subscribers to resources and resource types
Diff service that reconstructs and compares two versions of a resource
Consumer offset store so subscribers resume from their last acknowledged change
scalability_signals: Dual-writing the database and the notification path risks losing changes on a crash, so change capture reads the commit log rather than relying on the application to publish
Diffing by scanning the whole history would get slower over time, so changes are versioned per resource with sequence numbers that bound a diff to a range
Notification fan-out can be large and bursty, so dispatch is decoupled from the write path through a durable append-only log
Subscribers disconnect, so each tracks an offset and replays from the log instead of forcing the producer to retain per-subscriber buffers

title: Design an Ad Frequency Cap with Separated Read and Write Paths
problem_statement_markdown:
An ad platform limits how many times a given user sees a particular ad over a window. A frequency cap looks like a rate limiter but differs in one important way: the system reads a user's current count during the auction to decide whether an ad is eligible to bid, yet reading the cap does not mean the ad was actually served. The real increment happens later, in the event-tracking path, only when an impression fires. So the read that gates eligibility and the write that records an impression live on two different paths with different latency and consistency needs.

## Functional Requirements

- Read a user's current impression count for an ad or campaign during the auction
- Increment the count only when an impression event confirms the ad was shown
- Enforce a cap over a rolling or fixed window per user and campaign
- Support several cap scopes such as per-ad, per-campaign, and per-advertiser
- Expire counts when a window rolls over

## Non-Functional Requirements

- The eligibility read returns within single-digit milliseconds inside the auction
- A served impression is eventually counted even if it arrives seconds late
- The cap is enforced closely enough that overdelivery stays small and bounded
- The design handles millions of users and hundreds of thousands of active ads

## Out of Scope

- Ad ranking and bid pricing logic
- Budget pacing and advertiser billing

requirements: Read a user's frequency count fast enough to gate the auction
Increment counts only from confirmed impression events, not from reads
Enforce caps across per-ad, per-campaign, and per-advertiser scopes
Expire counts correctly when the window resets
Tolerate delayed impression events without losing or double-counting them
metadata.reference_diagram_description: During an auction the read service queries the Redis cluster for the user's frequency counters keyed by user, scope, and window bucket, and filters out ads that have hit their cap, all inside a few milliseconds. When an ad actually renders, the client emits an impression event into Kafka; an impression consumer reads it, applies an idempotency guard by event ID, and increments the matching Redis counters with a TTL that expires them at window roll-over. A reconciliation job periodically rolls confirmed impressions from the event stream into a cold store for auditing and to correct counter drift.
required_components: Redis cluster holding per-user frequency counters keyed by user and campaign scope
Auction-side read service that checks counters to filter eligible ads
Event tracking pipeline (Kafka) carrying confirmed impression events
Impression consumer that increments Redis counters with TTL-based window expiry
Counter key schema encoding user ID, scope, and window bucket
Idempotency guard keyed by impression event ID to dedupe replays
Cold store (relational or columnar) for audit and reconciliation of impression counts
Sharding layer partitioning counters by user ID
scalability_signals: Reading the cap does not prove an ad was served, so the auction read and the impression write are separate paths and the increment lives in event tracking, not in the read
The auction sits in a tight latency budget, so eligibility reads hit an in-memory Redis cluster rather than a database
Impression events can arrive late or be redelivered, so increments are idempotent by event ID and windows expire via TTL rather than manual cleanup
Counters span millions of users and hundreds of thousands of ads, so keys are sharded by user ID and scoped by campaign to spread load

title: Design a Natural Disaster Notification System for Vacation Rentals
problem_statement_markdown:
A vacation rental platform wants to warn travelers and homeowners when a natural disaster threatens a property. A third-party disaster feed reports events such as wildfires, floods, and hurricanes, and a geo service turns each event into a polygon describing the affected region. Internal services know property locations, active orders, homeowners, and travelers. When a disaster region arrives, the system has to quickly find every property inside the polygon and every order tied to those properties, then notify the right people. The core difficulty is answering the geospatial containment query efficiently across millions of properties.

## Functional Requirements

- Ingest disaster events and resolve each into an affected polygon
- Find all properties whose location falls inside an affected region
- Find all active orders and the travelers and homeowners tied to those properties
- Send notifications to affected travelers and homeowners
- Deduplicate notifications when overlapping disaster events hit the same property

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Affected properties for a new disaster region are resolved within minutes
- The geospatial query stays fast as property count grows into the millions
- No affected traveler with an active order is missed
- A single property is not spammed with repeated alerts for the same event

requirements: Ingest disaster events and convert each to an affected polygon
Query all properties contained in a disaster polygon efficiently
Resolve active orders, travelers, and homeowners for affected properties
Notify affected parties through their preferred channel
Dedupe alerts so one event triggers one notification per recipient
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The disaster ingestion service polls the third-party feed and passes each event to the geo service, which produces an affected polygon. The affected-set resolver queries the geospatial property index for every property inside the polygon, then joins against the property and order services to gather active orders, travelers, and homeowners. The resolved recipients flow through a queue into the notification service, which checks a dedupe store keyed by event ID and recipient before dispatching push, email, or SMS so each affected party is alerted once per event.
required_components: Disaster ingestion service polling the third-party disaster feed
Geo service that builds polygons from raw disaster event data
Geospatial index over property locations (PostGIS or geohash-based store)
Property and order services exposing internal lookups
Affected-set resolver that runs polygon containment and joins orders and users
Notification service with channel adapters for push, email, and SMS
Deduplication store keyed by event ID and recipient
Message queue decoupling resolution from notification fan-out
scalability_signals: A polygon containment query against millions of properties would be slow as a full scan, so property locations live in a geospatial index that prunes to a bounding region first
Disaster resolution and notification fan-out have different latencies, so they are decoupled through a queue so a slow channel does not stall the geo query
Overlapping events can flag the same property repeatedly, so a dedupe store keyed by event and recipient prevents alert spam
External feeds arrive irregularly, so ingestion polls and normalizes events before the system commits to expensive resolution work

title: Design a Like and Dislike System at Scale
problem_statement_markdown:
Users react to items with a like or a dislike, can see their own current reaction on any item, browse the items they have liked before, and see an exact like count per item. A user can flip from like to dislike, retract a reaction, and tap the button repeatedly on a flaky connection. The design has to keep each user's reaction correct under those flips and retries, store reactions for billions of item interactions, and serve exact counts fast. The hard parts are idempotent writes, correct like-to-dislike transitions, and counting at scale.

## Functional Requirements

- Like or dislike an item and flip between the two
- Retract a reaction so the item shows no reaction from that user
- Read a user's current reaction status for a given item
- List the items a user has liked, most recent first
- Show an exact like count and dislike count per item

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A reaction read or write returns within tens of milliseconds at p99
- Duplicate or retried taps never inflate or corrupt a count
- Counts are exact, not approximate, and converge quickly
- The system holds reactions across billions of user-item pairs

requirements: Record a like or dislike idempotently so repeated taps are safe
Flip a reaction from like to dislike with a correct net count change
Read a user's current reaction on an item quickly
List a user's liked items in recent-first order
Serve exact like and dislike counts under heavy read load
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A tap hits the API service, which builds an idempotency key from user, item, and reaction and writes the reaction row to the sharded reaction store; a replayed tap with the same key is ignored. On a flip the service computes the net delta and emits a counter-update event that the async consumer applies to the item's Redis counter, which flushes to the database periodically. A status read returns the user's row from cache, a count read returns the hot Redis counter, and the liked-items view is served from a secondary index on user and timestamp.
required_components: API service exposing react, retract, status, and count endpoints
Reaction store (sharded relational or wide-column store) keyed by user and item
Idempotency key derived from user, item, and reaction to dedupe retried writes
Per-item counter in Redis with periodic durable flush to the database
Secondary index on user plus timestamp for the liked-items history view
Cache layer holding hot per-item counts and recent user reactions
Sharding layer partitioning reaction rows by user or item ID
Asynchronous counter-update consumer applying net deltas on reaction flips
scalability_signals: A user can tap repeatedly on a bad connection, so writes are idempotent on the user-item-reaction key and a replayed tap is a no-op rather than a double count
A flip from like to dislike must move two counters atomically, so the system records the net delta and applies it through a single counter update path
Exact counts under high read volume cannot hit the database every time, so per-item counts live in Redis and flush to durable storage in batches
Reactions span billions of user-item pairs, so the store is sharded and the liked-items history is served from a secondary index on user and time

title: Design an Article Voting System Like Reddit
problem_statement_markdown:
A community platform lets users vote on articles the way Reddit or StackOverflow does. A user can upvote or downvote an article, and tapping the same direction again retracts the vote, while tapping the opposite direction flips it. The system tracks each user's current vote per article, maintains a running score, and can return the most recent articles where a given user flipped their vote. The interesting part is choosing data structures and storage so vote updates stay cheap, scores stay correct under flips, and the recent-flips query is fast even for active voters.

## Functional Requirements

- Add an article and assign it a unique ID
- Upvote or downvote an article, where a repeat tap retracts and an opposite tap flips
- Maintain a correct score per article as votes change
- Return a user's current vote on any article
- Return the most recent k articles where a user changed their vote

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A vote write and a score read both return in tens of milliseconds
- Scores stay exact under concurrent votes and rapid flips
- The recent-flips query returns quickly regardless of total vote history
- The system holds votes across millions of users and articles

requirements: Create an article with a unique identifier
Record an upvote or downvote with correct retract and flip semantics
Keep article scores accurate as votes are added, retracted, and flipped
Return a user's current vote on a given article
Return the last k articles a user flipped their vote on efficiently
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A vote request hits the API service, which reads the user's current vote for the article from the sharded vote store, decides whether the action is a new vote, a retract, or a flip, and writes the updated state. The service computes the net score delta and applies it to the article's Redis counter, which flushes to durable storage periodically, and it pushes the article onto the user's capped recent-flips structure when the direction actually changes. A score read returns the cached counter, a status read returns the stored vote state, and the recent-flips query reads the last k entries from the user's time-ordered structure.
required_components: API service exposing add-article and vote endpoints
Vote store (sharded relational store) keyed by article and user with current vote state
Per-article score counter cached in Redis with durable flush
Per-user recent-flips structure such as a capped, time-ordered list or deque
Idempotency check so a repeated identical vote does not double-apply
Article metadata store for titles and creation order
Cache layer for hot article scores and recent user votes
Sharding layer partitioning votes by article or user ID
scalability_signals: A repeat tap should cancel and an opposite tap should flip, so each vote is stored as explicit state per user-article pair and the score moves by a computed net delta, never by a blind increment
Recomputing a user's recent flips by scanning history would be slow, so each user keeps a capped time-ordered structure that makes the last k flips an O(k) read
Scores are read far more than they are written, so they are cached per article in Redis and flushed to durable storage in batches
Votes span millions of users and articles, so vote rows are sharded and hot scores are served from cache rather than recomputed

title: Design a Strictly Consistent Storage Quota Service
problem_statement_markdown:
Several products share one storage quota per user, the way Drive, Photos, and Gmail share a single Google account allowance. A service can reserve space before an upload, confirm it once the upload lands, cancel it if the upload fails, and release space when a user deletes a file. The platform must never let a user exceed their quota even by a byte, so reservations and confirmations need strict consistency. At the same time the service runs hot, tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of operations per second, with a tight latency budget and high availability. The tension is enforcing no-overdraft consistency while staying fast and available.

## Functional Requirements

- Reserve quota for a pending upload and return a reservation handle
- Confirm a reservation once the upload completes
- Cancel a reservation if the upload fails or is abandoned
- Release quota when a user deletes stored data
- Report a user's current usage and remaining allowance

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Strict consistency: a user can never exceed their quota, no overdraft ever
- P99 latency under 50ms for reserve and confirm
- Availability of 99.99 percent
- Throughput of tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of operations per second

requirements: Reserve space atomically so concurrent reservations cannot overdraft
Confirm or cancel a reservation idempotently
Release quota on deletion and reflect it immediately in usage
Report accurate current usage and remaining allowance
Hold consistency under failures, retries, and duplicate requests
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A product calls the quota API service to reserve space; the request carries an idempotency key and routes to the shard owning that user. The service runs an atomic conditional update against the UserQuota row, succeeding only if committed plus reserved usage stays within the allowance, and writes a pending row to the Reservation table. Confirm moves the reservation into committed usage, cancel and release reverse it, and all of these replicate synchronously across the shard's consensus group, while an expiry sweeper auto-cancels stale reservations so held space is returned.
required_components: Quota API service exposing reserve, confirm, cancel, release, and usage operations
UserQuota table holding allowance and committed usage per user
Reservation table tracking pending holds with state and expiry
Idempotency key store keyed by client request to dedupe retries
Conditional atomic update (compare-and-set or serializable transaction) on the quota row
Sharding layer partitioning quota and reservation rows by user ID
Synchronous replication (consensus-backed, Raft or Paxos) for the quota shard
Expiry sweeper that auto-cancels stale reservations to reclaim held space
scalability_signals: No overdraft is allowed, so a reservation succeeds only through an atomic conditional update that fails when committed plus reserved usage would exceed the allowance
All operations on one user touch the same balance, so the system shards by user ID and serializes per-user updates rather than locking globally
Strict consistency rules out lossy replication, so the quota shard replicates synchronously through consensus even though that costs latency
Clients retry on timeout, so reserve and confirm carry idempotency keys and abandoned holds are swept by an expiry job so space is never stranded

title: Design an In-Memory Query Engine with Tables, Inserts, and Filtered Select
problem_statement_markdown:
An internal tool needs a lightweight in-memory query engine that other services embed to hold structured data and run simple filtered lookups without standing up a real database. It supports creating a table with named columns, inserting rows that auto-increment a row ID and infer each value as an integer or string, and selecting rows by a set of AND conditions of the form column-operator-value, returning matching row IDs in a requested sort order. The design has to keep inserts cheap, make filtered selects fast as row counts grow, and stay correct about type inference and ordering.

## Functional Requirements

- Create a table with a fixed, ordered set of column names
- Insert a row that gets an auto-incrementing ID and per-value type inference
- Select rows matching all of a list of column-operator-value conditions
- Return matching row IDs ordered by a requested column and direction
- Reject inserts and queries that reference unknown tables or columns

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Inserts run in close to constant time
- A filtered select avoids scanning every row when an indexed column is queried
- Type inference is consistent so equality and comparison behave predictably
- The engine stays correct under interleaved inserts and selects

requirements: Create a table with ordered, named columns
Insert a row with an auto-incrementing ID and inferred value types
Filter rows by a conjunction of column-operator-value conditions
Return matching row IDs in a correct requested sort order
Validate table and column references and reject invalid operations
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A createTable call registers an ordered column list in the table catalog and provisions an empty row store and an ID counter. An insert assigns the next row ID, runs each value through the type inference module, appends the row to the store, and updates any secondary indexes on the affected columns. A select hands its AND conditions to the query planner, which chooses a hash or sorted index when a condition matches one and otherwise scans, passes candidates to the condition evaluator, and returns the surviving row IDs through the sort module in the requested order.
required_components: Table catalog mapping table names to ordered column definitions
Row store per table holding rows by auto-incrementing row ID
Auto-increment ID generator scoped per table
Type inference module classifying each inserted value as integer or string
Secondary indexes (hash for equality, sorted structure for range and order) per indexed column
Query planner that picks an index when a condition matches one, else falls back to scan
Condition evaluator applying AND filters with the inferred type semantics
Sort module ordering matched row IDs by the requested column and direction
scalability_signals: A select with many conditions over a full scan slows as rows grow, so equality columns get a hash index and order or range columns get a sorted structure the planner can use
Values are untyped on the way in but compared later, so type is inferred once at insert and stored so equality and comparison stay consistent
Row IDs must be stable and unique per table, so a per-table counter assigns them at insert in constant time
Most queries touch a subset of columns, so indexes are built only on columns that are filtered or ordered rather than on every column

title: Design a Cloud Storage Service with Files, Copies, Capacity, and Quotas
problem_statement_markdown:
A cloud storage service holds named files with sizes, lets callers copy a file to a new name, and looks up a file's size. Beyond the basics it grows into prefix-based listing, an account-wide capacity limit, and per-user quotas, the way a real bucket service layers features. Adding a file fails if the name is taken, copying fails if the source is missing or the target already exists, and a size lookup returns nothing meaningful when the file is absent. The design has to keep name lookups and copies cheap while enforcing capacity and quota rules correctly as the service grows.

## Functional Requirements

- Add a file with a name and size, failing on a duplicate name
- Copy a file to a new name, failing if the source is missing or the target exists
- Return a file's size, signaling clearly when the file does not exist
- List files by name prefix with their sizes
- Enforce an account capacity limit and per-user storage quotas

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Add, copy, and size lookups run in close to constant time
- Prefix listing avoids scanning every file in the account
- Capacity and quota checks are exact, with no overshoot
- The service stays correct under concurrent adds and copies

requirements: Add a file and reject a duplicate name
Copy a file with correct source-missing and target-exists failures
Look up a file's size and report absence clearly
List files matching a name prefix efficiently
Enforce account capacity and per-user quotas exactly
metadata.reference_diagram_description: An add request passes through the validation layer, which rejects a duplicate name, then an atomic update checks the account capacity counter and the owner's quota counter, writes the entry to the file metadata map, and increments both counters together. A copy validates that the source exists and the target does not, records a new metadata entry pointing at the content reference store, and applies the same capacity and quota update. A size lookup reads the metadata map directly, and a prefix listing walks the prefix index to return matching names and sizes without scanning the whole account.
required_components: File metadata map keyed by file name holding size and owning user
Content reference store so a copy shares or duplicates underlying bytes correctly
Prefix index such as a trie or sorted key structure for prefix listing
Per-user usage counters checked and updated on add, copy, and delete
Account-wide capacity counter enforced atomically before each add or copy
Validation layer rejecting duplicate names and invalid copy targets
Atomic update path so capacity and quota checks and the write commit together
Eviction or rejection policy for when capacity is reached
scalability_signals: Name lookups and copies must be cheap, so file metadata lives in a hash map keyed by name and a copy records a new metadata entry rather than rescanning storage
Prefix listing over a full key scan slows as the file count grows, so names are kept in a trie or sorted structure that bounds a prefix query to its matches
Capacity and quotas must never overshoot, so the check and the write happen in one atomic update so two concurrent adds cannot both slip past the limit
Usage is queried often, so per-user and account counters are maintained incrementally instead of summed on demand

title: Design a Redis-Backed Ad Frequency Capping System
problem_statement_markdown:
An ad serving platform limits how often a user is shown a given ad or campaign over a window. The whole design hinges on the Redis layer: what the key is, what the value holds, and how the window resets. With millions of users and hundreds of thousands of new ads each day, the key schema decides whether the system stays fast and small or blows up in memory. The cap is read during serving to filter eligible ads and incremented when an impression fires, so the counter design has to support cheap reads, cheap increments, and clean expiry.

## Functional Requirements

- Read a user's current impression count for an ad or campaign during serving
- Increment the count when an impression is confirmed
- Enforce a per-user cap over a fixed or rolling window
- Expire counts automatically when the window ends
- Support cap scopes at the ad, campaign, and advertiser level

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A cap read returns in single-digit milliseconds during ad serving
- The Redis key schema keeps per-user memory bounded as ad count grows
- Counts expire on their own without a manual cleanup sweep
- The system holds counters for millions of users and hundreds of thousands of ads

requirements: Read a frequency count fast enough for the serving path
Increment counts on confirmed impressions
Enforce caps across ad, campaign, and advertiser scopes
Expire counters automatically at window roll-over
Keep per-user Redis memory bounded under high ad cardinality
metadata.reference_diagram_description: During ad serving the read path queries the Redis cluster with a key formed from user ID and window bucket, reads the hash of ad or campaign counts, and filters out ads at their cap, all within a few milliseconds. When an impression is confirmed, an event flows through Kafka to the impression consumer, which applies an idempotency guard by event ID and increments the matching field inside the user's window hash, relying on the key's TTL to expire it at roll-over. A reconciliation job periodically folds confirmed impressions from the stream into a cold store for audit and to correct any counter drift.
required_components: Redis cluster storing per-user frequency counters
Key schema using user ID as the partition with scope and window bucket encoded
Hash value per user mapping ad or campaign ID to its count to bound key count
TTL on each user-window key so counts expire without manual cleanup
Serving-side read path that checks counters to filter eligible ads
Impression consumer (fed by an event stream such as Kafka) that increments counters
Idempotency guard keyed by impression event ID to dedupe replays
Cold store for reconciliation and audit of impression counts
scalability_signals: Per-user memory is the constraint, so the key is user plus window and the value is a hash of ad or campaign IDs to counts, instead of one flat key per user-ad pair that would explode key count
Windows reset on a schedule, so each user-window key carries a TTL and expires on its own rather than needing a cleanup job
Serving sits in a tight latency budget, so the cap read hits the in-memory Redis cluster and never a database
Counters span millions of users, so keys are partitioned by user ID across the cluster to spread both memory and request load

title: Design a Social Media Sentiment Tracking System
problem_statement_markdown:
A company wants to track how people feel about its brand on social media over time. The system pulls posts mentioning the brand from several platforms, cleans and aggregates them, runs sentiment analysis, and presents a trend of sentiment by day, region, and topic. Models are trained offline on labeled data and refreshed periodically, while scoring runs over the incoming stream. The design has to ingest from rate-limited third-party feeds, handle messy and duplicated text, aggregate at scale, and keep the offline training loop separate from the serving path.

## Functional Requirements

- Ingest brand-mention posts from multiple social platforms
- Clean, deduplicate, and normalize incoming text
- Score each post's sentiment with a trained model
- Aggregate sentiment over time, region, and topic
- Train and periodically refresh the sentiment model offline on labeled data

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Sentiment trends are available within minutes of posts being published
- Ingestion respects third-party rate limits without dropping data
- The pipeline handles spiky volume during viral moments
- Offline training does not disturb the live scoring path

requirements: Collect brand mentions from several platforms reliably
Clean and deduplicate noisy social text before scoring
Score sentiment per post with the current model
Aggregate sentiment across time, region, and topic dimensions
Retrain and roll out an updated model offline without breaking serving
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Per-platform ingestion connectors pull brand mentions within rate limits and push raw posts into Kafka. A stream processor cleans, deduplicates, and normalizes the text, then the sentiment scoring service applies the currently deployed model and writes scored records to the columnar aggregation store rolled up by time, region, and topic. In parallel, an offline training pipeline reads labeled data and features, produces a versioned model in the registry, and promotes it for the scoring service to load, while a dashboard and query API serve sentiment trends from the aggregation store.
required_components: Ingestion connectors per platform respecting API rate limits
Message queue such as Kafka buffering raw posts from ingestion
Stream processor (Flink or Spark Streaming) for cleaning, dedup, and normalization
Sentiment scoring service applying the deployed model to each post
Model registry and offline training pipeline producing versioned models
Aggregation store (columnar warehouse) for time, region, and topic rollups
Labeled-data store and feature pipeline feeding offline training
Dashboard and query API serving sentiment trends
scalability_signals: Third-party feeds are rate-limited and bursty, so ingestion buffers into a queue and the rest of the pipeline consumes at its own pace rather than blocking on the source
Social text is noisy and duplicated across reposts, so a stream-processing stage cleans and dedupes before scoring so aggregates are not skewed
Training is expensive and scoring is latency-sensitive, so the model is trained offline and published to a registry while the serving path loads versioned models
Trend queries slice by several dimensions, so scored sentiment is pre-aggregated into a columnar store instead of recomputed per query

title: Design an ML Platform Portal for Experiments, Models, and Deployments
problem_statement_markdown:
Machine learning engineers and data scientists need one web portal to manage the model lifecycle: record experiment runs with metrics and parameters, register trained models with versions, deploy a model version to an environment, and promote a deployment from staging to production. The portal is a full-stack system with a web UI, an API layer, a database, and integrations with the training and serving infrastructure. The design has to model experiments, models, and deployments cleanly, expose APIs the UI and CLI both use, and keep promotion safe so the wrong model version never reaches production.

## Functional Requirements

- Record an experiment run with parameters, metrics, and artifacts
- Register a trained model and create immutable versions
- Deploy a specific model version to a named environment
- Promote a deployment from staging to production with a controlled transition
- Browse experiments, models, and deployment status in the UI

## Non-Functional Requirements

- UI reads of experiment and model lists return in a fraction of a second
- A model version is immutable once registered so deployments are reproducible
- A promotion is atomic so production always points at exactly one version
- The portal handles concurrent users across many teams without conflicts

requirements: Log an experiment run with its parameters, metrics, and artifacts
Register models and produce immutable, addressable versions
Deploy a chosen model version to a target environment
Promote staging to production as a single controlled transition
Show experiment, model, and deployment state in the UI quickly
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The web frontend and a CLI both call the API layer, which validates team-scoped permissions and reads or writes the relational database holding experiments, models, versions, and deployments, with large artifacts stored in S3 and referenced by row. Logging a run writes metrics and parameters and uploads artifacts; registering a model creates an immutable version. A deploy or promote request goes through the promotion state machine, which drives the deployment controller against the serving infrastructure and updates the environment pointer atomically, while every deploy and promote action is written to an audit log.
required_components: Web frontend (single-page app) for browsing and actions
API layer exposing REST and GraphQL endpoints for the UI and CLI
Relational database schema for experiments, models, versions, and deployments
Artifact store such as S3 for run outputs and model binaries
Deployment controller integrating with the serving infrastructure
Environment and promotion state machine enforcing staging-to-production transitions
Authentication and team-scoped authorization layer
Audit log capturing who deployed or promoted what and when
scalability_signals: Deployments must be reproducible, so a registered model version is immutable and its binary lives in an artifact store referenced by the database, never overwritten in place
Production must point at exactly one version, so promotion runs through a state machine that swaps the pointer atomically rather than mutating rows independently
The UI and CLI need the same operations, so business logic sits behind the API layer and both clients call it instead of duplicating rules
Run and metric volume grows steadily, so list views are paginated and indexed by team and time rather than loaded wholesale

title: Design a Real-Time Top-Earner Tracking Service
problem_statement_markdown:
A large online platform runs many experiences such as games, features, and events, each generating profit that shifts constantly. A real-time analytics component has to track which experience is currently earning the most and answer that question instantly at any moment. It receives a stream of two operations: update, which adjusts an experience's profit by some delta, and query, which returns the name of the current top earner. The hard part is keeping both operations cheap as profits change rapidly across many experiences, so the max is always available without rescanning everything on each query.

## Functional Requirements

- Update an experience's running profit by a positive or negative delta
- Query the name of the experience with the highest current profit
- Handle experiences appearing and being updated over time
- Break ties deterministically when two experiences are tied at the top
- Process a continuous interleaved stream of updates and queries

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A query for the current top earner returns in close to constant time
- An update applies without rescanning all experiences
- The structure stays correct under a high rate of interleaved updates
- Memory stays proportional to the number of distinct experiences

requirements: Apply a profit delta to an experience efficiently
Return the current highest-earning experience in near-constant time
Support experiences that are added and updated continuously
Resolve ties at the top deterministically
Sustain a high rate of interleaved update and query operations
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The ingestion interface consumes a stream of update and query operations. An update looks up the experience in the profit map, applies the delta, and repositions its entry in the indexed max structure keyed by profit, using decrease-key or lazy deletion so the ordering stays accurate. A query reads the maximum from that structure in near-constant time, applying the tie-break rule when two experiences share the top profit. At high scale experiences are partitioned by ID across several such structures, and a top-of-tops merge returns the global top earner.
required_components: Profit map keyed by experience ID holding current total profit
Indexed max structure such as a balanced BST or order-statistics tree keyed by profit
Update path that adjusts the profit map and repositions the entry in the max structure
Query path reading the maximum from the indexed structure in near-constant time
Lazy-deletion or decrease-key handling so the max structure stays consistent on updates
Tie-breaking rule (such as lexicographic name) layered into the ordering
Ingestion interface consuming the stream of update and query operations
Optional sharding by experience ID with a top-of-tops merge for very high scale
scalability_signals: A plain hash map gives constant updates but an O(n) scan per query, so the design pairs the map with an indexed max structure that returns the top earner without scanning
A binary heap supports the max but not arbitrary updates well, so a balanced BST or order-statistics tree is used so an update can reposition an existing entry in log time
Stale entries from frequent updates can corrupt the max, so the structure uses decrease-key or lazy deletion to keep its top accurate
At very high scale one structure becomes a bottleneck, so experiences shard by ID and a small top-of-tops merge keeps the global max cheap

title: Design a Team Messaging Platform Like Slack
problem_statement_markdown:
A team messaging product supports direct messages and channels. Messages deliver in real time when recipients are online and wait for them when they are offline, and a user can be signed in on several devices that all stay in sync. Direct messages and small channels can push every new message to connected members, but a channel with tens of thousands of members would create a write storm on every post, so large channels need a different delivery strategy. The design has to handle real-time fan-out, large channels, multi-device sync, and recovery of messages missed during a disconnect.

## Functional Requirements

- Send and receive direct messages between two users
- Post and read messages in channels of varying size
- Deliver messages in real time to online members and queue them for offline ones
- Keep all of a user's devices in sync on read state and new messages
- Let a reconnecting client fetch messages it missed while disconnected

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A message reaches online recipients within a couple hundred milliseconds
- Posting in a very large channel does not stall on per-member writes
- Message ordering within a conversation is consistent across devices
- No acknowledged message is lost across a disconnect

requirements: Deliver direct messages in real time and queue them when offline
Support channels from tiny to tens of thousands of members
Keep multiple devices of one user in sync
Recover messages missed during a dropped connection
Maintain consistent message ordering within each conversation
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Clients hold WebSocket connections to a gateway, and the connection registry records which user and device sits on which gateway node. A sent message is written to the sharded message store with a per-conversation sequence number, then published over Redis Pub/Sub to the gateways holding online recipients; direct messages and small channels push directly while large channels are served pull-on-read when a member opens them. Each device tracks a cursor by sequence number, an offline notification service handles disconnected users, and a reconnecting client fetches all messages after its last cursor to recover anything missed.
required_components: WebSocket gateway maintaining persistent client connections
Connection registry mapping users and devices to gateway nodes
Redis Pub/Sub for routing messages to the gateways holding recipients
Message store (sharded by channel or conversation) with per-conversation sequence numbers
Push fan-out path for direct messages and small channels
Pull-on-read path for large channels where members fetch on open
Per-device inbox or cursor tracking the last delivered sequence number
Offline notification service for push notifications when a user is disconnected
scalability_signals: Pushing every message to every member of a huge channel is a write storm, so direct messages and small channels push while large channels switch to pull-on-read
A user is on several devices, so each device tracks a cursor by sequence number and syncs read state independently rather than assuming one session
Connections drop, so the message store assigns per-conversation sequence numbers and a reconnecting client requests everything after its last cursor
Recipients are spread across many gateway nodes, so Redis Pub/Sub routes a message only to the gateways that actually hold connected recipients

title: Design a Streaming Chat Playground System
problem_statement_markdown:
A developer playground lets people send a prompt to a language model and watch the response stream back token by token, the way a basic chat interface works. Beyond the single chat box, the playground keeps conversation history, lets users tune parameters such as model and temperature, and supports many concurrent sessions. The interesting parts are streaming partial output to the browser as it generates, holding a live connection open per active generation, and keeping the experience responsive when generation is slow or a user stops it midway.

## Functional Requirements

- Submit a prompt and stream the model's response into the UI as it generates
- Let a user stop an in-progress generation
- Persist conversation history per session
- Let users set parameters like model choice and temperature
- Support many concurrent generation sessions

## Non-Functional Requirements

- First tokens appear within a second of submitting a prompt
- A stopped generation halts model work promptly to free capacity
- A dropped connection does not corrupt saved conversation state
- The system scales to many simultaneous streaming sessions

requirements: Stream model output to the client token by token
Allow a user to cancel an in-flight generation
Persist conversation turns per session reliably
Apply per-request parameters such as model and temperature
Hold many concurrent streaming sessions without exhausting connections
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The frontend chat component opens a streaming connection (SSE or WebSocket) through the API gateway, which hands the prompt and its parameters to the inference orchestration service. That service calls the model serving backend and relays each token back over the open stream while the component renders incrementally. A stop action or a dropped connection fires the cancellation channel, signaling the backend to end generation, and each completed turn is written to the conversation store so history and parameters survive independent of the live stream. A session and rate-limit layer caps how many concurrent generations a user can run.
required_components: Frontend chat component rendering streamed tokens incrementally
Streaming transport such as Server-Sent Events or a WebSocket per active generation
API gateway routing prompt requests and managing stream lifecycles
Inference orchestration service that calls the model backend and relays tokens
Model serving backend producing the token stream
Conversation store (database) persisting session history and parameters
Cancellation channel that signals the inference backend to stop a generation
Session and rate-limit layer scoping concurrency per user
scalability_signals: Users expect to see output as it forms, so tokens stream over SSE or a WebSocket rather than waiting for the full completion before responding
Abandoned generations waste GPU time, so a cancellation channel propagates a stop to the inference backend the moment a user halts or disconnects
A dropped stream should not lose the conversation, so completed turns are persisted to the conversation store independently of the live connection
Long-lived streams tie up connections, so the gateway scopes concurrent sessions per user and sheds or queues load past a limit

title: Design an Auto-Slide Image Feed with Dwell-Time Prediction
problem_statement_markdown:
A single-page swipeable feed shows one image at a time, like a TikTok feed but images only. The product wants the page to advance on its own once a user has likely finished looking, so the system predicts how long a user will dwell on a given image and auto-scrolls to the next one when that time elapses. This is a machine learning recommendation problem with a twist: alongside choosing what to show next, the system models per-user, per-image dwell time and uses the prediction to drive the auto-slide. The design covers candidate generation, ranking, the dwell-time model, feature handling, and serving the prediction in time to act on it.

## Functional Requirements

- Generate candidate images for a user's feed
- Rank candidates for relevance and engagement
- Predict expected dwell time per user and image
- Auto-advance the feed when predicted dwell time elapses
- Log actual dwell and swipe behavior as training signal

## Non-Functional Requirements

- The next image and its dwell prediction are ready before the current one ends
- Predictions reflect recent user behavior, not only stale offline features
- The feed stays smooth with no visible stall between slides
- The pipeline retrains on fresh engagement data regularly

requirements: Generate a candidate set of images per user
Rank candidates by predicted engagement
Predict per-user, per-image dwell time
Trigger auto-advance based on the dwell prediction
Capture real dwell and swipe events to retrain the models
metadata.reference_diagram_description: When a session starts, the candidate generation service produces images from embeddings and recent interest signals, and the ranking model scores them while the dwell-time model predicts expected view duration per image, both reading the feature store for online and offline features. The online inference service returns the next items with their dwell predictions, which a client-side controller uses to prefetch the upcoming image and auto-advance when the predicted dwell elapses. Real dwell and swipe events stream into Kafka and feed an offline training pipeline that retrains both the ranking and dwell models on fresh data.
required_components: Candidate generation service using embeddings and recent interest signals
Ranking model scoring candidates for engagement
Dwell-time prediction model producing expected view duration per image
Feature store serving user, image, and context features online
Real-time event pipeline (Kafka) logging dwell and swipe outcomes
Online inference service returning ranked items with dwell predictions
Offline training pipeline retraining ranking and dwell models on logged data
Prefetch and client-side controller advancing the feed on the prediction
scalability_signals: The next slide and its dwell prediction must be ready before the current one ends, so candidates and predictions are prefetched a few items ahead rather than computed on demand at swipe time
Dwell depends on recent behavior, so the feature store serves fresh online features beside offline ones instead of relying on a stale snapshot
The dwell model needs ground truth, so the real-time event pipeline logs actual view durations and swipes to close the training loop
Ranking and dwell prediction are distinct objectives, so they are separate models composed at serving time, with the dwell output driving the auto-advance

title: Design a Distributed Ad Frequency Cap System at Scale
problem_statement_markdown:
An ad platform limits how many times a particular ad is shown to a single user. At platform scale this means counting impressions across millions of users and a large catalog of ads, then checking those counts fast enough to filter ads during serving. The counting has to survive node failures, stay roughly consistent across a distributed fleet, and not balloon in storage. The design centers on how counts are stored, how they are incremented as impressions happen, and how the whole thing scales horizontally without a single counter becoming a bottleneck.

## Functional Requirements

- Count impressions per user per ad or campaign
- Check a user's count during serving to decide if an ad is still eligible
- Enforce a cap over a defined time window
- Increment counts as impression events arrive across the fleet
- Expire counts when their window ends

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A cap check returns within single-digit milliseconds during serving
- Counting scales horizontally as users and ads grow
- Storage stays bounded as old windows expire automatically
- The system tolerates node failures without losing the cap guarantee broadly

requirements: Count impressions per user and ad across a distributed fleet
Check caps fast during the serving path
Enforce caps over a defined window
Increment counts reliably as impression events flow in
Expire counts and bound storage as windows roll over
metadata.reference_diagram_description: Confirmed impressions flow through Kafka to increment consumers, which apply an idempotency guard by event ID and update counters in the Redis cluster keyed by user, scope, and window bucket, each with a TTL. During serving the cap-check service reads the relevant counters, consulting a local cache for hot users to avoid cross-node round trips, and filters out ads that have reached their cap within single-digit milliseconds. A reconciliation job periodically folds impression totals from the event stream into a cold store for auditing and to correct counter drift.
required_components: Distributed in-memory counter store (Redis cluster) sharded by user ID
Key schema encoding user, ad or campaign scope, and window bucket
Impression event pipeline (Kafka) carrying confirmed impressions
Counter increment consumers updating the store with TTL-based expiry
Serving-side cap-check service filtering eligible ads
Idempotency guard keyed by impression event ID
Local serving cache for hot user counts to cut cross-node reads
Cold store for reconciliation and audit of impression totals
scalability_signals: One global counter per ad would be a hotspot, so counts are sharded by user ID across a Redis cluster so load spreads with the user base
The serving path is latency-bound, so cap checks hit in-memory counters and frequently seen counts are cached locally on the serving node
Impression events can be redelivered, so increments are idempotent by event ID so a replay does not inflate a count
Old windows must not pile up, so each counter key carries a TTL and expires automatically instead of needing a sweep job

title: Design a Real-Time Messaging Service with Missed-Message Recovery
problem_statement_markdown:
A messaging product focuses on the send and receive path: a message a user sends must reach the recipient in real time when they are connected, and the recipient must be able to recover anything they missed if their connection drops. Real-time delivery runs over persistent connections, but connections are fragile, clients cold-start, and the order a recipient sees messages matters. The design has to deliver fast over a live connection, decide the tradeoff between strict ordering and immediate notification, and let a reconnecting client fetch exactly the messages it missed using sequence numbers backed by a durable queue.

## Functional Requirements

- Send a message and deliver it to the recipient in real time when connected
- Persist every message durably with an ordering sequence
- Notify a recipient who is offline so they open and catch up
- Recover missed messages after a dropped or cold-started connection
- Preserve a consistent message order within a conversation

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A message reaches a connected recipient within a couple hundred milliseconds
- No acknowledged message is lost across a disconnect
- A reconnecting client fetches only what it missed, not the whole history
- Ordering within a conversation is consistent for the recipient

requirements: Deliver messages in real time over a live connection
Persist messages with per-conversation sequence numbers
Notify offline recipients to reconnect and catch up
Recover exactly the missed messages after a disconnect
Keep message ordering consistent within a conversation
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A sent message lands in the durable message queue, which assigns a per-conversation sequence number and persists it to the message store. The real-time delivery path looks up the recipient in the connection registry and publishes to their WebSocket gateway if connected, otherwise the offline push notification service prompts them to reconnect. Each recipient tracks a cursor by last acknowledged sequence number, and on reconnect the catch-up service returns only the messages after that cursor in order, so nothing is lost and nothing is redelivered wholesale.
required_components: WebSocket gateway holding persistent client connections
Connection registry mapping users to gateway nodes
Durable message queue assigning per-conversation sequence numbers
Message store persisting conversation history in order
Per-recipient cursor tracking the last acknowledged sequence number
Real-time delivery path publishing to the recipient's gateway
Offline push notification service for disconnected recipients
Catch-up service serving messages after a client's last cursor
scalability_signals: Connections drop and clients cold-start, so every message gets a per-conversation sequence number and a reconnecting client requests everything after its last cursor rather than refetching all history
Strict ordering and instant notification pull against each other, so the design persists and sequences first, then delivers, accepting a tiny delay to keep order consistent
A live push can be missed, so the durable queue is the source of truth and the real-time path is an optimization layered on top of it
Recipients sit on many gateway nodes, so the connection registry routes a delivery only to the node holding the recipient

title: Design the Cart Backend for a Food Delivery Marketplace
problem_statement_markdown:
A food delivery marketplace needs a backend for the shopping cart across its full lifecycle: a user creates a cart, adds and removes items, updates quantities, checks out, and the cart becomes an order that flows to fulfillment, while abandoned carts eventually expire. Checkout is the delicate moment, where item availability, pricing, and inventory have to agree at the instant the order is created, and the platform handles enormous concurrency at peak. The design has to model the cart and its items, index them for fast reads, and keep checkout consistent so a user never pays for something out of stock or is double-charged.

## Functional Requirements

- Create a cart for a user and a chosen merchant
- Add, remove, and update quantity of cart items
- Check out a cart, validating availability and price
- Convert a checked-out cart into an order for fulfillment
- Expire carts abandoned past a time limit

## Non-Functional Requirements

- Cart reads and edits return within tens of milliseconds
- Checkout is consistent so an order never includes an unavailable item
- A retried checkout never creates two orders for one cart
- The system handles very high concurrent order volume at peak

requirements: Create and manage a cart tied to a user and merchant
Add, remove, and update items with correct totals
Validate availability and price atomically at checkout
Create an order idempotently from a checked-out cart
Expire abandoned carts to reclaim reserved state
metadata.reference_diagram_description: The cart service handles create and edit requests against the cart and cart_item tables, sharded by user ID, with hot active carts cached in Redis. At checkout the service runs a transaction or saga that consults the inventory service to validate availability and price, applies an idempotency key for the checkout attempt, and on success hands a validated cart to the order service, which creates exactly one order for fulfillment. A TTL-driven expiry job clears carts abandoned past the limit so reserved state is reclaimed.
required_components: Cart service exposing create, edit, and checkout endpoints
Cart and cart_item tables indexed by user and cart ID
Cache layer (Redis) for hot active carts
Inventory or availability service consulted at checkout
Idempotency key store keyed by cart and checkout attempt
Order service creating the order record from a validated cart
Transaction boundary or saga coordinating checkout across cart, inventory, and order
Expiry job (TTL-driven) clearing abandoned carts
Sharding layer partitioning carts by user ID
scalability_signals: Carts are read and edited constantly but only checked out once, so active carts live in a cache fronting the database and the edit path stays cheap
Checkout must agree across cart, price, and inventory, so it runs inside a transaction or saga that validates availability before the order is created
Clients retry checkout on timeout, so an idempotency key per cart attempt guarantees one cart yields exactly one order
Peak order volume is huge, so carts shard by user ID and abandoned ones expire via TTL so dead state never accumulates

title: Design a Scalable Like Counter with Change Data Capture
problem_statement_markdown:
A content platform shows a like count on every post and updates it as users tap like. Likes arrive in huge bursts on popular posts, so writing each like straight into a strongly consistent database would overwhelm it, yet the displayed count still needs to be accurate and fast to read. The design splits the write path that absorbs raw likes from the read path that serves stable counts, and uses change data capture to flow aggregated changes between them. The core idea is dual databases: a write-optimized store for ingesting likes and a read-optimized store for serving counts, kept in sync through a CDC stream.

## Functional Requirements

- Record a like (or unlike) on a post idempotently
- Aggregate raw like events into a per-post count
- Serve an accurate like count fast on read
- Keep the read count converging quickly toward the true total
- Handle viral posts with very high like rates

## Non-Functional Requirements

- A like write is accepted within tens of milliseconds even during a burst
- A count read returns within tens of milliseconds at p99
- Counts converge to the true value within seconds, not minutes
- The system absorbs viral spikes without overwhelming the read store

requirements: Accept like and unlike events idempotently under burst load
Aggregate raw events into per-post counts
Propagate aggregated counts to the read store via CDC
Serve fast, accurate counts on read
Sustain very high like rates on viral posts
metadata.reference_diagram_description: A like tap is written to the write-optimized ingestion store with an idempotency key on the user-post pair, so a replayed tap is a no-op. A change data capture pipeline tails that store and emits events to Kafka, where a stream aggregator folds them into per-post deltas and updates the read-optimized count store. Count reads are served from a Redis cache backed by the read store, both sharded by post ID, while a reconciliation job periodically compares raw events against served counts and corrects any drift so the displayed number converges to the true total within seconds.
required_components: Write-optimized ingestion store capturing raw like and unlike events
Idempotency key derived from user and post to dedupe repeated taps
Change data capture pipeline (Debezium-style) tailing the write store
Stream aggregator (Kafka plus a stream processor) folding events into per-post deltas
Read-optimized count store serving current counts
Cache layer (Redis) holding hot post counts for the read path
Reconciliation job correcting drift between raw events and served counts
Sharding by post ID across the ingestion and read stores
scalability_signals: Writing every like into a strongly consistent store would overwhelm it on viral posts, so a write-optimized store absorbs raw events and a separate read store serves counts
The two stores must stay in sync without dual writes, so change data capture streams changes from the write path into aggregation rather than the app writing both
Repeated taps and redelivered events would inflate counts, so each like carries an idempotency key on the user-post pair
Hot posts dominate reads, so served counts are cached in Redis and the read store is sharded by post ID to spread the rest
